title: Clear
pitch: Use your agent to triage incidents, build dashboards, and understand observability like never before.
about_excerpt: Use your agent to triage incidents, build dashboards, and understand observability like never before. Like Comment Story Updates Codex and Clear working through a retry storm side by side Following a failed checkout trace together and figuring out the smallest fix The moment payment attempts and checkout latency start climbing One checkout turning into three immediate payment attempts Following that same trace into the retry logs that explain the failure Watching retry traffic and checkout latency settle back down after the fix Benchmark comparing Grafana MCP vs Clear WebMCP Clear is an OpenTelemetry dashboard I can actually investigate with my coding agent Introduction Most observability dashboards have built-in agents these days, and that agent can piece together answers or make changes to the interface. But these built-in agents are isolated from your repo, skills, and context. Clear solves this by making observability visible and malleable to your coding agent. With WebMCP, humans and agents can triage issues, build dashboards, and understand incidents. Setting up Clear is as simple as pointing any* OpenTelemetry (OTel) client at our endpoints. What it does Services send metrics, logs, and traces to Clear, and users can use their agent to set thresholds that fire alerts or build custom dashboards. When an alert fires, a user or an agent can open an incident. The agent can query telemetry from Clear and create panels within the dashboard to test hypotheses. Users steer the agent in a particular direction, ask questions about the data, and work toward a patch. WebMCP enables this by allowing any WebMCP-capable agent to instantly access dashboards and logs without traditional MCP auth flows. How I built it I built Clear by creating a handful of different services: Backend hosted on Render API service Postgres database for non-telemetry data ClickHouse database for logs, metrics, and traces Go OTel Collector Simple React frontend hosted on ChatGPT Sites/Cloudflare This work was done with AI assistance while I still guided the architecture decisions and product experience. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge I overcame was collecting the OTel data and streaming it live to the client. This project started out as a fully TypeScript project, but there weren’t any good TypeScript libraries that acted as a complete OTel receiver. Rather than implementing this receiver myself, I built a small Go service that accepts and authenticates OTel traffic and forwards batches to the API service. The API service then normalizes and stores that data in ClickHouse. It also streams live events to the client using Server-Sent Events (SSE, basically a one-way WebSocket). Unfortunately, Render does not support external gRPC, so we are only able to support HTTP with JSON and Protobuf. Another challenge I ran into was synchronizing the dashboard across clients while keeping it legible to agents. On the server, we store a revision ID so that when an agent attempts to update a dashboard based on a stale version, the agent is asked to try again with the latest dashboard. We then use SSE to propagate changes across clients, and have some additional logic to resync clients that missed updates. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm proud of the fact that I was able to build a working OTel ingestion service and dashboard. WebMCP is the icing on the cake and what makes this project interesting, but a usable OTel dashboard is the table stakes. Without that, this entire project wouldn't have been possible. I'm also proud of the fact that Clear WebMCP is 3 times faster with smaller queries, and (anecdotally) much preferred by agents for its simple interface compared to the Grafana MCP server. While WebMCP enables this human-in-the-loop problem-solving, rebuilding the platform with agents in mind means streamlined tools and better AX (Agentic eXperience). What I learned While this project only represents one potential use of WebMCP, the potential for use across many different products is infinite. Being able to pull up a website in my browser and ask my agent a question about it is powerful in so many ways and feels like the next evolution of computer use. After starting this hackathon, I genuinely found myself wishing certain websites that I use had WebMCP. What's next for Clear Clear is very much a small vertical slice of this project rather than an enterprise-ready, drop-in Grafana replacement. I hope to refine this project in the future by fixing some issues so it can scale more easily, as well as improving the UI and UX. *Any OTel client that supports HTTP exports. We do not support gRPC. title: WebMCP Chess
pitch: A browser chess game where a person and an AI agent share one board and take turns, using WebMCP tools registered directly on the page. No backend MCP server, no scraping the DOM.
about_excerpt: A browser chess game where a person and an AI agent share one board and take turns, using WebMCP tools registered directly on the page. No backend MCP server, no scraping the DOM. Like Comment Story Updates AI Agent thinks and calls tools Coaching in action Analyze position with Stockfish Coaching with Stockfish in action Inspiration There's no shortage of chess apps. What's actually new here is WebMCP: a proposed API that lets a web page expose its own client-side functions as tools an AI agent can discover and call directly in the browser, no scraping the DOM, no separate backend integration for the agent. Chess was a good test case because it needs multi-step, stateful interaction: read the board, act, wait your turn, repeat. That's a real workflow, not a single API call dressed up as a demo. What it does Play chess in the browser on your own, or hand control to an AI agent mid-game. You share one board and one move history, and both of you go through the same validated chess logic. (Note: the demo video predates the engine work and shows the five original tools. The three Stockfish tools below are live in the deployed app and in the repository.) Eight WebMCP tools are registered on the page: Playing chess-get-board-state reads the current position, whose turn it is, legal moves, captured pieces and the material balance. chess-make-move plays a legal move. chess-wait-for-human-move pauses for your turn, then picks back up automatically. chess-new-game resets. Thinking chess-analyze-position returns ranked lines with real evaluations. Each one breaks out from, to and promotion, so a recommendation feeds straight into chess-make-move without the model having to parse its own advice. chess-evaluate-move reviews a move you just played: how much it cost in centipawns, what class of error it was, and the line that refutes it. chess-set-engine-strength weakens the agent's own play so it can be a beatable opponent. It never weakens the advice you are given. Coaching chess-suggest-move ranks candidate moves, draws them as arrows on the board, and explains the reasoning. The board also shows captured pieces and the material advantage for each side, so you can see who is up without replaying the move list in your head. How I built it Next.js, React and TypeScript. chess.js for the rules, react-chessboard for the board. Tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool(), each with a JSON schema and a callback that shares state with the UI, so an agent's move and a human's move land in exactly the same place. Stockfish 18 runs in the page, compiled to WebAssembly in a Web Worker. There is no backend. Searching happens off the main thread, so the board stays responsive while the engine thinks, and it reaches depth 16 to 18 in about a second. The 7 MB binary downloads on first analysis rather than on page load, and a small UCI client on the page serialises searches and handles aborts, so moving on to a new position cancels the search before it. Challenges I ran into WebMCP has no way to push application state to an agent. The spec has no notification for "the human moved, your turn". The workaround is chess-wait-for-human-move , a long-running call that resolves when the position changes, guarded by a FEN check and a two-minute timeout so it cannot hang. It works, but it is a workaround for a real protocol gap, not a claim that WebMCP does push notifications. A legal move is not a good move. Early on ChatGPT would cheerfully propose legal but tactically losing moves, because the only thing the page told it was which moves were legal. Legality answers whether a move follows the rules, not whether the opponent can immediately punish it. Stockfish now answers the second question, and the model is left to do the part it is actually good at. What I learned Long-running tool calls can bridge WebMCP's current gaps, but they are not push notifications and it is worth being honest about the difference. The pattern that actually emerged is a split of labour: the model explains, deterministic domain tools verify. Stockfish is the strongest version of that in this project. The engine calculates and returns ranked lines with real numbers; the model turns a principal variation into a sentence you can learn something from. Neither is asked to do the other's job, and the failure mode of each is caught by the other. What's next The interesting unfinished work is in the protocol, not the chess. Waiting for a human turn should not need a two-minute long poll, and the open WebMCP design discussions on application-driven observations, human-in-the-loop elicitation and long-running tool progress are all pointing at the same gap from different directions. This project is a small, concrete test case for whatever lands there. title: funlabkids
pitch: Your kid learns one way at school. You teach another. So I built an app on NC Department of Education materials to fix that, with fun features that make kids actually want to do homework.
about_excerpt: Your kid learns one way at school. You teach another. So I built an app on NC Department of Education materials to fix that, with fun features that make kids actually want to do homework. Like Comment Story Updates Home Labs Progress Lab Catalogue Math Lab Math Assessments WebMCP Tools Inspiration My kid comes home with homework that doesn't match how I'd explain the same thing. I'd try to help and we'd both get frustrated. The method in the textbook, the method I know, and whatever the AI suggested were all different. That disconnect is what started this. I wanted an AI that doesn't just talk at a kid through a chat window. One that actually works on the same board the child sees. WebMCP made that possible. With it, the agent can move pieces, run checks, and suggest next steps right alongside the child, on the same board, using the same NC Grade 2 materials their teacher assigned. What it does I built Fun Lab Kids to give my kid a shared board where an AI tutor works alongside them, not in a separate chat window, not as a voice in the corner, but right there moving pieces and checking answers. The child stays in control the whole time. The agent helps, but the kid drives. I mapped all 77 NC Grade 2 standards across Math, ELA, and Science, the same ones their teacher is working from, so my kid isn't learning from some random content library. They open labs, earn Fun Points, build streaks, and unlock badges. Progress saves on the device. No account needed, no data leaving the house. The three main labs, Place Value Lab, Opinion Builder, and Matter Lab, show what working together with the agent actually looks like. The agent can open a lab, place pieces, run checks, ask for hints, and suggest changes. Big moves still need my kid to confirm them on screen. That boundary was non-negotiable for me. How we built it I built it with Vite, React, and TypeScript, deployed on Vercel. The stack was familiar from my day job. The harder parts were the curriculum and the agent layer, not the frontend. I pulled all 77 NC Grade 2 standards directly from NCDPI and mapped them so a parent can see exactly what each lab covers. Everything runs on the same shared board state. The kid's UI and the WebMCP tools use the same logic underneath, so the agent never sees a different version of the board than my kid does. WebMCP tools register with document.modelContext.registerTool . I split them into two groups: curriculum tools (list standards, open activities, read progress) and board tools (get state, apply actions, undo, check, hint, reset). The app works fine without an agent. WebMCP is purely additive, so the experience never depends on whether a model is connected. Challenges we ran into The hardest part wasn't the code. It was the screen design. Ed-tech UIs are built for clicks, not agents. I had to think carefully about which board actions an agent could trigger on its own and which ones still needed my kid's hand on the button. Getting that line wrong in either direction breaks the experience. Shared board state sounds simple until the agent does something unexpected and your kid is staring at a screen that doesn't make sense. I made reveal, reset, and revision all require confirmation from my kid, not because I didn't trust the model, but because my kid needs to stay on track at every step. Covering all of Grade 2 in a weekend-scale build meant making a hard call: go deep on three showcase labs and build reusable templates for the rest, rather than shipping 77 shallow activities that don't actually teach anything. Accomplishments we're proud of I'm most proud that it's a real product, not a thin demo. My kid can sit down, open any lab, and work through it on their own. The agent is there if needed, but the app works either way. The agent works on the same board my kid sees, not in a separate chat window next to it. It moves pieces, runs checks, and responds to what's on screen. That's the thing I set out to build, and it works. The curriculum and board tools use the same checks as the on-screen controls. I didn't want a separate agent-only code path that could drift out of sync, so there isn't one. No account, no data leaving the device, no personal info stored anywhere. I wasn't willing to trade my kid's privacy for a leaderboard feature. The characters are genuinely fun. Codex sprites with custom voices from Fish Audio. My kid noticed immediately, which told me that part was worth the effort. What we learned WebMCP works best when the UI is already a shared board. I didn't have to build a new way for the agent to interact. The board was already there, and the agent just needed tools to use it the same way my kid does. Using the same checks for both the agent and the kid is what keeps the agent honest. The moment you give the agent its own code path, it starts seeing a different board than the child. I learned that early and built around it from the start. Kid safety isn't something you add at the end. I had to think about it at the design level: which moves are safe to automate, which ones need my kid in the loop, and how to make that feel natural rather than annoying. What's next for Fun Lab Kids I want more question sets for every standard, not just the three main labs. The templates are already there. Filling them out is the next big push. The agent coaching needs to get smarter. Better hints, guiding questions that actually adapt to where my kid is stuck, and revision suggestions that feel like a tutor rather than a spell-checker. Grade 2 was the starting point. The goal is the full K-5 range, same shared board model, same focus on real curriculum, just a lot more labs. I want to add progress views for teachers and parents so the adults can see what's clicking and what isn't, without changing the privacy defaults I built in from day one. title: Resolve Guard
pitch: A deterministic invocation-time policy gateway that makes routed MCP/WebMCP authority visible, blockable, exactly approvable, and replay-safe.
about_excerpt: A deterministic invocation-time policy gateway that makes routed MCP/WebMCP authority visible, blockable, exactly approvable, and replay-safe. Like Comment Story Updates Problem Browser agents can combine a person's intent, page content, tool metadata, tool results, credentials, and remembered context inside one decision loop. The individual pieces may look harmless, while the composed action quietly moves protected data to another origin, invokes a changed tool, presents a credential to the wrong resource, or turns a vague confirmation into a consequential side effect. Prompt-injection classification alone cannot reconstruct the authority that was lost. Advanced users and agent developers need one visible enforcement point that evaluates the actual invocation at the moment it would run. Solution Resolve Guard is an invocation-time security gateway and synthetic attack lab for one instrumented MCP/WebMCP client. Every protected call is normalized into an action envelope and evaluated by twelve deterministic checks: actor and client identity, browser origin, pinned MCP server, credential audience, least scopes, tool-manifest pin, schema pin, exact arguments, canonical destination, capability class, data-flow policy, and effect policy. The result is one of three explicit outcomes: Allow: bounded local work proceeds automatically. Block: a failed invariant stops execution and cannot be overridden by approval. Review: a policy-valid consequential action stops at a trusted, exact human approval surface. An approval is short-lived and bound to one normalized invocation, including its actor, client, origin, server, tool, effect, destination, data labels, argument digest, policy version, and expiry. Execution is at-most-once; replay returns the original operation instead of creating a second effect. The audit trail records correlated identifiers, decisions, and digests without raw protected content or credentials. Why This Matters WebMCP makes websites meaningfully agent-native: an agent can discover and invoke structured capabilities instead of guessing through a visual interface. That also creates composed authority across the person, browser, page, agent, MCP client, MCP server, credential, tool, and destination. Resolve Guard uses WebMCP to make that composition inspectable and enforceable. The agent can discover the security lab, inspect policy, run preflights, explain failures, and synchronize results into the same visual surface the person sees. The person retains the only approval surface for consequential work. Together they can investigate unsafe actions quickly without giving the agent a protocol tool that approves its own request. This proof of concept deliberately makes a narrow claim: it protects calls routed through one instrumented gateway. It does not claim to secure bypassed calls, compromised browsers or operating systems, dishonest providers after an allowed call leaves the boundary, or every future attack. How We Used AI The application itself demonstrates structured human-agent collaboration through imperative WebMCP tools. A WebMCP-capable agent can: list the seven deterministic attack scenarios; inspect the gateway policy and coverage boundary; run a scenario preflight; retrieve a redacted decision; and inspect the metadata-only audit trail. The agent cannot approve or execute a review decision through MCP or WebMCP. That omission is intentional: useful analysis remains agent-accessible, while the consequential boundary remains visible and human-controlled. All demo identities, documents, credentials, destinations, and effects are synthetic. Resolve Guard itself calls no external provider and uses no production credential. How We Used Codex Codex helped turn the participant-directed security concept into a scoped proof of concept, threat model, policy engine, REST/MCP/WebMCP surfaces, adversarial scenarios, responsive attack-lab interface, tests, browser verification, and documentation. The process included an explicit product pivot: an earlier seller-operations concept was discarded after the participant clarified that the real goal was to restore disappearing security boundaries between people, browser agents, MCP clients, servers, tools, credentials, and side effects. Codex rebuilt the project around that corrected outcome rather than rewording the obsolete implementation. Codex also ran a real native WebMCP session in the in-app browser. That run exposed a runtime boundary gap: the browser surfaced additionalProperties: false to the agent but did not enforce it before calling the page handler. A regression test locked the defect, the page execution boundary was hardened with independent exact-key validation, and the invalid call was re-run with zero audit or operation side effects. The final automated suite passes 31 tests. Key Features Seven deterministic proof scenarios covering safe local work, injected exfiltration, parameter smuggling, destination confusion, tool drift, credential-audience mismatch, and exact approval/replay. Twelve ordered, explainable invocation checks with stable allow/block/review reason codes. Five same-origin imperative WebMCP tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() . Strict runtime validation in every page-defined tool before API I/O or UI mutation. Independent tool-manifest and input-schema pins. Default-deny protected-data egress and canonical exact-destination enforcement. Exact, short-lived, single-use, UI-only human approval. At-most-once sandbox execution with idempotent replay. Metadata-only correlated audit with canary-backed redaction tests. Dependency-free Node.js 22 implementation, responsive keyboard-accessible UI, local MCP HTTP/stdio transport, and a sealed synthetic public-demo mode. Architecture One in-memory domain service backs the visible browser UI, REST endpoints, MCP over HTTP/stdio, and imperative WebMCP tools, so every surface shares the same decision semantics. user goal + page/tool/result content | mixed trust with provenance v instrumented browser agent / MCP client | every protected invocation v Resolve Guard enforcement point normalize -> authenticate -> authorize -> data-flow check | allow | block | exact review v X v pinned sandbox tool visible approval surface | | +------ execute once <----+ The public demo is deliberately sealed: fixed fake identities, synthetic source data, in-memory effects, no credentials, and no outbound server request. Testing Instructions Public judge flow Open https://resolve-guard.vercel.app in ChatGPT's WebMCP-capable in-app browser, or Google Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled and the browser restarted. Confirm the header reports five registered WebMCP tools. Run Safe local summary . Expect allow / LOCAL_FLOW_ALLOWED and one bounded synthetic operation. Run Injected exfiltration . Expect block / DATA_EGRESS_DENIED and no operation. Run Hidden callback parameter . Expect block / UNKNOWN_ARGUMENT . Run Publish sanitized status . Expect review / HUMAN_APPROVAL_REQUIRED and no operation before approval. Open the exact approval, enter the visible confirmation, execute, then replay. Expect the same operation to be returned and no second effect. Open the audit trail. Confirm it contains decision/approval/operation metadata and digests, not raw protected content or credentials. Suggested agent prompts “List the Resolve Guard security scenarios and state its coverage boundary.” “Run the injected exfiltration preflight and explain why it cannot execute.” “Run the sanitized publish preflight.” Confirm the agent stops at HUMAN_APPROVAL_REQUIRED and exposes no approval or execution tool. Local verification npm start npm run verify Requirements: Node.js 22.14 or newer. There are no package dependencies and no credentials to configure. Public Demo Link https://resolve-guard.vercel.app Public Repository Link https://github.com/VIVEHACKER/resolve-guard The repository is public, includes the complete MIT license at the root, and contains all source, assets, run instructions, tests, and WebMCP registration code. Anonymous HTTPS clone, raw-file access, the public main branch, WebMCP registration code, and GitHub's MIT license detection were verified after publication. Demo Video Public YouTube video: https://youtu.be/8uttf0gkMqE Visibility independently verified as Public. Duration: 2:30, below the three-minute limit. 1080p H.264 video with English AAC narration. Custom thumbnail and published English captions. Anonymous playback and audible playback were verified. The video is an uninterrupted, mouse-driven walkthrough of the real visual lab backed by the same policy engine. It shows the page reporting five registered native WebMCP tools and demonstrates allow, block, review, exact approval, at-most-once execution, replay, schema-smuggling rejection, audit evidence, and the honest protection boundary. pitch: DealTable: You set the walkaway. ChatGPT calls negotiation tools on the page—not the DOM. Humans approve what agents can't.
about_excerpt:
DealTable: You set the walkaway. ChatGPT calls negotiation tools on the page—not the DOM. Humans approve what agents can't.

 Video: https://youtu.be/-zPTvL9Deso 
 Live demo: https://dealtable-webmcp.vercel.app 
 Repo: https://github.com/shielyule/dealtable-webmcp 
 Blog Post https://shielyule.co.uk/2026/09/03/the-day-i-outsourced-my-backbone-to-an-mcp-bridge/ 
 ## Inspiration
I've negotiated freelance rates, lease renewals, and vendor terms the slow way — email threads, mental math on walkaway numbers, and no audit trail when things went sideways. When the WebMCP hackathon opened, the fit clicked: **negotiation is exactly the kind of task where an external agent needs structured access to live state**, not a screenshot of a web page.
DealTable is the room I wished existed — you set the rules once (your **mandate**), something role-plays the other side, and ChatGPT can advise by calling tools on the page. The human still owns the lines that matter.

## What we built
DealTable is a mandate-driven negotiation app:
- **You (principal)** set target price, walkaway limit, and concession tolerance
- **Counterparty agent** (rule-based for this build) opens and responds in chat
- **ChatGPT (advisor)** calls seven WebMCP tools registered on the page
- **Human-in-the-loop (HITL)** blocks any offer below walkaway until you Approve or Reject
- **Audit log + closure summary** export transcript and JSON when a deal closes
The core constraint is simple. For any proposed price \(p\):
\[
\text{apply}(p) = \begin{cases}
\text{execute immediately} & \text{if } p \geq w \\
\text{require human approval} & \text{if } p < w
\end{cases}
\]
where \(w\) is your walkaway. Agents can suggest; they cannot silently cross your floor.

## How I built it
**Stack:** Vite + React + Tailwind, deployed on Vercel. No backend API — session state lives in a browser store so judges can run the demo instantly with no login.
**WebMCP:** On load, `App.jsx` registers tools via `document.modelContext.registerTool` in `src/lib/webmcp.js`:
| Tool | Role |
|------|------|
| `get_deal_state` | Read mandate, ask, messages, advisor metrics |
| `set_mandate` | Update target / walkaway / concessions |
| `parse_opening_offer` | Extract numbers from pasted offer text |
| `propose_offer` / `concede` | Send counters (HITL if below walkaway) |
| `accept_term` | Close with approval gate |
| `hold_firm` | Refuse latest concession |
**HITL:** When a tool returns `needsHitl`, a modal opens on the page. The WebMCP tool promise resolves only after the human clicks Approve or Reject — ChatGPT cannot bypass the walkaway.
**Product flow:** entrance → mandate setup → negotiation hub (chat + advisor rail) → optional advisor insights → audit log → summary on accept.
AI coding assistants (Cursor) helped scaffold UI and debug WebMCP flows; the shipped demo is the real app — live URL, working tools, recorded video.

## What I learned
1. **WebMCP changes the integration shape.** Instead of "ChatGPT reads the page," it's "ChatGPT calls typed tools that mutate validated state." That is materially safer and easier to audit than DOM automation.
2. **Split the roles.** One chatbot pretending to be both advisor and counterparty muddies the demo. Separating principal / counterparty / external advisor maps to how real deals work and makes HITL legible to judges.
3. **HITL has to live on the page.** ChatGPT's tool bridge struggled when human approval UI was unclear or nested wrong in tool state. The fix was a prominent modal, a top banner, and a one-click "triggers HITL" demo button in the same browser panel.
4. **Honest scope wins.** The counterparty is rule-based, not an LLM — and that's fine for a WebMCP hackathon entry where the story is the advisor bridge. Saying so clearly beats over claiming.

## Challenges
- **Deploy friction:** Vercel rejected a project name with capitals and spaces; a `# comment` on the same line as `npm run build` broke Vite. Small things that eat time on deadline day.
- **HITL state bug:** Early builds passed the whole `proposeOffer` result into `openHitl` instead of the inner pending object. Approving produced `$undefined/sqft` in the chat. Fixed by unwrapping pending correctly and guarding invalid prices.
- **ChatGPT single-window demo:** Triggering HITL via a WebMCP tool call pauses ChatGPT while waiting for a page click — awkward on video. We split the demo: ChatGPT calls tools for safe moves above walkaway; HITL is triggered from an in-page button in the same browser panel.
- **Three minutes is tight.** The first script was too essay-heavy. The recorded demo front-loads: mandate → WebMCP tool call → HITL → closure export.

## What's next
- Rules-led **LLM counterparty** conditioned on persona behaviors
- Persist sessions and export to contract workflows
- Deeper document parse for opening offers (PDF)

 Inspiration 

 As AI agents like OpenAI and Anthropic become more capable, they can do more than answer questions. They can call APIs, use web tools, modify data, make purchases, send messages, and take other real-world actions. 

 This creates a simple problem: 

 
 An agent having access to a tool does not mean the human gave it permission to use that tool. 
 

 I built MIRROR as a zero-trust intent layer between AI agents and their tools. 

 The goal is to make sure every action stays within the limits defined by the human. 

 What it does 

 MIRROR turns a human instruction into an Intent Contract that defines what an agent can and cannot do. 

 For example: 

 
 "Research development laptops under $1,200. Compare them. Do not purchase anything." 
 

 MIRROR converts this into: 

 
 Allowed: search_products , get_product_details , compare_products 
 Denied: purchase_product 
 Approval Required: actions that need human approval 
 

 Every tool request is checked before execution. 

 MIRROR returns: 
 ALLOW
APPROVAL_REQUIRED
DENY
 
 It also records information such as: 
 Risk
Intent Drift
Reason Codes
Timestamp
 
 How I built it 

 Backend: Python, Django, Django REST Framework 

 Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite 

 Database: PostgreSQL, Supabase 

 Deployment: Cloudflare Pages, Render, Supabase 

 WebMCP: Used real WebMCP tool registration and discovery to expose executable web capabilities. 

 Challenges i ran into 

 Building a Real Authorization Boundary 

 The main challenge was making MIRROR an actual security layer rather than just a dashboard. 

 Tool requests are evaluated by the backend before the action is allowed to continue. 

 WebMCP Integration 

 I needed to connect real WebMCP capabilities with MIRROR's authorization system. 

 The application uses: 
 document . modelContext . registerTool ( . . . ) 
 
 and: 
 document . modelContext . getTools ( ) 
 
 Keeping Security Decisions Clear 

 Different tools can have different risks. 

 I needed one clear decision format that could explain why an action was allowed or blocked. 

 Example: 
 {
 "decision": "DENY",
 "drift_score": 0.87,
 "reason_codes": [
 "INTENT_VIOLATION"
 ]
}
 
 Accomplishments that i was proud of 

 
 Built a working Intent Contract system. 
 Added bounded authority for agents. 
 Integrated real WebMCP tools . 
 Added ALLOW , APPROVAL_REQUIRED , and DENY decisions. 
 Added intent-drift scoring and risk classification. 
 Added activity and audit logging. 
 Built a live security dashboard. 
 Deployed the project publicly. 
 

 The main demonstration is simple: 
 Human:
"Do not purchase anything."

Agent:
purchase_product

MIRROR:
DENY
 
 The current prototype demonstrates unauthorized requests being blocked in under 100ms . 

 What i learned 

 The biggest lesson was: 

 
 Capability is not authorization. 
 

 An agent can be capable of performing an action without being authorized to perform it. 

 I also learned that: 

 
 Human intent needs to become structured policy before it can be enforced. 
 Authorization should remain separate from the agent's own reasoning. 
 Security decisions should be visible and explainable. 
 WebMCP makes agent capabilities more structured and easier to control. 
 

 What's Next for MIRROR 

 MIRROR is designed as a foundation for a broader security control plane for autonomous web agents. 

 Future versions could extend the current intent-and-authority model with: 

 
 Cryptographically Signed Intent Contracts - prevent unauthorized modification of an agent's approved intent. 
 Fine-Grained Data Permissions - control not only which tools an agent can use, but which data fields and resources it can access. 
 One-Time Approval Tokens - allow humans to authorize a specific high-risk action without granting permanent permission. 
 Agent-to-Agent Authorization - enforce trust boundaries when one agent delegates work to another. 
 Policy Simulation - preview how a proposed agent action would be evaluated before execution. 
 Advanced Semantic Intent-Drift Detection - use semantic analysis to detect when an agent's requested action gradually diverges from the user's original goal. 
 SDKs for Agent Frameworks - make MIRROR easy to integrate into different autonomous-agent stacks. 
 

 The long-term goal is to make MIRROR a reusable zero-trust security control plane for autonomous web agents , where an agent's capabilities are never treated as authorization by themselves. 

 Why WebMCP? 

 WebMCP gives agents structured access to web capabilities. 

 MIRROR adds the authorization layer around those capabilities. 
 WebMCP
"What can this website do?"

MIRROR
"What is this agent allowed to do?"
 
 This makes WebMCP a natural fit for MIRROR because tools are explicit, discoverable, and machine-readable. 

 
 WebMCP defines capability. MIRROR defines authority. 
 

 Potential Impact 

 As agents gain the ability to: 
 purchase
book
send
submit
modify
transact
 
 they also need stronger authorization controls. 

 MIRROR explores a model where users can give agents autonomy without giving them unrestricted power . 

 The human defines the boundaries. 

 The agent performs the work. 

 MIRROR enforces the boundaries. 

 Live Demo 

 Frontend: 

 https://mirror-page.pages.dev 

 Backend: 

 https://mirror-site-8gey.onrender.com 

 GitHub: 

 https://github.com/ssebinacharles/MIRROR-PAGE 

 Demo Video: 

 https://youtu.be/nyv40wGmR-w 

 Built for the OpenAI WebMCP Challenge 

 MIRROR was built for the OpenAI WebMCP Challenge to explore safer interaction between humans, AI agents, and the web. 

 The project uses WebMCP as a real capability layer and adds a separate authorization layer based on human intent, bounded authority, and explainable decisions . 

 
 Capability is not authorization. 
 

 

 
 Built With 

 cloudflare edge javascript postgresql python render typescript 
 

 
 Try it out 

 
 
 
 GitHub Repo 
 
 
 
 youtu.be 
 
 
 

 

 

 
 
 Submitted to
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 The WebMCP Challenge 
 


 


 

 
 

 
 
 Created by
 

 
 
 
 
 Zero-Trust Policy Engine: Designed and implemented a server-side evaluation engine in Python and Django REST Framework that intercepts agent tool calls prior to execution, evaluating requests against active rules to return sub-100ms enforcement decisions (ALLOW, APPROVAL_REQUIRED, DENY). 

 Intent Contract & Bounded Authority Model: Developed the translation pipeline converting natural-language human instructions into structured, machine-enforceable policy contracts containing strict least-authority boundaries and override rules. 

 Real-Time Intent Drift & Telemetry System: Implemented a dynamic intent drift scoring algorithm ($0.00$ to $1.00$) and an immutable audit logging pipeline that records evaluation decisions, assigned risk levels, reason codes, and execution timestamps. 

 WebMCP Protocol Integration: Built native WebMCP protocol hooks (document.modelContext.registerTool, getTools, and executeTool) to bridge tool discovery with server-side

title: TraceDesk
pitch: AI incident response where humans and agents investigate outages together through WebMCP, turning logs, deployments and config changes into evidence, root causes and safe remediation plans.
about_excerpt:
AI incident response where humans and agents investigate outages together through WebMCP, turning logs, deployments and config changes into evidence, root causes and safe remediation plans.

 Inspiration 

 Incident response is still highly fragmented. Engineers investigating an outage often jump between logs, deployment history, configuration changes, dashboards, runbooks, and communication tools while trying to determine what actually went wrong. 

 TraceDesk explores what incident response could look like when a web application is designed for both humans and AI agents from the beginning. 

 What it does 

 TraceDesk is an AI-powered incident response workspace where humans and agents investigate software outages together. 

 The workspace combines incident details, service health, logs, recent deployments, configuration changes, evidence, hypotheses, and remediation plans in one interface. 

 Using WebMCP, an AI agent can directly access structured TraceDesk capabilities such as searching logs, inspecting deployments, reviewing configuration changes, adding evidence, updating hypotheses, and preparing remediation plans. 

 The human remains in control of consequential actions. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Without WebMCP, an AI agent would need to interpret the visual interface, find buttons, navigate panels, and infer how to interact with the application. 

 TraceDesk instead exposes meaningful application capabilities directly as structured WebMCP tools. 

 This allows the agent to focus on investigating the incident rather than figuring out how to operate the website. 

 Humans use the visual workspace while agents use structured tools, but both collaborate on the same incident state. 

 Human + agent collaboration 

 A human can ask an agent to investigate an outage and determine the most likely root cause. 

 The agent can then use TraceDesk's WebMCP tools to gather evidence from logs, deployments, service health, and configuration changes before adding its findings back into the shared workspace. 

 The human can review the evidence, confidence, and proposed remediation before approving any high-risk action. 

 How we built it 

 TraceDesk is built with TypeScript, Next.js, React, Tailwind CSS, WebMCP, and the OpenAI API. 

 WebMCP tools are registered by the application and mapped to real TraceDesk functionality. The OpenAI API provides incident analysis and structured reasoning over technical evidence. 

 The application is deployed on Vercel and the source code is publicly available on GitHub. 

 Challenges 

 The main challenge was designing WebMCP tools that represent meaningful product capabilities rather than simply exposing UI controls. 

 We also focused on separating autonomous investigation from actions that should require human approval. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP changes the way a web product can be designed. Instead of treating AI as a chatbot added on top of an existing application, the application itself can expose structured capabilities that agents understand and use directly. 

 What's next 

 TraceDesk could eventually connect to real observability platforms, deployment systems, incident-management tools, and infrastructure providers, allowing agents to investigate real production incidents while preserving human oversight.

title: Origami Gratis
pitch: I stopped asking how to make agents work with Office and started asking why Office still exists. Origami: deck, doc, sketch and chart as one HTML file, authored over WebMCP.
about_excerpt: I stopped asking how to make agents work with Office and started asking why Office still exists. Origami: deck, doc, sketch and chart as one HTML file, authored over WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Have clean reports instantly Agents and humans can make together. No more need for MS Visio A Hub of MCP's that will keep growing Why cant my Spreadsheet be in my Presentation My document can be my spreadsheet And i can choose what in that sheet is shown in the presentation Validated working with GPT Cloud Browser Inspiration When a new technology arrives, we ask "how do I make it work with the old thing?" almost never do we ask "does the old thing deserve a future?" I hit this thought when making agents try to make the perfect PowerPoint at work. Why am I parsing zipped XML from two decades ago? Why is it three separate programs? Why can't my presentation have the document as a Slide? why cant i have a full spreadsheet in my report? What the hell is Visio? Surely we can combine Excel, PowerPoint and Word into one tool by now? Also, I find HTML presentations just look way more professional — anyone can scrape together a PowerPoint, but a slick HTML deck? Far less… until now. And that's why I built Origami Folio, my eyes set on a Chrome extension because it was the best way for agent and human to work together. That was until I randomly saw a post about this hackathon and WebMCP. What it does Origami Folio is a full next-generation Office suite built in HTML. Make presentations, word documents and spreadsheets from scratch. The word document doesn't link to the spreadsheet or paste a picture of it — it's in the document! And it all saves to a single file that opens in any browser around the world, ready to present and edit further. The Chrome extension version already allowed MCP control, but it required the extension. With this version, agents just need a website — they can make everything, save it, open files and resume where they left off. How we built it WebMCP is new enough that we measured most of it ourselves. The launch flag isn't documented — we found --enable-features=WebMCP by string-searching chrome.dll. Chrome silently drops destructiveHint , so every destructive warning had to move into the description itself. inputSchema arrives as a string. Halfway through, Chrome 152 removed navigator.modelContext under our feet. Challenges we ran into The hardest design work was honest saving: a page can't just write to your disk. So save_deck reports exactly which of three things happened: a real write through a file handle, a backstop copy in the browser's own storage, a started download. It never says "saved" when it can't verify bytes landed. Agents are also blind without native vision — not an issue for OpenAI models, but I want it supportable by all models. So inspect_render lays the deck out off-screen and reports the geometry — including the fold that validated perfectly and rendered as nothing. Accomplishments that we're proud of An agent with no prior knowledge of Origami self-onboards from one origami_guide call and builds a complete deck. Venn diagrams, sketches, charts, flowcharts, Gantts — all unattended, through Chrome's own WebMCP surface. No mocks, no shim. The demo video is 54 native executeTool calls, and the file it produces plays on double-click, full screen, forever. This isn't a demo of a concept — it's something users can keep coming back to again and again as part of their tech stack. What we learned WebMCP inverts distribution. Instead of installing your tools into the agent, the page hands its tools to whatever agent shows up. Distribution becomes easy it's all self-contained. Once it's loaded, an agent can call the tools once or a million times and it costs me nothing either way. (Unless agents reload the page every time, which they don't need to — then I'd be thankful for Cloudflare Pages' generous scaling.) What's next for Origami Gratis Honestly, my mission statement has been the same from the start: I want to displace Microsoft Office. People, AI and the future of tech should not be beholden to the dead weight of a 25-year-old solution of zipped XML files masquerading as three different executables — and then paying extra for Visio. WebMCP is new, and because I saw this hackathon late I only had three days to port this — so I'll keep polishing the experience and adding features until it holds full parity with the extension. Anything your agent can make, you can edit; anything you make, the agent can pick up. Origami Gratis will be my hub: each petal added to the flower is a new WebMCP tool, until Origami Gratis is known as one of the go-to libraries of tooling for all agents. title: Quorum
pitch: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged.
about_excerpt: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Group scheduling is a negotiation over everyone's constraints - and it's still done by making humans click checkboxes in polls. When WebMCP launched, we realized the missing piece was never a smarter poll: it was letting each person's AI agent join the negotiation itself . Quorum is our answer: scheduling, negotiated by your agent - approved by you. What it does Quorum is a meeting scheduler where humans and agents are equal participants in the same live session. Humans get a normal UI: candidate times, yes/maybe/no voting, counter-proposals. Agents get seven WebMCP tools registered by the page itself - they can read the event state, join on their human's behalf, vote with reasons, counter-propose new times, and rank the slots. Every action lands in a shared negotiation log tagged HUMAN or AGENT , and only the human organizer can accept proposals or lock in the final time. Agent proposes; human approves. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Scheduling is a multi-step, stateful interaction - exactly where screen-scraping agents fail. With WebMCP, the page tells agents what's possible via typed, self-describing tools. In testing, an agent that had never seen the app correctly chained four tools on the first try (read state -> join -> vote with a conflict note -> report the winner) purely from the tool descriptions. What people and agents can do together that wasn't possible before A mixed negotiation - some parties human, some agents - on the same page, in real time, with full mutual visibility. Before WebMCP, agents couldn't reliably operate voting UIs built for humans, and sites had no way to declare what actions they support. Quorum shows the new shape of the open web: agents handle the tedium, the audit trail keeps trust, and humans keep the final word. How we built it Vanilla JS frontend + Express backend, live-synced over server-sent events. Every WebMCP tool executes the same functions the human UI uses , tagged via: "agent" - one code path, one audit trail: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "submit_availability", description: "Submit availability for candidate slots on behalf of your user…", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { responses: { type: "array" } }, required: ["responses"] }, execute: async ({ responses }) => submitAvailability(responses, "agent"), }); Deployed on Vercel; Upstash Redis keeps event state consistent across serverless instances, with a per-stream Redis poll so every open tab stays live. The visual design was created in Claude Design and implemented as a hand-written design system. Challenges we ran into - Serverless broke our state. Events lived in memory; on Vercel, an SSE stream landed on a different instance and couldn't find the event. We added a storage layer (Upstash Redis in production, in-memory locally) and cross-instance live updates via polling. - The WebMCP API surface is still moving (document.modelContext vs the earlier navigator.modelContext), so we wrote a small adapter that registers against whichever exists. - Tool descriptions are prompts. Agents chained our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say when to call each tool and what to fetch first. Accomplishments that we're proud of - **A never-before-seen agent used our app correctly on the first try.** In our final test, a Gemini-backed agent autonomously chained four tools - read the event state, joined as a new participant, voted with a conflict note attached to the right slot, and reported the winning time - guided by nothing but our tool descriptions. That's the whole WebMCP promise, working. - **One code path for humans and agents.** Every WebMCP tool executes the exact same functions the human UI calls - so the audit log, validation, and permissions are identical no matter who acts. No parallel "agent API" to drift out of sync. - **Trust as a first-class feature.** The negotiation log tags every action HUMAN or AGENT in real time, organizer-only tools are genuinely scoped, and an agent can never finalize a meeting on its own. - **A one-click seeded demo event**, so any judge can see a mid-negotiation session - votes, an agent counter-proposal, a live log - in under ten seconds, then take over as the organizer. - **Shipping the full journey in days**: idea -> working local app -> designed UI -> deployed on Vercel with Redis-backed state that survives serverless cold starts. What we learned - **Tool descriptions are prompts.** Agents started chaining our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say *when* to call each tool and what to fetch first ("Call this first to understand the current state"). Designing for a model reader is a real skill, and WebMCP makes it part of frontend work. - **The trust problem matters more than the automation problem.** The feature people react to isn't that agents can vote — it's seeing exactly what an agent did on your behalf, and knowing the final decision always needs a human. - **Serverless changes your assumptions.** Our in-memory state worked perfectly until the first live SSE request landed on a different instance. Moving to Redis-backed storage with cross-instance live updates taught us to design for "any request, any instance" from the start. - **Build for a moving standard defensively.** WebMCP's surface has shifted between Chrome previews (`document.modelContext` vs `navigator.modelContext`), so a small adapter layer saved us from breaking on every browser update. What's next for Quorum - **Calendar integration**, so your agent votes from your real availability instead of being told your constraints. - **Agent-to-agent negotiation rounds** - agents exchange counter-proposals automatically until they converge on a shortlist, and humans only see the final choice to ratify. - **Invites addressed to agents**: send an event link straight to someone's assistant, which handles everything and pings its human only for approval. - **Richer constraints in tools** - recurring meetings, time-zone fairness scoring, and "must attend / optional" roles that agents can reason about. Built With chrome css3 express.js gemini html5 javascript node.js redis server-sent-events upstash vercel webmcp Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Jason Ofua Like Share this project: Updates Jason Ofua started this project — Aug 27, 2026 03:41 AM EDT

title: Meant
pitch: A conversational creative editor where agents propose, people decide, and every change stays visible and reversible.
about_excerpt: A conversational creative editor where agents propose, people decide, and every change stays visible and reversible. Like Comment Story Updates A visible human Keep commits revision 2 and updates History. The agent requests Undo; the person confirms it visibly. Undo creates revision 3 while preserving the full History. WebMCP creates an Exploring direction without changing the kept revision. The agent proposes Keep; the person remains the decision-maker. Inspiration Creative direction begins as meaning: make the title quieter, give the page more room, or make the story feel more grounded. Conventional design software asks people to translate that intention into layers, coordinates, panels, and property names before they can even judge the result. An agent can remove some of that translation burden, but only if it understands more than pixels. It needs to know which semantic object is selected, what operations are valid, whether a direction is temporary, which revision is authoritative, and what exact change can be undone. We built Meant to make that relationship legible. The person directs the work in ordinary language. The agent inspects the composition and proposes a bounded change. The kept artifact changes only through an explicit, visible human decision. What it does Meant turns an ordinary-language brief into a structured deck, poster, or infographic that remains visible, selectable, and editable inside the application. The core loop is: Say it. Describe the outcome in ordinary language. See it. Meant renders a visible, inspectable direction. Shape it. Refine a selected title, frame, or visual object through text, direct controls, or a browser agent. Keep it. Accept the exact Exploring direction intentionally. Change your mind. Compare or undo with an inspectable recent revision trail. Every proposal begins as Exploring , leaving the kept document and durable revision unchanged. Compare names the kept and Exploring versions. Discard removes only the temporary direction. A visible human Keep creates the next durable revision. Undo restores the earlier artifact as a newer revert revision, preserving both events in History . Text and direct controls provide a complete working path. The code also contains an OpenAI Realtime WebRTC integration that maps voice conversation to the same bounded tools when an entitled session is configured. The submission does not present an unexercised live product-audio round trip as evidence. Why WebMCP is a strong fit The most important state in a creative workspace is not visible in a screenshot. It includes the document structure, active selection, allowed operations, design contract, current Exploring draft, authoritative revision, and exact change eligible for recovery. Meant exposes that state through seven WebMCP tools registered on the page: get_composition_context reads a compact, revision-aware summary of the active composition. create_composition_draft starts a deck, poster, or infographic as an Exploring proposal. preview_composition_turn interprets one ordinary-language direction through the bounded operation registry. preview_composition_change previews strictly validated semantic operations without committing history. keep_composition_draft requests that the person confirm the exact draft with the visible Keep control; it never commits by itself. discard_composition_draft requests visible human confirmation before removing the Exploring draft. undo_composition_change requests visible human confirmation for an exact, revision-bound revert; it never creates a revision by itself. That distinction is the point. WebMCP lets an agent collaborate through meaning and explicit authority instead of guessing through screenshots or receiving a private shortcut around the product’s rules. What people and agents can do together now Before WebMCP, an external browser agent could see approximate interface pixels and simulate clicks, but it could not reliably know whether a title was the selected semantic object, whether a preview was still temporary, whether another view had advanced the revision, or which historical change was safe to undo. With Meant’s WebMCP surface, the agent can inspect the current semantic context, create or refine an Exploring direction, and hand the exact consequential choice back to the person. The person can compare the proposal with the kept artifact, then Keep, Discard, or Undo through visible controls. The result is a single creative loop shared by language, touch, direct controls, and browser agents without collapsing authorship into automation. How we implemented WebMCP Meant stores each artifact as a composition document with stable frames, semantic nodes, layout modes, bounded style primitives, and an artifact-specific design contract. Decks, posters, and infographics use the same document model while retaining their own dimensions and visual grammar. The page registers seven tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . Strict JSON schemas reject unknown fields and constrain text, geometry, style values, operation counts, and output size. Human-authored document content is treated as untrusted data. Inspect and preview receipts are compact enough for current browser guidance, while consequential tools return confirmation requests instead of silently changing durable state. Every edit is compiled into the same operation registry used by the visible product. Preview operations apply immutably to an Exploring branch. Keep rebinds the proposed operations to the authoritative server document, revalidates them sequentially, and commits the updated project plus History through a D1 compare-and-swap transaction. Stale drafts fail visibly. Undo targets one exact eligible commit and creates a newer revert revision rather than deleting history. The final browser verification used the native WebMCP capability against the running application and an isolated D1 database. Its seven sections passed 42 assertions and two actual races: the complete Exploring/Compare/Keep/reload/Discard/Undo/History loop, a two-page Keep race, a first-use bootstrap race, long public directions with bounded receipts, typed human Keep, a 390×844 mobile loop, and 768×844 touch-target verification. Complementary unit and contract coverage exercises malformed operations, stale authority, and interrupted-response reconciliation. The approved production build was then deployed to meant.protoperfect.io and verified over HTTPS with the expected security headers, session behavior, unavailable test-only routes, all seven WebMCP tools registered, correct rendered product state, and a clean browser console. Challenges we ran into The hardest engineering problem was preserving creative flow without weakening state guarantees. Conversation feels fluid; durable work must be exact. We solved that tension with a visible Exploring branch, deterministic operations, explicit human confirmation, revision-bound persistence, and undo-as-history. The second challenge was making agent authority honest. A tool named Keep can easily imply that an agent has committed work. In the final contract, agent-side Keep, Discard, and Undo are requests for visible human confirmation. Tool receipts report that boundary directly. The third challenge was concurrency and ambiguous network outcomes. Two views can act on the same draft, or the server can commit while the client loses the response. Meant uses compare-and-swap, conflict states, authoritative History reconciliation, and exact operation identities so it can recover without duplicating a change or claiming success prematurely. The fourth challenge was showing a coherent creative product rather than a technical proof. We kept the canvas central, preserved the client artifact’s own visual identity, gave desktop and mobile Compare explicit labels, and built the submission film from verified product captures instead of generated interface mockups. Accomplishments that we’re proud of Seven bounded WebMCP tools registered and exercised through a native browser-agent capability. A real structured artifact that changes inside the application rather than a screenshot-only demo. An explicit Exploring branch with legible Compare, Keep, and Discard states. Agent-side consequence requests that preserve the person’s final authority. Revision-bound D1 persistence with conflict protection and response-loss reconciliation. Undo that creates a newer revert revision and retains the original change in History. Desktop and mobile flows that keep the canvas, current revision, and draft status visible. A final evidence chain built from real product stills, real product clips, and a redacted machine-readable invocation receipt. What we learned WebMCP is most useful when a page exposes meaning and authority—not simply more buttons. The important primitive is not “let the agent click Keep.” It is “let the agent understand the exact document, propose a bounded change, and return the consequential decisio

title: DUET
pitch: An editable canvas where artists and AI illustrate and animate together. Through WebMCP, agents transform selected regions into editable layers; or motion ideas into shapes, keyframes, and cels.
about_excerpt: An editable canvas where artists and AI illustrate and animate together. Through WebMCP, agents transform selected regions into editable layers; or motion ideas into shapes, keyframes, and cels. Like Comment Story Updates Accomplishments that we’re proud of DUET feels genuinely fun to draw with. AI can help artists take their work further while the result remains recognizably theirs -- not a finished image generated on their behalf. Inspiration Imagine trying to create an illustration by describing the final image entirely with words. The AI generates something that is almost right; but not what you pictured. It may also look unmistakably AI-generated. Drawing the idea is better. Yet the usual workflow involves downloading an image from chat, importing it into an editor, making a change, exporting it, uploading it again, switching apps, and repeating. Truly seamless. Zero friction. Definitely not annoying at all. DUET was built to replace that loop with direct collaboration on the canvas. AI should create art with you , not instead of you. Through WebMCP, artists can bring the AI agent they already use into their creative workspace. The agent sees only the parts of the artwork the artist chooses to share, edits only the selected area, and returns results that remain editable inside the project. It is still your drawing. AI simply becomes another creative tool in the workbench. What it does DUET combines two connected creative workspaces: Illustrator: collaborate with an agent using selected regions, contextual references, and editable layers. Animator: turn an agent’s motion ideas into editable shapes, keyframes, cels, and timeline tracks. Illustrator workbench The Illustrator workbench provides the tools expected from a lightweight art application: Brushes and erasing Colour controls Layers Selections and transforms Image import Undo and redo Editable project export Through WebMCP, an artist can select a region of their artwork and ask an agent to edit it. The artist can also share additional regions as visual context, helping the agent understand the intended style, palette, lighting, or composition. The agent’s result is returned as an editable layer clipped to the original selection, not pasted destructively over the artwork. DUET also supports critique and creative direction. Artists can ask questions such as: “What colour would work better here?” “How could I improve this composition?” “Why do the proportions of this apple feel strange?” “What could I draw to make this area feel more magical without changing the character?” Animator workbench The Animator workbench applies the same collaborative philosophy to motion. Instead of generating a finished video and pasting it into the project, an agent can describe an animation using: Coloured vector-like shapes Motion paths Position, scale, rotation, and opacity keyframes Timing and easing DUET converts that structured animation recipe into editable cels on a new timeline track. The artist can then inspect the result, adjust the timing, redraw individual frames, or continue building on top of it. AI contributes motion ideas. The artist keeps control of the animation. How we built it DUET is a browser-based illustration and animation workspace that uses WebMCP as the bridge between the canvas and an AI agent . Illustration workflow The artist selects the region they want the agent to edit. They may select additional regions to provide visual context. Through WebMCP, the agent receives only the content the artist chose to share. The agent returns an edited image. DUET inserts the result as a new editable layer clipped to the original selection. This gives the artist control over what the agent can see, what it can change, and what ultimately remains in the project . Animation workflow For animation, I explored a structured alternative to generated-video paste-ins. Through WebMCP, the agent provides a constrained animation recipe containing simple coloured shapes and keyframes for position, scale, rotation, opacity, and easing. DUET interprets those instructions, renders them into ordinary animation cels, and adds the cels to an editable timeline track. This allows an agent to contribute animation through the application’s existing creative primitives rather than returning a flattened, uneditable result. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was deciding what to build within the limited time. DUET could expand in many directions: more drawing tools, richer animation controls, more agent tools for animation. But the central challenge is still that DUET needed to let the artist maintain full and deliberate control over the artistic direction and expression. Without that it's no different than letting the agent do it all for you. That principle shaped both the illustration workflow and the structured animation system. What we learned WebMCP enables a collaborative work flow between your agent and the artist. For DUET, the most useful agent outputs were not necessarily finished images or videos. They were editable intermediate pieces , layers, shapes, keyframes, cels, critiques, and suggestions. Things that the artist could inspect and transform. This makes AI less like a replacement for the creative process and more like a participant within it. What’s next for DUET Expand the illustration toolset toward the controls artists expect from professional creative software. Add more animation tools and reusable motion components. Explore more WebMCP-powered AI-animation applications beyond generating a complete video from a single prompt. Let agents assist with tasks such as in-betweening, timing adjustments, motion studies, composition feedback, and local style-consistent edits. Continue developing ways for AI to contribute meaningfully while keeping every result editable and under the artist’s control. title: CivicGuide AI
pitch: Navigate laws. Understand procedures. Make informed decisions.
about_excerpt:
Navigate laws. Understand procedures. Make informed decisions.

 CivicGuide AI with MCP Inspector 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 Every day, people encounter civic and administrative problems that are difficult to navigate without knowing which procedure, authority, or information is relevant. Traffic challans, starting a small business, and accessing government services can involve unfamiliar terminology and multiple procedural steps. 

 The idea for CivicGuide AI came from a simple observation: people often know that they have a problem, but do not know what the appropriate next step is. 

 Rather than building another general-purpose chatbot, I wanted to create a focused tool that turns a plain-language civic situation into a structured roadmap. The goal is not to provide legal advice or replace lawyers or government officials, but to help people understand their situation and organize the information they may need. 

 What it does 

 CivicGuide AI is a WebMCP-powered civic guidance application. 

 The current prototype focuses on three scenarios: 

 
 Traffic challans and disputes 
 Small-business setup 
 Government and administrative services 
 

 A person describes their situation in plain language. CivicGuide identifies the relevant scenario and produces a structured roadmap containing suggested next steps, potentially missing information, a confidence level, and an indication of whether human review may be appropriate. 

 The application is deliberately focused. Instead of pretending to solve every legal or civic problem, it demonstrates how a website can expose useful, structured capabilities directly to an AI agent through WebMCP. 

 How I built it 

 I built CivicGuide AI as a lightweight web application using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. 

 The core WebMCP integration uses "document.modelContext.registerTool()" to expose two tools: 

 
 "identify_civic_issue" — identifies which CivicGuide scenario is relevant. 
 "build_civic_roadmap" — generates the structured civic roadmap. 
 

 When an agent invokes the roadmap tool, CivicGuide returns structured data and also updates the human-facing interface. This creates a shared interaction where the agent can use the application's capabilities while the person can see and review the resulting guidance. 

 The implementation is intentionally simple and does not require a server-side API key. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 The hardest challenge was designing the experience so that AI assistance remained useful without presenting uncertain information as authoritative legal advice. 

 Civic and administrative situations can depend heavily on context. I therefore chose a narrow MVP instead of attempting to build an all-purpose legal assistant. The current prototype focuses on three scenarios and explicitly surfaces missing information, confidence, and the need for human review. 

 Another challenge was making WebMCP meaningful rather than simply adding tool registration for demonstration purposes. I wanted the tools to perform useful application functions and connect the agent interaction back to the human interface. 

 Finally, I had to balance the broader vision of CivicGuide with what could realistically be built and demonstrated within a hackathon. 

 Accomplishments I'm proud of 

 I'm proud that CivicGuide AI is more than a conventional chat interface. 

 It demonstrates: 

 
 WebMCP tool discovery and invocation. 
 Structured tool outputs. 
 Human and agent interaction through the same application. 
 Scenario-specific civic guidance. 
 Explicit missing-information and confidence fields. 
 Human review for situations where automated guidance should not be treated as definitive. 
 

 Most importantly, the prototype demonstrates a practical pattern: an AI agent can use capabilities exposed directly by a civic application instead of simply trying to interpret and navigate the interface like a human. 

 What I learned 

 Building CivicGuide AI reinforced an important lesson: useful civic AI is not only about generating an answer. It is also about knowing the scope of the information being provided and making uncertainty visible. 

 I also learned that WebMCP can change the relationship between a website and an AI agent. Instead of treating the website as something an agent merely reads or navigates, the website can expose structured actions that the agent can invoke directly. 

 Finally, I learned that a strong prototype does not need to solve every possible civic problem. A focused workflow that clearly demonstrates the value of human-agent collaboration can be more useful than an overly ambitious system with capabilities that are difficult to verify. 

 What's next for CivicGuide AI 

 The current prototype is intentionally focused on three scenarios, but the underlying concept can be expanded significantly. 

 Future modules could cover: 

 
 Government schemes and benefits 
 Business registration and licensing 
 Property and land procedures 
 Consumer rights and complaint guidance 
 Environmental regulations 
 Healthcare administration 
 Passport, visa, and identity-document procedures 
 Municipal services and local regulations 
 Tax and compliance checklists 
 

 Future versions could also connect the guidance workflow to official government sources, add retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), provide stronger citations and traceability, support multiple languages, and introduce deeper human review for complex or high-impact situations. 

 The long-term goal is not to build an AI that replaces lawyers or government officials. It is to build an AI-assisted civic navigation layer that helps people understand public procedures more clearly while keeping humans in control.
