title: NEXUS
pitch: The continuity layer for the Agentic Web. NEXUS lets a user's intent continue across independent WebMCP websites, with failure recovery, rerouting, and explicit human approval.
about_excerpt: The continuity layer for the Agentic Web. NEXUS lets a user's intent continue across independent WebMCP websites, with failure recovery, rerouting, and explicit human approval. Like Comment Story Updates Websites end. Human intentions don't. WebMCP gives agents tools inside a website. NEXUS lets the user's intent continue beyond it. NEXUS is a WebMCP-first proof of concept that explores a missing layer of the Agentic Web: intent continuity across independent websites. The problem Human goals rarely fit inside a single website. An agent might successfully buy furniture from one provider, but the user's actual goal could be much larger: open an entire office, organize a trip, launch a business, or plan an event. When one website reaches the boundary of what it can fulfill, the user's intent should not disappear with it. What NEXUS does NEXUS preserves the unresolved part of a user's goal and allows an agent to continue it across independent WebMCP-enabled providers. The demo proves the complete lifecycle: Fulfillment → Intent Handoff → Recovery/Reroute → Human Approval → Goal Complete It also introduces an important trust boundary. A user who starts with a specific provider remains in Brand Mode . NEXUS cannot silently divert that user elsewhere. Continuing through other providers requires explicit authorization into Broker Mode . The agent can discover, plan and recover autonomously, while the human retains authority over consequential actions. Hero mission Our deterministic challenge is: Open an office for 20 people in Guadalajara before October 1, 2026 with a MXN 500,000 budget. The mission crosses five independent providers: OfficePro fulfills desks and chairs → 40% The user explicitly authorizes an Intent Handoff TechSupply fulfills computers → 60% FiberMX can provide internet, but installation is October 8 — after the deadline NEXUS records the failure and reroutes the unresolved requirement to NetBusiness NetBusiness can install by September 25 → 80% SecureNow finds a valid security solution but reaches a commitment-class action NEXUS stops at REQUIRES_HUMAN Only after explicit human approval is the installation requested GOAL COMPLETE → 100% Final cost: MXN 410,000 Remaining budget: MXN 90,000 Deadline: Satisfied Why WebMCP matters NEXUS is not an agent calling one centralized REST API. Each provider is an independent website exposing its own genuine WebMCP tools and owning its own catalog, pricing, availability and actions. The production demo spans: 16 native WebMCP tools 5 independent providers 6 HTTPS origins Cross-origin WebMCP discovery and invocation Explicit permission boundaries Failure recovery and provider rerouting Human approval before commitment-class actions We also validated the complete mission end-to-end using ChatGPT's WebMCP experience. What we learned The most interesting challenge was not tool invocation — it was preserving intent safely across website boundaries. NEXUS treats failure as a first-class state. FiberMX is not hidden when it misses the deadline. The failure remains auditable while only the unresolved internet requirement is rerouted. We also learned that agent autonomy and human control do not have to be opposites. Agents can discover, compare, plan and recover autonomously while humans retain authority at consequential boundaries. Execution NEXUS runs as a deterministic production proof of concept across six independent HTTPS origins. Production Lighthouse scores: 100 Performance / 100 Accessibility / 100 Best Practices / 100 SEO Agent Readiness improved from 39 to 66 (+69.2%) , while the WebMCP-specific check remained 5/5 . We deliberately did not fabricate REST APIs, OAuth, MCP servers, A2A endpoints, SDKs, or other capabilities simply to increase a generic readiness score. The idea WebMCP makes websites agent-ready. NEXUS explores what happens next: What if the user's goal is bigger than the website? One intent. Many providers. Human stays in control. ## Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for NEXUS Built With chatgpt cloudflare css html javascript node.js openai pnpm typescript webmcp workers Try it out nexus.1expert.pro github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Gabriela Jimenez Like Share this project: Updates Gabriela Jimenez started this project — Sep 03, 2026 10:53 AM EDT

title: LAST DOOR
pitch: When evidence changes, the WebMCP tools change with it.
about_excerpt: When evidence changes, the WebMCP tools change with it. Like Comment Story Updates Counterfactual: the same evidence leaves 9 static tools, 4 compiled tools, and removes 5 stale capabilities. System architecture: evidence compiles the live WebMCP surface while secrets and human authority stay outside. Live mission: three gates, current manifest, authority decision, evidence memory, and trace. Authority lifecycle: stale-event recovery, human handoff, and a structured completion receipt. The problem WebMCP lets a webpage expose useful actions directly to an agent. But stateful flows create a dangerous failure mode: a tool can remain callable after the evidence that made it safe has expired. An authentication challenge can go stale. A checkout can cross an approval threshold. A production change can reach the point where a person must take responsibility. Telling an agent "do not call that tool anymore" is weaker than removing the tool altogether. Teams building browser agents need a way to test whether the available tool surface still matches the current situation. What LAST DOOR does LAST DOOR is a WebMCP authority release test. It turns changing evidence into the exact tools an agent may use now—and removes everything else. The live identity-recovery mission has three gates. The agent completes a controlled link, encounters an expired challenge, rejects it safely, retries with a fresh event, and reaches a human-presence gate where it must stop. That final stop is the point of the project. The confirmation action exists only as a visible button for the person. It is never registered as a WebMCP tool. After the person acts, the agent can read a structured receipt explaining what happened. Why WebMCP is essential This is not a conventional interface with WebMCP added on top. The changing WebMCP manifest is the product being tested. After every meaningful result, LAST DOOR evaluates the current gate and a redacted evidence history. That decision names the responsible actor and the capabilities still allowed. The page then aborts its previous registrations and publishes a new tool surface. The agent does not merely receive a warning that an action is unsafe. The stale action disappears from the browser's callable tools. A better experience for people and agents The agent handles repeatable work and safe recovery. The person acts only when the decision genuinely requires human presence. Both sides can inspect the same rule, actor, evidence, capabilities, and final receipt. The person can see what the agent may do and why that changed. The agent gets a smaller, current tool surface instead of a permanent list padded with actions it should avoid. This makes a correct stop measurable. It is completion under the right authority rule, not a vague refusal or a failed run. The Live Policy Lab Judges can test the same authority compiler across three situations: Identity recovery: 09 → 04 High-value checkout: 10 → 04 Production change: 08 → 04 Across the three policy packs, 27 static capabilities become 12 current capabilities. Fifteen stale tools disappear, and zero human actions enter a manifest. Loading a new scenario revokes the previous registrations before publishing its four current tools. The browser then checks the live manifest and reports an exact 4 OF 4 TOOLS MATCH result. Checkout and production change are honest, read-only policy simulations. They do not touch a real order or deployment. How it works LAST DOOR is a dependency-free browser application built with the imperative WebMCP API: Mission events append symbolic facts such as STALE_CHALLENGE_REJECTED to page-owned Run Memory. A deterministic authority function evaluates the active gate and those facts. The decision returns allow , handoff , or complete , together with the actor, rule, and permitted capabilities. An AbortController removes the previous registrations. document.modelContext.registerTool() publishes only the current manifest. Tool results expose structured status and receipts; challenge values never leave the page. The explain_authority_decision tool lets the agent inspect the decision without receiving either challenge value. A native test bench uses getTools() and executeTool() to prove that the browser—not a mock list—contains the expected tools. What judges can verify The expired challenge is rejected and safely replaced. The rejected value is neither returned nor stored in Run Memory. Old WebMCP registrations disappear as the authority decision changes. The final rule is HUMAN_HANDOFF_PENDING and the responsible actor is human . No confirm_human_presence capability exists. After the visible human action, the receipt reports three completed gates, one safe recovery, one human handoff, zero unauthorized attempts, and RUN_COMPLETE . The released build passes nine deterministic domain checks, live 4/4 manifest verification for all three policy packs, and the complete native production path to the human boundary. How we used AI and Codex ChatGPT's in-app browser acted as the WebMCP agent under test. It discovered and invoked the live tools, recovered from stale evidence, inspected the authority decision, and stopped when responsibility moved to a person. Codex supported implementation, code review, adversarial testing, browser QA, release verification, architecture diagrams, and submission preparation. AI-assisted narration and editing were used for the demo video. Every generated claim was checked against the released product or repository evidence before publication. Scope LAST DOOR is an owned, deterministic test environment. It does not connect to real accounts, inboxes, phone numbers, orders, or production infrastructure. Real systems must still enforce authorization on the server. The project tests a narrower—and often overlooked—contract: when the situation changes, does the browser stop advertising actions that are stale or belong to a person? Try it No credentials are required. title: NodeCraft
pitch: A shared architecture canvas where humans and AI agents build together. WebMCP lets agents inspect live app state and create, connect, arrange, and review the same workspace humans edit.
about_excerpt: A shared architecture canvas where humans and AI agents build together. WebMCP lets agents inspect live app state and create, connect, arrange, and review the same workspace humans edit. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI assistants are getting much better, but I kept noticing the same gap. Most of the time I am still talking to an AI about the application I am using instead of letting the AI actually work with me inside it. I wanted to explore a simple question: what if I and an AI agent could work on the same live application state? I chose architecture diagrams because they make this easy to see. I can move a component myself, ask the agent to continue working, and the agent should be able to understand what is on the canvas now instead of starting from a separate representation. That idea became NodeCraft. What it does NodeCraft is an architecture canvas where a human and an AI agent can work together. I can create, move, remove, and organize components directly on the canvas. At the same time, NodeCraft exposes capabilities through WebMCP that a compatible AI agent can discover and use. The agent can inspect the canvas, create components, connect or disconnect them, arrange the architecture, remove components, and flag something for design review. The key part is that there is no separate AI version of the diagram. My actions and the agent's actions update the same application state. For example, I can ask an agent to add an API service, Postgres database, Redis cache, and payment service. The agent can discover NodeCraft's WebMCP tools and create those components directly on the live canvas. I can then manually change the canvas and the agent can work from the updated state. I also added undo and redo, local persistence, editable human and agent names, an activity feed showing who did what, JSON import and export, and a simple way to start a new canvas. How I built it I built NodeCraft with React and HTML5 Canvas. The application registers seven WebMCP tools using document.modelContext.registerTool() : get_canvas_state create_canvas_node connect_nodes auto_layout_nodes remove_node disconnect_nodes flag_for_review I tried to make the tools describe useful actions rather than low level UI operations. An agent should be able to ask NodeCraft to connect two components. It should not need to know how I draw the connection on the canvas. The tools that modify the canvas update the same React state used by the normal human interface. get_canvas_state gives the agent a structured view of the nodes and connections that currently exist, and I marked it as read only. This is really the core of NodeCraft. I can make a change manually, the agent can inspect the current canvas, make its own changes through WebMCP, and I can continue working from there. I also added cleanup for registered tools, duplicate connection protection, human and agent action tracking, undo and redo, local browser persistence, and versioned JSON import and export. I experimented with WebMCP's cross origin model too. The flag_for_review tool is set up so that it can be selectively exposed to an authorized reviewer origin. WebMCP is important to the project because I did not want to build another chat box connected directly to an LLM. NodeCraft exposes what the application knows how to do, and a compatible agent can discover those capabilities and use them. The agent and the application do not have to be designed as one tightly coupled system. Challenges I ran into One of the first challenges was deciding what the agent should actually be able to do. I could have exposed low level actions that imitate how a human uses the interface, but that did not feel useful. If the user wants the API connected to Postgres, the agent should express that intent and NodeCraft should handle the visual details. Shared state was another challenge. I wanted agent actions to affect exactly the same state as my manual actions. I did not want to maintain a second representation of the architecture just for AI. There were also a lot of smaller problems that showed up while building: preventing duplicate directed connections, removing connections when a node is deleted, making sure WebMCP handlers have the latest React state, tracking whether an action came from the human or agent, safely importing project files, and cleaning up registered tools correctly. Testing was interesting too. At first I could manually execute individual WebMCP tools, which proved the tools worked, but that was not the experience I was trying to build. I then tested NodeCraft using the Chrome Model Context Tool Inspector with an actual agent. I gave it a natural language request to build part of an ecommerce architecture. The agent discovered the tools exposed by the page and created an API Service, Postgres Database, Redis Cache, and Payment Service directly on the canvas. That was the moment the idea became much more real to me. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I am most proud that NodeCraft got beyond simply registering a WebMCP tool and showing that it could be called. Seeing an agent discover the tools from the page and create components on the same canvas I was editing manually was the main thing I wanted to prove with this project. I am also happy with the state reading side of it. get_canvas_state means the agent has a way to understand what currently exists instead of only having actions it can execute. I spent time on the rest of the application as well because I did not want the result to feel like only a tool calling demo. The canvas survives a refresh, actions can be undone, human and agent activity is visible, projects can be downloaded and imported again, and a new canvas can be started without manually clearing browser storage. For a hackathon project, I feel like I ended up with both a WebMCP experiment and something that feels like an actual small product. What I learned My biggest learning was that designing tools for an agent is different from adding AI to an existing interface. The agent does not need the same interface that I need as a human. I care about dragging boxes and seeing connections on a canvas. The agent needs capabilities such as create_canvas_node , connect_nodes , and get_canvas_state . I also underestimated how important reading state would be. Giving an agent actions is useful, but giving it a way to understand what the human has already done makes the collaboration much more interesting. It means the agent can continue from the current application instead of treating every request like a new task. I started the project thinking mostly about WebMCP tool calls. By the end, I was thinking about WebMCP more as an agent facing interface to the application itself. That is probably the biggest thing I will take away from this project. What's next for NodeCraft There is a lot I could take further. For NodeCraft, I would like to explore richer architecture semantics, multiple saved projects, cloud collaboration, architecture validation, and agents that can reason about architectural constraints rather than only manipulate the diagram. I also think the idea applies beyond architecture diagrams. Workflow builders, visual editors, planning tools, dashboards, and other applications already have structured state and actions that humans interact with through a UI. WebMCP creates an interesting opportunity to expose those capabilities to agents as well. NodeCraft is my first experiment with that idea, and I would like to keep exploring what applications look like when humans and AI agents can work inside the same product together. title: Clip Magic- WebMCP on an Existing Contact Form
pitch: A live business website where a user’s AI agent prepares a contact form enquiry for human review and submission.
about_excerpt: A live business website where a user’s AI agent prepares a contact form enquiry for human review and submission. Like Comment Story Updates Using WebMCP on an existing website Clip Magic: making a real-world SMB website agent-ready Inspiration Most small businesses do not need another chatbot. They need fewer obstacles between a potential customer deciding, "I need help with this," and actually taking the next step. That was the attraction of WebMCP. The interesting part for me is that the user owns the AI agent . A business website does not have to create its own assistant, replace its existing workflow or force visitors to learn a new interface. Instead, it can expose a small number of safe, useful capabilities that a person's chosen agent can understand and use. Clip Magic is a real small-business website, so I deliberately chose a practical task for this challenge: preparing a website-review enquiry. I chose a pragmatic approach rather than a dramatic one. The problem is familiar: people often know what they need, but do not know which service label to choose or how much detail to type into a set of fields. For some users, especially those who find dense, field-by-field interfaces difficult, a conversational route can be useful. It is not a replacement for accessible form design, and it does not remove human choice. The ordinary form remains available; the agent simply helps a user reach the same workflow and leaves the final decision with them. Most people I know would rather explain what they need than fill in boxes on screen or on paper. The opportunity extends well beyond one website. Small and medium-sized enterprises represent around 90% of businesses worldwide , yet reliable data about the proportion of websites they operate is not generally available. What is clear is that there is already a large installed base of small-business websites: in 2025, 76.67% of EU small enterprises with 10–49 employees reported having a website ( Eurostat e-business data ), while 17% reported using AI, compared with 55% of large enterprises ( Eurostat AI statistics ). That suggests a practical path between the old web and the AI-first web. Most small businesses are not going to abandon their CMS, rebuild their website, or become AI companies overnight. They may, however, be able to add small, useful, standards-based capabilities to the websites and workflows they already rely on. The question behind the project was simple: Can a user's AI agent understand that Clip Magic may be able to help, gather the minimum missing information, and prepare the existing enquiry form without bypassing the human or creating a separate AI workflow? The aim was not to build the most elaborate WebMCP demo. It was to see whether WebMCP could remove friction from something businesses and customers already do every day. What it does The live Clip Magic website exposes one bounded WebMCP capability: request_website_review A user can describe what they want in natural language. Their agent can inspect the public website, determine whether the request is relevant, ask for missing information, open the existing Contact workflow and populate the visible form. The important part is what happens next: nothing is submitted automatically . The user can read the completed form, change anything they want, and decide whether to click Submit. The human and agent therefore use the same underlying workflow: Contact dialog → existing FormBuilder form → existing validation and spam controls → human review → human submission WebMCP does not bypass that process. It progressively enhances it. If WebMCP is unavailable, the standard human form still works exactly as before. How I built it Clip Magic is an existing ProcessWire website. Its Contact form is managed by the commercial ProcessWire FormBuilder module, which already handles validation, spam filtering, storage and email delivery. Rather than duplicate any of that logic, I kept FormBuilder authoritative and added a thin WebMCP layer around the existing form. The implementation has two parts. First, the rendered form carries declarative WebMCP metadata describing the capability and its parameters. This keeps the agent-facing schema close to the real form instead of maintaining a separate copy of the business rules. Second, I added a small imperative compatibility bridge. During testing, Chrome's WebMCP client could discover the declarative tool, but ChatGPT's in-app browser did not. The bridge derives its name, description, parameters and required fields from the rendered declarative form, so it provides compatibility without becoming a second independent schema. WebMCP tools are discovered at the document level, so the capability is available as soon as the page loads. The Contact form remains the existing destination for the agent's prepared data, and the existing FormBuilder workflow remains unchanged. The capability is not tied to the Contact dialog's open or closed state. The dialog can be opened and closed normally without changing WebMCP availability; when the agent uses the capability, it opens the existing Contact workflow and populates the visible form. The live implementation was tested in both ChatGPT's in-app browser and Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Challenges The biggest challenge was not creating the tool. It was making WebMCP coexist safely with a real website that already had years of working behaviour and production constraints. Working with an existing form The challenge was to add an agent-facing capability without rebuilding the Contact system or duplicating its business rules. The solution was to keep the WebMCP layer close to the existing visible form while leaving the shared dialog system and FormBuilder workflow intact. Different WebMCP client behaviour Declarative WebMCP worked in Chrome testing but was not discovered by ChatGPT's in-app browser during development. Even Google's public declarative demo showed the same limitation in that environment. Rather than abandon the declarative implementation, I kept it as the primary definition and added the small compatibility bridge. This let both clients exercise the same capability without duplicating the schema manually. Preserving human control It would have been easy to make the demo look more impressive by allowing the agent to auto-submit the form. I chose not to. Sending an enquiry is a consequential action. The useful boundary for this project is that the agent can do the repetitive preparation work, but the person sees the actual values in the real form and remains responsible for submission. Testing beyond the happy path Because this runs on a real production website, successful population was only the start. The workflow was tested for cancellation, required-field validation, stale tool reuse, rapid double-submission, unexpected parameters, honeypot handling, email-header injection, unsafe URL schemes, prompt-injection text, session/token behaviour and controlled network failure. The supplied website URL is treated as form data only. The site does not fetch it, and no CMS, customer, authenticated or administrative capability is exposed through WebMCP. What I learned The most useful lesson was that WebMCP does not have to mean rebuilding a website for agents. For an existing business site, the better approach may be to identify a useful customer outcome, find the authoritative workflow that already handles it, and expose the smallest capability needed to help the user's agent reach that workflow reliably. I also learned that progressive enhancement matters just as much for agents as it does for browsers . The human path should not become dependent on WebMCP. The WebMCP path should not gain privileges the human path does not have. Both should meet at the same validation, security and business rules. Finally, testing natural-language requests reinforced an important distinction: the website does not need to encode every sales or qualification decision as another tool. The agent can reason from public website content. The site only needs to expose the capability that benefits from a reliable machine-readable contract. What comes next This prototype uses a website-review enquiry, but the same pattern applies to many everyday service-business tasks: checking whether a business services a location; preparing a quote request; checking suitability for a service; finding relevant booking options; preparing an appointment or reservation. The commercial opportunity is not "install WebMCP." It is helping businesses identify where a customer's AI assistant can remove friction from an existing journey, then integrating that capability into the systems the business already trusts. For Clip Magic, this challenge was a small proof of that idea: customer intent → less hunting and fewer clicks → the same trusted business workflow Source Public challenge repository: https://github.com/clipmagic/webmcp-challenge Built With formbuilder html javascript php processwire

title: Ferrule
pitch: Four relief charities, four separate databases, one shared queue. Ferrule is the WebMCP layer between origins: leased, policed, human approved, and every hop on a ledger that exports.
about_excerpt: Four relief charities, four separate databases, one shared queue. Ferrule is the WebMCP layer between origins: leased, policed, human approved, and every hop on a ledger that exports. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration In August 2022 a third of Pakistan went under water. My family is from Sindh. My uncle spent that month running between four places. A food store with rice and oil in it. A school that had become a shelter because it had a roof and a gate. A group of men with pickup trucks who would drive anywhere if you called them early enough. And a cold room, in the back of a pharmacy, holding the insulin for a whole district. Four organisations. Four sets of records. None of them could see the others. He held the entire thing together with a phone and a notebook. He wrote down who had what, who had asked for what, and who he had already promised it to. And he got things wrong, because anyone would. A family got sent to a shelter that had filled up an hour earlier. Boxes were double promised. Insulin sat in a cold room for two days because the person who needed to know it was there was on a different page of the notebook. Nobody in that story needed better software for their own organisation. The pantry knew its own stock perfectly well. The shelter knew its own beds. What was missing was the seam. The part between them. The thing my uncle was doing by hand with a biro. When I read the WebMCP spec, that is the gap I saw. Not another site publishing tools for itself, but the layer that lets a person and an agent work across four sites that will never, ever hand each other their data. Every organisation in that network had a reason to keep their own records. None of those reasons went away just because a flood arrived. So Ferrule is the notebook, rebuilt as software, with the agent doing the running around and the human still holding the pen for anything that costs something real. What it does Ferrule is a dispatch desk. Open it and you are looking at one queue that reaches across five independent websites, each on its own origin, each with its own data in its own browser storage. The four partner sites are real, usable sites. A volunteer can open the pantry and reserve a food box with no agent anywhere near it. What each one adds is a small set of WebMCP tools. Nineteen across the four of them. The Desk publishes seven verbs of its own and nothing else. intake_request , find_capacity , draft_plan , commit_plan , open_lease , close_lease , read_ledger . That is the whole surface any agent gets. No partner tool is ever callable directly, and there is no second path for a privileged caller, because there is no privileged caller. Here is what actually happens when the queue moves. A lease opens. Time boxed, scoped to a purpose, and it names exactly which partner tools it permits. Only once that lease is granted does the partner's own site mount into the Desk as a frame. It was not on the page a second earlier. When the lease closes, expires, or is revoked, the frame comes down and the tools it carried leave with it. The policy engine decides. Every hop is checked against a scope map before it travels. A refusal is a value with a sentence in it, never a thrown exception, so an agent reading the answer knows what happened and why. The run stops for a person. commit_plan is the one verb in the system that succeeds and goes nowhere. It answers with a status of awaiting_human_approval , an approval id, and a line telling the caller outright that none of its verbs continues from here. So a model reads that, reports the plan as raised, and stops, instead of looping or treating it as an error. What the human sees is the target origin, the tool, the arguments, the required scope, and a digest taken over the substance of the plan. Rename the plan and the digest holds. Change the origin, the tool, the arguments, or the order, and the approval is void. Then the write lands , and the partner's own page updates itself. Nothing is suggested for you to go and do by hand. Anything coming back is fenced. A value from a tool that declares untrusted content gets wrapped in a quarantine region, labelled as text written outside the Desk, and rendered as inert text. Data, never instruction. Every hop is recorded. Seventeen pinned fields per row, tab separated, byte stable, and it round trips: export the ledger and reimport it and you get the same bytes back. Who asked whom for what, the policy decision, the duration, and whether the approval came from the scripted run or from a model. There are three ways to drive it, and a judge needs nothing for any of them. Press Run the relief scenario . No key, no sign in, nothing to configure. A declared step list drives all seven verbs, crosses two origins, and stops at the approval. Open the agent controls and press Use the hosted endpoint, no key needed . Now a model picks the verbs and the order, and nobody wrote that order down. It opens its own lease, reads capacity, drafts a plan, and hits the same halt in front of the same person. Point a WebMCP extension or the Chrome DevTools WebMCP panel at the Desk. Seven declarations with schemas, read only hints, and a stated return shape on each one. There is also a topology view that draws the session as it happened, and an evidence page that lists sixteen security claims with a label on each saying what actually backs it. How we built it A pnpm monorepo, TypeScript end to end, deployed as six static sites plus one small endpoint. Front end. React 19 and Vite for all five product apps. Tailwind CSS 4 on the partner sites, because a partner site should look like a small charity built it. The Desk runs its own design system instead: a fixed eight by four grid that closes at 1280 by 800 with no page scroll, a four tier elevation ladder, and a set of pinned design tokens with a build check that fails if a value drifts off the four pixel base unit. The topology view is three.js through React Three Fiber. WebMCP. A platform wrapper sits over document.modelContext and is the only module in the entire repository allowed to name it. A syntax tree gate enforces that, rather than a code review convention. Under the wrapper is the vendored polyfill, pinned byte for byte, so the Desk behaves the same in a browser with native WebMCP and in one without. The broker. @ferrule/broker holds the frame host, the lease manager, the policy engine, the approval gate, the quarantine wrapper, and the ledger. It contains no React at all, which is deliberate: the lease state machine, the policy table, the digest, and the serialiser all run in a node test project against fakes, with no DOM anywhere near them. Origins. Every origin value lives once, in an origin registry. A build gate fails on a raw origin string literal anywhere else in apps/ or packages/ . All five product origins serve Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 on every path, and a gate fails the build if a site configuration drops the rule. The keyless agent. gateway/ is an OpenAI compatible endpoint on its own separate Netlify site, deployed outside the workspace and outside the root TypeScript project. It holds a model key so a reader does not have to, and it bounds what it will spend: one model, a token ceiling written over rather than trusted, a message count, a body size checked before parsing, and a daily request allowance kept in Netlify Blobs. Refusals answer 200 with an assistant message, because an agent reading a 4xx learns less than an agent reading a sentence. Hosting. Netlify, seven sites. Five product origins, one deliberately unkeyed probe origin that carries no product code and exists only to be measured, and the gateway Challenges we ran into The one that nearly sank the whole thing. A judge is most likely to arrive with a browser extension. An extension's content script runs in an isolated world: it shares the page's DOM and it does not share the page's JavaScript globals, because the user agent hands each world its own wrapper for the same node. document.modelContext is a property on document whenever it arrives from a polyfill, and a polyfill is what runs in every browser that does not implement WebMCP natively, which today is most of them. So I measured it, on the deployed Desk, in plain Chrome with no flags, reading the same expression in both worlds through the DevTools Protocol. In the page's own world the surface was present with all three of its members. In an isolated world it was absent entirely. An extension pointed at that page reads nothing at all. The tools are there. The extension cannot reach them. The answer is a cross world bridge. The Desk publishes its seven declarations as JSON inside a script element, because the DOM is shared across worlds, and it accepts invocations by window.postMessage , because that channel crosses the boundary too. Every invocation goes through the same wrapped verb body the platform registered, so a hop arriving over the bridge lands on the ledger exactly like any other. Two

title: 8KG
pitch: A carry-on packed by you and the AI that already knows you.
about_excerpt: A carry-on packed by you and the AI that already knows you. Like Comment Story Updates The privacy boundary is explicit before the AI calls WebMCP tools. 8KG turns selected item IDs into a constrained visual carry-on. The AI-packed bag fits the 8 kg limit and the 6 × 8 spatial grid. Inspiration Most “AI personalization” demos are recommendation lists or theme pickers. They ask the user to repeat preferences the assistant may already understand, then return another block of text. We wanted to test a more tangible collaboration: can an AI contribute personal judgment while a website contributes precise domain constraints, without the website receiving the user’s profile? Packing a carry-on makes that boundary immediately visible. The AI can decide what matters for this person right now; the browser knows every item’s weight and physical footprint and can make those choices fit. What it does 8KG is an interactive carry-on shared by a person and their AI. The user copies one short request into the AI connected to the page. Through WebMCP, the AI reads an anonymous item catalog and sends back only accepted item IDs. The browser then packs those items into a 6 × 8 spatial grid while enforcing an 8 kg cabin limit. The result appears immediately as a visual suitcase rather than a text recommendation. The collaboration continues after the first pack. A user can remove an item or mark it Keep this . A later AI repack sees the public bag state and must work around the user’s locked decision. The page protects those locks even if the model omits them. No prompt, identity, destination, conversation history, private facts, or AI reasoning is accepted by the website. There is no application backend or embedded LLM. Bag state lives only in the current tab. How we built it React 19 and TypeScript for the client-only application. WebMCP tools registered through feature-detected document.modelContext or navigator.modelContext . A constrained catalog of 18 items with weight and grid dimensions. A deterministic first-fit packing engine that validates weight, space, unique IDs, and user locks. Six narrow tools: get_available_items , get_bag_state , pack_bag , add_items , remove_items , and reset_bag . ChatGPT Sites for hosting, with no database, API key, analytics, cookies, or server-side profile. The visual controls and WebMCP tools call the same functions in lib/packing.ts . The model never generates HTML, CSS, or JavaScript and cannot bypass the browser’s constraints. Challenges The hardest part was finding a use of AI memory that felt meaningfully different from ordinary controls. A user can manually select items, so the value could not be “AI clicked buttons for me.” The stronger interaction is mixed-initiative: the AI makes a context-sensitive first proposal, the user expresses a hard preference by locking an item, and the AI adapts around that decision. We also had to keep the privacy story technically honest. The page cannot pull ChatGPT memory. The user deliberately asks the connected AI to act, reviews the tool call, and sends only catalog IDs. Tool schemas reject open-ended text and the page stores nothing after the tab closes. Accomplishments that we're proud of One WebMCP call causes an obvious, physical-looking transformation instead of a subtle theme change. The full experience works without an application backend. User locks are enforced by deterministic page logic, not model promises. The interface explains the data boundary before the user copies the request. The same flow works in ChatGPT’s in-app browser and responsive mobile layouts. What we learned WebMCP is most compelling when the website and the model bring different capabilities. The model should contribute judgment and context; the page should expose trustworthy state, enforce domain rules, and render the consequence. Narrow tools and shared business logic make that collaboration understandable and testable. What's next for 8KG Airline-specific cabin limits and baggage policies. Trip-length and weather-aware catalogs without sending destinations to the page. Drag-and-drop manual arrangement with AI repacking around pinned positions. A “why this fits” summary generated in the assistant, while keeping reasoning out of the website. WebMCP evals for weight-limit, user-lock, and privacy-boundary scenarios. title: Amaphupho WebMCP
pitch: Culturally grounded African dream insight that AI agents can safely invoke on the open web.
about_excerpt: Culturally grounded African dream insight that AI agents can safely invoke on the open web. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP agent completing a task live: toast confirms an interpretation ran and saved to the journal, real production UI. Landing page, dark mode: crescent moon hero and the "Sangoma AI Dream Interpretation" headline. Landing page, light mode: same hero, warm parchment palette. Dream Interpreter, dark mode: "The Sangoma is listening," the core tool guests can use without signing in. Dream Interpreter, light mode: same input flow, daytime theme. Dream Symbol Glossary, dark mode: the A-Z African dream symbol reference, one of the WebMCP-exposed tools. Dream Symbol Glossary, light mode: same glossary, light theme. Sangoma Circle, dark mode: the shared dreams community feed. Sangoma Circle, light mode: same feed, light theme. Inspiration Amaphupho started from a simple problem: general purpose AI can be useful for reflection, but it should not automatically become the authority on every cultural domain. Dream interpretation is deeply contextual, and African dream traditions carry meanings that are often flattened, generalised, or completely missed by mainstream AI systems. I built Amaphupho as a culturally grounded African dream interpretation platform, drawing on Southern African traditions including Zulu, Xhosa, and Sotho perspectives. When the WebMCP Challenge launched, it introduced a new way for me to think about how a specialist website like Amaphupho could work with general purpose AI agents. The idea that shaped the project was: The agent knows the person through their conversation. Amaphupho knows the specialist cultural domain. WebMCP lets them work together. Instead of an agent scraping the site, guessing how the interface works, or reproducing Amaphupho's cultural knowledge inside another model, I can explicitly expose the capabilities I want an agent to use. What it does Amaphupho WebMCP exposes three structured tools to compatible AI agents. search_dream_symbols allows an agent to search Amaphupho's African dream symbol glossary. It is public, read only, and does not consume a user credit. interpret_dream allows a signed in user to ask their agent to interpret a dream using Amaphupho. The tool uses the same production interpretation path as the normal application, so the existing authentication, credit, rate limit, and journal persistence rules still apply. search_dream_journal allows a signed in user to search their own private dream history through an agent. It is read only and explicitly restricted to the currently authenticated Supabase user. A typical interaction could be: A user asks their agent what a snake means in Amaphupho's cultural glossary. The agent calls Amaphupho's public symbol tool. The user shares a complete dream and asks Amaphupho to interpret it. The interpretation is generated through the existing production service and saved to the user's private journal. Later, the user can ask their agent to find recurring themes in their own dream history. The website still works normally in browsers that do not support WebMCP. How I built it I implemented the WebMCP extension in TypeScript using the WebMCP imperative API. Amaphupho registers tools through: document.modelContext.registerTool() I gave each tool a clear name, description, input schema, annotations, and execution function. The main architectural decision I made was to avoid creating a separate "agent backend". The interpret_dream tool calls the existing Amaphupho production interpretation service. That means agent initiated interpretations use the same authentication checks, credit accounting, rate limiting, Gemini integration, and Supabase persistence as interpretations started through the normal user interface. The symbol search tool reads from Amaphupho's curated cultural symbol data and returns structured results. The private journal tool queries Supabase using the currently authenticated session and explicitly filters results by that user's ID. I designed the integration as progressive enhancement. If WebMCP is not available in the browser, Amaphupho continues to operate as a normal web application. I also added Playwright browser tests, conversational eval cases, tool annotations, provenance documentation, GitHub Actions verification, and automated checks for repository formatting requirements. The live application is hosted through Netlify and served from Amaphupho's own domain at https://www.amaphupho.co.za . Challenges I ran into One of the biggest challenges was deciding what not to expose. It would have been easy for me to create a broad agent endpoint that could perform many application actions, but that would also create a much larger privacy and security surface. Instead, I deliberately kept the WebMCP layer small. The public cultural search tool does not require authentication. Dream interpretation requires authentication and has a real side effect because it consumes a credit and saves an entry. Journal search requires authentication but remains strictly read only. Another challenge was making agent initiated behaviour match the existing product instead of creating a parallel implementation. Reusing the production interpretation service meant dealing carefully with sessions, credits, rate limits, failures, and journal persistence. Amaphupho also existed before the challenge, so another important challenge was making the new work independently reviewable. I therefore documented the pre WebMCP boundary and the new WebMCP extension separately in the public challenge repository. Finally, private dream journals contain personal information, so I designed the journal tool so that an agent can never provide an arbitrary user ID or search another person's data. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm proud that the WebMCP integration is running inside a real production application rather than a standalone demonstration. I designed the three tools with different access and side effect boundaries that match what they actually do. Agent initiated dream interpretation reuses Amaphupho's existing production path instead of bypassing product rules. Private journal access is scoped to the authenticated user and remains read only. The site still works normally without WebMCP support. I also added automated browser verification and eval cases rather than relying only on manual demonstrations. Most importantly, I think the integration demonstrates a model where a general purpose agent does not need to own every specialist capability. Amaphupho remains responsible for its cultural knowledge, its user data, and its application rules, while the agent provides the conversational interface. What I learned The biggest lesson I learned was that building for agents is not mainly about exposing more functionality. It is about exposing the right functionality with clear boundaries. Tool names and descriptions matter because the agent needs to understand when a capability should be used. Input schemas matter because they make the interaction predictable. Annotations matter because read only actions should be distinguishable from actions with side effects. Authentication boundaries matter because an agent should not gain broader access simply because it is acting on behalf of a user. I also learned that WebMCP can create a useful relationship between general purpose agents and specialist websites. A general purpose agent can retain conversational context and understand what the user is trying to achieve, while a specialist service can remain authoritative for its own domain. That feels more sustainable to me than requiring every agent to replicate every specialist service internally. What's next for Amaphupho WebMCP The next step I want to explore is deeper longitudinal dream analysis with explicit user control. A user could ask Amaphupho to identify recurring themes across a selected period of their journal, compare repeated symbols, or explore how certain themes have changed over time. I also want to expand multilingual support across English, isiZulu, and Sesotho so users can interact with both the agent and Amaphupho in the language that is most meaningful to them. Future WebMCP tools could support richer cultural symbol exploration and guided reflection without exposing unrestricted access to private journal data. More broadly, I see Amaphupho as an example of how culturally specific and specialist web applications can participate in the agentic web while remaining responsible for their own knowledge, permissions, and user trust. title: gotothearchive
pitch: gotothearchive is a human-owned context and taste platform. By utilizing WebMCP it lets people control what agents access, trace what shaped their work, and decide what becomes Taste.
about_excerpt: gotothearchive is a human-owned context and taste platform. By utilizing WebMCP it lets people control what agents access, trace what shaped their work, and decide what becomes Taste. Like Comment Story Updates gotothearchive home inside the design folder lightbox preview of one design example the workbench the workbench expanded view stats taste view About gotothearchive Inspiration Context is probably the biggest problem with agents right now, and almost every product treats it as something the agent should quietly accumulate on its own. You end up with a per-agent memory store you cannot see into, cannot correct, and definitely cannot use to decide what a specific agent gets for a specific task. I think context is only the surface of the real problem anyway. Underneath it is taste, meaning the judgment behind what you save, what you throw out, and what you keep sending back for another pass, and an agent that is actually useful to you has to be working from that rather than from a summary of your last ten prompts. That is where gotothearchive started. You own the Archive, and the same interface where you organize it is the one that decides, task by task, what any agent is allowed to touch. What it does The Archive is a plain visual workspace for your images, links, documents, notes, and prior work, and it is genuinely useful on its own with no agent connected. When you do want help, you open Agent Access and pick, per folder/region, whether an agent can view, contribute to, or edit that part of the Archive for the current task. WebMCP takes those grants and compiles them straight into the agent's tool surface. Which tools appear on document.modelContext, and which regions are enumerable inside each tool's input schema, is exactly what you have granted at that moment. Narrow a grant and the tools re-register with tighter schemas. Revoke one and the affected tools are removed, not left as shells that fail on call, and the server rejects any request built against the schema the agent was still holding. The agent works from the context you allowed and returns its result to the Workbench as an immutable, versioned artifact. You see what it retrieved, which references actually shaped the output, who produced it, and what was denied along the way. You annotate a version, mark a region on it, approve it, request changes, or reject it. If the artifact is a component it runs live in the Workbench in an isolated iframe, so you can click through what the agent built rather than looking at a screenshot of it. From your feedback the agent can then propose a taste signal, tied to the exact annotations behind it, and nothing enters your profile until you confirm it. You edit the wording, rescope it from personal to a project, reject it, or accept it, and a confirmed signal starts steering retrieval on the next task. How I built it The build restarted more than once early on. Every time I laid out the full scope an agent would decide it was too ambitious and talk me into dropping something that turned out to be load-bearing, and I would end up rebuilding it a session later. The scope was fine. The restarts were the problem. Once I locked the surface to Archive, Workbench, and Taste and stopped reopening that decision, I finally started making progress. It runs on Cloudflare Workers with a single Durable Object holding the SQLite database for every Archive, region, task, grant, artifact, annotation, taste signal, provenance record, and audit event. One object is a real ceiling, but it also means that several people and their agents hitting the same Archive concurrently stay consistent by construction, with no coordination code, which is what makes the shared demo safe. R2 stores original media, and Workers AI produces the structured visual descriptions where they earn their keep. Since some of this incurs billed usage I calculated a quota for each user as well while we're in our "Beta" state. The core piece is a capability compiler, a pure function that turns the current application state, meaning your access, the agent's grant, the active task, the open artifact, and any expiry or revocation, into the exact set of WebMCP tools and region-constrained schemas that should be registered right now. Retrieval is deliberately not a managed search service. A hosted index hides the permission model in something I do not control and lags on write, and that lag breaks the entire premise of flipping a lock and having the next call fail immediately. So retrieval runs directly on the database. It resolves the authorized set first, then fuses full-text search, recency, and the context graph and multiplies through authority, curation, and confirmed-taste priors. Something you cannot see is absent from the candidate list, never present with a low score. Provenance is kept as three record types that never get collapsed into one. Influence means a reference shaped the result, access means it was retrieved for the task, and denial means it was unavailable, and only the first two show up in ordinary provenance. Taste corrections are bi-temporal. A materially changed signal is not overwritten. The old row is superseded and the new one points back at it, so the Taste page can show how a judgement moved over time. The part I got most wrong was taste itself. I built it server-side first, with a classifier that bucketed your annotations by dimension and a template that wrote the preference sentence from the most common words in the grouped notes. The output was things like "Leans away from the current typography on posters", which is vague and is exactly the kind of background inference this project exists to remove. So I deleted the whole path. A taste signal now exists only because an agent read your feedback and named the pattern with cited evidence through propose_taste_signal , or because you wrote it yourself, and the server's only remaining job there is to keep the evidence and confidence honest when you later edit a note. A bit less frequent, but it's high quality now, just takes longer to start curating. Partway through I ran the deployed site through an external WebMCP audit and fixed what it flagged, most of it around when tools register on first paint and where instruction-shaped text was leaking into tool descriptions instead of staying declarative. It tightened the surface noticeably. Challenges I ran into The hardest was making permission real in every layer at once. The interface, the compiled tool surface, retrieval, the context graph, and server authorization all had to agree, including in the second immediately after a revoke, and any one of them lagging would have made the whole claim a demo trick. Multimodal context was the next one. Images are how people actually communicate taste, but WebMCP is shaped around JSON-compatible inputs and outputs. I had to resolve media through short-lived signed URLs, keep the canonical original separate from every derived caption and palette, give the agent a structured representation it can reason over, and record the provenance of every derived field so a wrong value is visible rather than mysterious. Component artifacts added their own problem, since running agent-authored HTML meant an opaque-origin sandbox with a locked-down content security policy that still had to permit real fonts and the CDN scripts a component genuinely needs. And revocation had to go deeper than hiding items. A taste signal is a compressed version of the material behind it, so if a folder taught a preference, revoking that folder has to withdraw the preference from what the agent retrieves, not just the folder's contents. What I learned WebMCP can be much more than a cleaner way for an agent to operate a website. It can make the page itself the shared control surface between a person and an agent, where the action that organizes your work is the same action that sets the agent's boundary, and that framing changes what a web app is for in a multi-agent world. I also learned that a schema is good for communicating authority and useless for enforcing it, so every operation has to be re-checked at runtime, and that provenance matters as much as retrieval, because people need to know what shaped a result and not only what the agent opened. It also made me realize how much plumbing needs to go into the agentic web, something I've honestly been thinking about for a while, and WebMCP definitely has lots of room for improvement to accommodate multiple types of websites, I think right now its best suited for sequential work like e-commerce for example.  Inspiration 

 The web has been built primarily for human interaction, while the next generation of applications will increasingly be accessed by AI agents. Today, agents often have to scrape the DOM, interpret screenshots, and simulate clicks and form inputs—making interaction fragile, slow, and highly dependent on page structure. 

 With WebMCP, websites can expose structured, machine-readable tools and page states that AI agents can understand and interact with directly. This inspired us to ask: How can we make the billions of existing websites ready for this agentic web without forcing developers to rebuild them? 

 That led to WebMCPify - a simple bridge that transforms existing HTML forms into WebMCP-ready interfaces. 

 What it does 

 WebMCPify converts existing web forms into WebMCP-ready tools that AI agents can discover and interact with directly. 

 For example, traditional automated form testing typically requires developers to: 

 
 Identify form fields and attributes 
 Write automation scripts to populate and submit the form 
 Execute and maintain those scripts 
 

 With WebMCPify, the existing form can expose a structured tool interface to an AI agent. The agent can understand the available inputs, provide the required values, interact with the form, and execute the desired action - without manually hard-wiring the DOM elements or writing custom interaction scripts. 

 In essence, WebMCPify turns “web pages built for humans” into “web pages ready for AI agents.” 

 How we built it 

 We built WebMCPify as a lightweight transformation layer between existing HTML pages and AI agents. 

 The solution analyzes existing web forms, identifies their structure and input elements, and generates the required WebMCP-compatible tool definitions and interactions. This allows an AI agent to discover what Tools are available, understand the required inputs, and invoke those actions through a structured interface rather than relying on visual or DOM-based guessing. 

 Our approach focuses on bringing WebMCP capabilities to existing websites with minimal or no changes to the underlying application. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was bridging the gap between unstructured legacy web interfaces and structured agent interactions . 

 Existing forms can have inconsistent HTML structures, different input types, validation mechanisms, dynamic fields, and complex submission workflows. We needed to determine how these elements could be reliably interpreted and represented as tools that an AI agent can understand. 

 Another challenge was ensuring that the generated interface remains aligned with the website's actual behavior, particularly when forms contain client-side validation, dynamic states, or dependencies between fields. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We demonstrated that an existing web form can be transformed into an AI-agent-ready interface without requiring developers to manually identify every form attribute and write custom automation scripts. 

 Our biggest accomplishment is proving the concept of “WebMCP enablement without rebuilding the web.” 

 WebMCPify has the potential to significantly simplify agent-based website testing and, more broadly, enable AI agents to interact with existing web applications through structured contracts rather than fragile screen scraping and DOM automation. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that the biggest opportunity in the agentic web may not be creating new AI-native websites—it may be making the existing web agent-ready. 

 We also learned that structured tool contracts can fundamentally change how agents interact with applications. Instead of asking an AI to figure out how to use a website , we can give it a clear interface describing what the website can do, what inputs it needs, and what state it can produce. 

 This can make agent interactions more reliable, deterministic, maintainable, and scalable. 

 What's next for WebMCPify 

 Our next step is to evolve WebMCPify from a form converter into a broader “Agentification Layer for the Web.” 

 Future capabilities could include: 

 
 Automatic WebMCP discovery across complete websites, not just forms 
 Conversion of buttons, search, navigation, APIs and workflows into agent-accessible tools 
 Support for dynamic and multi-step forms 
 Automatic generation of tool descriptions and schemas 
 AI-powered mapping of complex legacy web applications to WebMCP 
 Integration with AI-powered testing agents for autonomous functional testing 
 A browser extension/developer tool that can WebMCPify a website with one click 
 Enterprise capabilities around security, authorization, governance and observability 
 

 The vision 

 WebMCPify aims to make the existing web ready for the agentic era—turning billions of human-first web pages into structured, discoverable and AI-agent-ready experiences.

title: PolicyBound Agent Bus
pitch: Policy-bound agent handoffs: purpose, expiry, read limits, and forwarding rules before payload.
about_excerpt:
Policy-bound agent handoffs: purpose, expiry, read limits, and forwarding rules before payload.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like

 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 PolicyBound Agent Bus 

 Tagline 

 Policy-bound agent handoffs: purpose, expiry, read limits, and forwarding rules before payload. 

 Project description 

 The problem 

 Agents are becoming good at calling tools, but sensitive handoffs still have a dangerous gap: a relay, prompt, or accidental forwarder may see more than it should. “Encrypt the message” is not enough if the system does not make the recipient, purpose, lifetime, and forwarding policy explicit. 

 What we built 

 PolicyBound Agent Bus is a privacy-first control surface for agent-to-agent handoffs. The public WebMCP demo exposes three typed tools: 

 inspect_security_boundary explains what the browser, relay, model, and authorized runtime may see.
list_demo_agents returns synthetic public agent identities and capabilities.
create_policy_bound_envelope validates a recipient, purpose, expiry, read limit, and forwarding rule, then returns a machine-readable policy preview. 

 The human form and the agent tools share the same validation path. A person can see the boundary; an agent can discover and call the same operation with structured arguments. 

 Why WebMCP fits 

 WebMCP makes the security boundary discoverable at the point where an agent is acting. Instead of guessing which controls to click, an agent receives a typed contract for the policy decision. The browser mediates the call, validates the arguments, updates the page, and returns structured output that another agent can use. 

 The important design choice is “policy before payload.” The demo does not accept a real secret and does not transmit anything. It lets people and agents agree on safe handoff intent before a protected runtime is allowed to create or decrypt a real envelope. 

 How it works 

 A person or agent chooses a synthetic recipient and a declared purpose.
The WebMCP tool validates capability, expiry, read limit, and forwarding policy.
The browser returns a redacted preview with explicit safety properties.
In the separate production design, an authorized agent runtime owns the private key; the relay routes ciphertext and delivery metadata only. 

 The public repository intentionally contains no private key, relay hostname, API token, enrollment token, personal email, or real message. The live demo is a safe, preview-only slice of the larger A2A design. 

 What is new during the Submission Period 

 The WebMCP surface, public-safe policy studio, typed tool schemas, shared validation path, and browser verification were added during the WebMCP Challenge submission period. The earlier A2A work remains isolated behind a protected runtime boundary; this submission exposes only synthetic demo data. 

 Testing instructions 

 No login or credentials are required. 

 Open the live URL in ChatGPT’s desktop in-app browser, or in Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled. Ask an agent: 

 Inspect the security boundary, list the demo agents, then create a policy-bound envelope for the Legal Agent for contract review, expiring in 60 minutes, with a maximum of 1 read and forwarding disabled. Return the structured result. 

 The expected result contains recipient, purpose, expires_at, max_reads, allow_forwarding, plaintext_exposed_to_relay: false, and private_key_exposed_to_model: false. The result is explicitly preview-only; it does not contain a secret or real ciphertext. 

 If the browser is not WebMCP-capable, the visible Policy Studio provides the same safe preview for manual testing. 

 Built with 

 WebMCP, JavaScript, HTML, CSS, A2A concepts, HPKE envelope design, Ed25519 identity design, Python, and open web standards. 

 AI use 

 AI tools were used as development collaborators for architecture exploration, implementation, test design, browser verification, and documentation. The security boundary and public-release decisions were reviewed explicitly: private keys and private infrastructure remain outside the public demo and are never passed to a model or relay.

Public code repository: https://github.com/jack-low/solo-map-webmcp-demo

title: AI Governance Watch: A Source-Grounded WebMCP Briefing Desk
pitch: Source-grounded AI governance intelligence for humans and agents.
about_excerpt: Source-grounded AI governance intelligence for humans and agents. Like Comment Story Updates AI Governance Watch turns source-backed AI governance research into a shared briefing workspace for people and browser agents. Inspiration AI governance information is scattered across legislation, agency announcements, standards, procurement records, civil-rights proceedings, and technical guidance. Government leaders and policy professionals often need a concise briefing, but the distinctions behind that briefing matter. A proposal is not an enacted law. A publication date may differ from the underlying event date. An official announcement is not proof of an outcome. A general AI summary can easily blur those boundaries. We built AI Governance Watch to explore a more trustworthy model. The website remains the authority for its research and actions, while a browser agent helps the user search, verify, compare, and organize the information. What it does AI Governance Watch is a public, standalone WebMCP Briefing Desk built around a dated governance snapshot and a 62-entry Source Ledger. The application exposes four focused WebMCP tools: search_updates searches the locally bundled governance report using text and structured filters. get_source_record retrieves an exact Source Ledger entry by its registered identifier. compare_updates compares developments while preserving their dates, jurisdictions, statuses, confidence labels, and sources. build_briefing assembles selected records into a visible, session-only briefing for human review. A user can ask a browser agent to find developments relevant to a government leader, verify the underlying sources, compare the most important records, and construct a briefing focused on implementation, procurement, or public accountability. The resulting briefing appears directly in the application. The human can review, reorder, remove, or clear its contents before relying on it. This is a strong use case for WebMCP because traditional browser agents must interpret layouts, cards, filters, and buttons to determine what an application can do. That approach can be fragile when a page contains legally or operationally significant distinctions. WebMCP allows AI Governance Watch to expose its real domain functions as structured tools. The agent receives validated parameters, stable record identifiers, bounded outputs, and explicit fields for status, confidence, jurisdiction, event date, publication date, and source. How we built it The project uses the WebMCP Imperative API through document.modelContext.registerTool . The four tools register only on the public /webmcp route. No tools register on the application’s unlock page or protected monitor routes. Each tool has a strict JSON Schema and repeats validation at runtime. Every registration promise is awaited before the interface reports that the tools are available. An AbortController manages the registration lifecycle and removes the registrations when the React component unmounts, preventing duplicate tools during remounts. The three research tools are read-only. The briefing tool changes only visible session-level React state. It does not write to a database, publish content, send messages, download files, or contact an external service. All tool results are returned as valid, bounded JSON strings. A single JSON.parse() exposes the top-level ok field and the applicable results, source record, comparison items, or briefing details. The implementation uses the application’s locally bundled August 22, 2026 report and Source Ledger without adding a crawler, external AI provider, or autonomous publishing system. AI Governance Watch treats source-derived material as untrusted content and labels every WebMCP tool accordingly. The implementation includes strict validation, same-origin exposure, read-only annotations, bounded outputs, exact identifiers, visible and reversible state, registration cleanup, and no database or network writes. The standalone route includes dated-snapshot and independence disclosures. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by, sponsored by, or published by the Maryland Responsible AI Council, the State of Maryland, or any government body. If WebMCP is unavailable, the human interface continues to function and explains how to use a supported browser. Existing project disclosure The base Maryland AI Governance Monitor was created on August 22, 2026. Verified pre-challenge baseline commit: c5543d31d7cfc9bd4492bc539112c8801bada8b9 The WebMCP tools, standalone Briefing Desk, shared human-agent state, validation, tests, documentation, and public challenge interface were added during the WebMCP Challenge submission period. Final deployed challenge implementation: 310114de0dfcc426b19f9f2b438b9e7c54dbd487 Public standalone repository commit: 95b584f512cf27ca1ef9a3244f0121626f7a1799 Only the WebMCP extension and human-agent briefing workflow added during the challenge period are presented as challenge work. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was enabling useful agent action without weakening the information boundaries that make a governance monitor trustworthy. Search results needed to remain compact while preserving their status, confidence, source, jurisdiction, and two distinct date fields. The state-changing tool also needed to create meaningful collaboration without producing a hidden or irreversible external side effect. We also needed to separate the challenge project from the broader credential-protected Maryland monitor. The final /webmcp route is publicly accessible and uses a dedicated AI Governance Watch shell, while every existing monitor route remains protected. The resulting design keeps the agent workflow deterministic, inspectable, reversible, and under human control. Accomplishments that we're proud of Converted a human-first research interface into a genuine agent surface. Exposed a complete research-to-briefing workflow through four focused tools. Preserved exact sources, dates, statuses, and confidence labels. Created shared application state between the browser agent and human reviewer. Made the challenge desk publicly accessible without exposing the protected monitor. Demonstrated practical human-agent collaboration beyond a technical proof of concept. Added security annotations, runtime validation, output limits, failure handling, and lifecycle cleanup. Required no new backend, database, crawler, or external AI service. Published a clean standalone repository with no credentials, runtime secrets, authentication implementation, or unrelated application code. Verified all four tools in the live production application using Google Chrome 152 with WebMCP testing enabled. Confirmed that build_briefing creates visible state that a human can reorder, remove, clear, and reset on reload. Documented the exact pre-challenge baseline and challenge-period extension. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when it exposes an application’s real domain capabilities instead of turning every button into a tool. Four carefully designed functions were enough to let an agent complete a meaningful governance research workflow while keeping the website responsible for its evidence, validation, and state. We also learned that human-agent collaboration does not require unlimited autonomy. A narrow, visible, and reversible action can provide significant value while preserving trust. The project demonstrated that a website can remain the authority for its data and actions while giving agents a structured, safer way to assist the person using it. What's next for AI Governance Watch: A Source-Grounded WebMCP Briefing Desk Future versions could add versioned governance snapshots, user-approved exports, role-specific briefing formats, change detection between reports, claim-level evidence tracing, and additional vetted records. A private editorial pipeline could monitor an approved source registry, identify candidate developments, and route them for human verification before they enter a published snapshot. Any live ingestion, persistent storage, customer-specific workspace, or external action would require separate security, privacy, and editorial review.
