title: Live Canvas
pitch: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface.
about_excerpt: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For as much as marketers have optimized for conversion, they haven't been able to cut through the number one reason that people leave open carts. they're not ready to buy. It had just happened to me while shopping for a microphone: I started at one site, then realized I needed more information to determine which was going to be the best fit. What if the shopping interface could have met me where I was at--researching the options, ranking the matches, explaining its rationale, and then designing a search result layout to fit its conclusions? That's just one glimpse of how web-interfaces of the future will adapt to their users' needs through a Live Canvas. What it does Each demo walks you through a conventional user interface, and then cordons off a bounded portion of it as WebMCP to redesign (the Live Canvas) The Storefront demo lets the agent curate the search results with a toolbox of approved card presets and badges. This constrained design is a good fit for the untrusted nature of the public internet, keeping users safe from XSS attacks. The Dashbord demo scales the idea up by giving you an entirely blank page. It imagine how the future of CRM / ERP dashboards might function. Prompt the agent to onboard you, collaborate on a vision with the agent as you would with your analytics team, and the end result is an entirely personal dashboard of controls, visualizations and reports. The Distribution demo scales the idea outwards by asking whether you distribute a Live Canvas as part of conventional component libraries. It demonstrates what a future Datatable component could be, with the ability to generate bespoke reports and save them to your browser - all without backend engineering or ai-vendor lock-in. How we built it The architecture north star is "agent composition, application execution". The application exposes its UI primitives through WebMCP. The agent supplies a composition, and then the live canvas renders that composition using application-owned components. This solution prevents data from leaking out of the organization's security boundary, and also prevents token bloat. Challenges we ran into and accomplishments that we're proud of There are two large challenges that required creativity: The largest challenge was discoverability. WebMCP is not bidirectional: an agent can invoke tools, but there's no mechanism for the website to initiate a conversation. The past 30 years of the web have trained users for the affordance of buttons and forms. I built a new set of visible prompts and verbs to communicate to surface the new modality which was an interesting accomplishment, but does highlight an apparent shortcoming in the standard. The second challenge is the built-in approval flow of agentic browsers. ChatGPT would auto-deny requests to access the user's simulated library to make recommendations, e.g. In the short term, this is solved with instructional text to ask for permission in advance. However, what WebMCP needs is a built in consent layer where tools are tied to required consent artifacts. What we learned WebMCP shows great potential to break interfaces out of the "ai chatbot jail". What's next for Live Canvas The most likely next step is to select an existing open-source component library and use it to build the first end-to-end WebMCP UI framework. That would turn the Live Canvas from just a demo pattern into a production-hardened implementation. title: Sivan AI
pitch: Autonomous multi-chain settlement and Service Agreement layer for browser AI agents, enabling milestone payments on Solana, Base, Stellar, Celo, and bank payouts.
about_excerpt: Autonomous multi-chain settlement and Service Agreement layer for browser AI agents, enabling milestone payments on Solana, Base, Stellar, Celo, and bank payouts. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents inside web browsers (ChatGPT, Google Gemini in Chrome, Claude) are rapidly advancing from passive text generators to active digital workers capable of negotiating deals, booking services, and coordinating freelance work. However, when browser agents attempt commercial transactions, they hit a major bottleneck: UI Fragility: Scraping DOM elements or simulating blind clicks often fails when layouts shift. Direct Transfer Risk: Upfront payments carry severe counterparty risk with zero delivery guarantees. Disconnected Financial Rails: Agents lack unified multi-chain settlement capabilities and cannot bridge crypto assets into local fiat banking. Sivan AI was built to solve this by providing the first autonomous, multi-chain settlement and Service Agreement layer for browser AI agents using the open W3C WebMCP standard. What it does Sivan AI enables AI agents in browsers to negotiate, draft, fund, and complete commercial Service Agreements with milestone protection. By registering typed financial tools on document.modelContext, web pages allow browser agents to interact with Sivan AI natively: Create Milestone Agreements: The agent drafts clear deliverables and milestone terms. Query Spendable Balances: The agent checks available USDC balances across Solana, Base, Stellar, Celo, and BSC. Human-in-the-Loop Safety: Every funding action and milestone payout requires on-screen human approval via interactive review cards before any blockchain transaction moves. Instant Local Fiat Settlement: Settled USDC can be off-ramped directly into local bank accounts (e.g. Nigerian Naira via instant NGN bank rails). How we built it WebMCP Client Layer: Implemented in TypeScript using official webmcp-types declarations, registering document.modelContext tools on https://staging.sivantech.online . Multi-Chain Core: Node.js and Fastify microservices orchestrating Privy embedded wallets, Stellar Horizon RPC, Solana web3.js, and EVM adapters. Edge Gateway: Cloudflare Workers (sivan-gateway) managing edge routing, CORS, and Model Context Protocol streaming. Cloud Backend: High-availability microservices deployed on Render with PostgreSQL persistence on Neon. Challenges we overcame Multi-Chain Fan-Out Latency: Grouped multi-chain RPC reads into deduplicated queries, preventing public RPC rate limits and timeouts from blocking balance rendering. Agent Security Boundaries: Designed a strict human-in-the-loop authorization modal so autonomous agents can never drain or move funds without explicit user confirmation. Cross-Chain Key Unification: Unified distinct cryptographic wallet families (ed25519 Solana, secp256k1 EVM, Stellar StrKey) under a single cohesive WebMCP tool schema. Accomplishments that we are proud of Delivering a fully functional, live multi-chain settlement platform on staging ( https://staging.sivantech.online ) and Telegram AI (@SivanStaging_Bot). Achieving sub-second Solana and Base transaction broadcasts with verifiable block explorer receipts. Creating an open-source, standards-compliant WebMCP tool provider available on GitHub ( https://github.com/Sivan-Technologies/Sivan ). What we learned WebMCP fundamentally transforms web applications from human-only interfaces into dual-purpose environments where humans and AI agents collaborate seamlessly without breaking authentication or state boundaries. What is next for Sivan AI Extending WebMCP tools to background service workers for asynchronous milestone monitoring. Enabling automated recurring service agreements and escrow-free micro-payouts. Onboarding global freelance marketplaces to Sivan AI agentic settlement rails. title: CourseMCP
pitch: An agent can take your course, and edit it. 33 WebMCP tools scoped by route and permission.
about_excerpt: An agent can take your course, and edit it. 33 WebMCP tools scoped by route and permission. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent operating a live course GIF Authoring in motion One prompt, one new screen 33 total tools Reading live learner state Answering through the agent 33 tools on document.modelContext Tool surface follows the route The boundary: humanOnly Tools vary by route. Inspiration Online courses are built for one participant: the person clicking through them. An AI agent can read visible text or try to operate the page, but it does not reliably know what counts as a lesson, where the learner is, which choices belong to a question, or which edits the application actually permits. The same wall exists on the other side. Course authoring tools are dense forms. An agent asked to add a knowledge check has to find the right screen, open the right panel, fill a question prompt, create the right number of answer choices, mark exactly one correct, and write feedback for each, and a run that fails halfway leaves a broken question in a real course. On the learner side, a failed agent action wastes a turn. On an authoring side, it corrupts the course content. CourseMCP began with a question that applies to both: what if the course itself could explain its structure and capabilities to the agent working beside you? What it does CourseMCP turns a prompt or an uploaded TXT, Markdown, PDF, or DOCX file into a polished, shareable micro-course. A course can remain private, belong to an optional account, or be deliberately published to a public gallery. The human interface works in any modern browser. In a WebMCP-capable browser, the course also describes itself to an agent, but never the same way twice. CourseMCP defines 33 distinct tools. An agent is never offered all 33. Depending on the route and the signed-in user's permissions, it receives between 3 and 24: Route Purpose Tools /auth/callback Authentication callback 3 /gallery Public gallery 5 /account My Courses 5 /sign-in Passwordless sign-in 5 / and /#create Course builder 6 /c/:slug Learner course 17 /edit/difficult-conversations-demo Session-only demo editor 23 /edit/:slug Persistent course editor 24 Three tools are global, context, account status, and navigation. Everything else is earned by being somewhere specific. The learner route adds 14. Read the outline, get course info, inspect the current screen, read screen content, search real course text and receive stable screen IDs, list learning objectives, read progress, list questions, read notes, then navigate to a screen, submit an answer, reset the course, add a note, or bookmark content. Nothing on this surface can alter course content. The editor route adds 21. It begins with all 14 learner tools, because an author is also a reader: the agent can add a question, navigate to it, submit an answer, and confirm the feedback renders correctly. On top of that sit four authoring tools, add_screen , update_screen , add_question , update_question , and three management tools for sharing status, visibility, and opening the learner view. Four authoring tools cover the entire editing surface: lesson bodies, titles, image URLs, alternative text, image prompts, question prompts, answer choices from two to eight, the single correct answer, per-choice feedback, and summary takeaways. That is deliberate. Stable screen and answer IDs let a small number of well-typed tools compose, instead of exposing one tool per form field. Every agent action uses the same application state as the visible UI. When an agent moves to a lesson, the learner sees the player move. When it adds a knowledge check, the editor updates immediately. A visible activity trail records what happened. Why WebMCP Learning is semantic and stateful. A useful assistant needs stable screen identifiers, course structure, question models, progress, and clearly bounded actions, not DOM selectors. CourseMCP uses WebMCP as its capability contract. On the learner side, an agent can search the course, receive matching screen IDs, and pass one into the navigation tool. It can inspect assessment prompts without being told the correct answer. On the authoring side, the argument is stronger. Adding a knowledge check means a question prompt, between two and eight answer choices, exactly one correct answer, feedback for each choice, and a position in the outline. Through a DOM, that is a long sequence of interactions in which every intermediate state is a partially valid course. As a WebMCP tool it is one call against a strict schema: it either produces a complete, valid knowledge check or it produces nothing. The clearest expression of route and permission scoping is the difference between the two editors. The session-only demo editor exposes 23 tools. The real editor exposes 24. The difference is exactly one tool, set_course_visibility , because the demo is permanently public and must not be publishable or unpublishable by anyone. Not a guard clause inside a handler that refuses the call. The tool is never registered on that route, so an agent inspecting the demo editor cannot see that publishing is even a concept there. The same logic runs in the other direction. /auth/callback is a transient route, so its surface collapses to the three globals and nothing else. /sign-in offers get_sign_in_state and prepare_sign_in , an agent can fill the form, but there is no tool to send the magic-link email, because that decision belongs to the person. How I built it The frontend uses Vue 3, Pinia, Vue Router, and Tailwind CSS. WebMCP tools feature-detect the browser API and register against the top-level document. Route-scoped registration managers remove stale tools during navigation, and course tools do not appear until the exact requested course has finished loading. Every handler calls the same Pinia actions used by the human interface, there is no separate agent-only course engine. Inputs use strict JSON schemas, results are serializable and bounded, and stable IDs allow small tools to compose safely. The Node.js and Express server extracts supported documents and calls the OpenAI Responses API with a strict Zod course schema. Supabase provides passwordless accounts and PostgreSQL persistence for courses and redacted activity metadata. Row-level security is forced on the course tables, browser roles have no direct table access, and private editor credentials are stored only as SHA-256 digests. A single Render web service serves both the API and the built Vue app. Additional guardrails include pagination, explicit publication confirmation, permission-gated authoring tools, revision checks for visible drafts, and idempotent generation so retries do not create duplicate courses. Challenges I ran into The hardest problem was lifecycle correctness, and authoring is what made it hard. A tool set that belongs to one course must never survive navigation to another course, a loading screen, or an invalid route, and the consequence of a leaked authoring tool is an edit landing on the wrong course. I built isolated registration scopes with abort-based cleanup and tested rapid navigation explicitly. A second challenge was keeping human and agent state genuinely shared. Reimplementing actions inside tool handlers would have produced subtle drift between what an author saw and what an agent had done, so I routed both interfaces through the same stores and validation paths. Generation also needed production-grade failure handling. Document extraction, model latency, retries, and duplicate requests can all fail in different ways. I added bounded uploads, extraction limits, concurrency controls, timeouts, idempotency keys, and safe error messages. Finally, authentication and sharing required careful boundaries. Accounts remain optional, private courses stay private by default, and publication requires an explicit acknowledgement. Accomplishments that we're proud of A tool surface that ranges from 3 to 24 by route and permission, with the demo and real editors differing by exactly one deliberately withheld tool. 33 composable WebMCP tools where four authoring tools cover an entire editing surface, because the IDs are stable and the schemas are strict. An editor that is a superset of the learner surface, so an agent can verify its own authoring by reading the result back. A coherent creator, gallery, account, learner, and editor, not a disconnected tool demo. A no-login demo that lets judges inspect, navigate, annotate, bookmark, and edit a real course. Persistent signed-in courses with private-by-default sharing and an opt-in public gallery. 124 automated tests plus linting and a production build check. What I learned WebMCP is most powerful when tools expose application concepts rather than reproducing buttons. Small capabilities with stable identifiers compose better than one giant "do everything" tool, four authoring tools cover more editing surface than a per-field design would have, and they compose with th

title: ClearPath — WebMCP accessibility planning studio
pitch: Agents cannot measure a floor plan from a screenshot. ClearPath exposes real centimetre geometry over WebMCP, proposes constraint-safe layouts, and keeps every change human-approved and undoable.
about_excerpt: Agents cannot measure a floor plan from a screenshot. ClearPath exposes real centimetre geometry over WebMCP, proposes constraint-safe layouts, and keeps every change human-approved and undoable. Like Comment Story Updates Studio Inspiration I kept coming back to a specific failure. Ask an agent to help with a floor plan and it looks at a picture of one. It can tell you a desk "looks close" to a walkway. It cannot tell you the desk leaves 20 cm of centred clear width where 90 cm is needed, that the desk is desk-3 at (600, 130), that you locked desk-4 ten minutes ago, or that moving it costs two seats. Accessibility planning is exactly the domain where that gap matters, because the answer is a measurement, not an impression. And it is also the domain where you least want an agent acting alone — a layout change is a physical, consequential decision that belongs to a person. So ClearPath is built around one claim: the agent and the human should reason over the same structured model, and only the human should be able to commit. What it does ClearPath models one classroom — North Hall, 9 × 6 m — in centimetres. Not a picture of a classroom: walls, an entrance, a route polyline, thirteen objects with footprints, rotations, locks and seat-capacity contributions, a 150 cm turning zone, and a door approach/recovery zone. A deterministic geometry engine recomputes, on every change: segment/rectangle intersection along the route centreline-to-obstacle distance and centred clear width destination-wall clearance with terminal-contact semantics turning-space overlap and entrance approach conflicts active capacity, route length, and changed-object count On the shipped fixture that yields a baseline of score 61, 20 cm centred clear width, 24 seats, 1,048 cm route, and one critical issue: route-corridor:desk-3. A bounded beam search then looks for a way out. On this fixture the top result moves Desk 3 from (600, 130) to (530, 130) — 70 cm — reaching 90 cm centred clear width, clearing every issue, preserving all 24 seats, and scoring 98. The agent gets twelve page-scoped tools: get_plan_summary get_plan_geometry audit_access_routes focus_audit_issue set_planning_constraints generate_route_alternatives stage_route_proposal compare_plan_versions apply_staged_plan reject_staged_plan undo_plan_change get_audit_history apply_staged_plan is the important one, because of what it does not do. It never commits geometry. It records an approval request, opens the visible comparison, and returns approvalRequired: true, committed: false. Only a human clicking Approve and apply can change the committed plan — and the commit function re-checks the actor and re-validates the staged geometry at runtime, so the boundary is enforced in the domain layer rather than in the UI. Undo restores the exact stored prior plan rather than reconstructing it. How I built it Geometry first, UI second. lib/planning-engine.ts owns the domain: types, geometry primitives, the audit, the scoring heuristic, and the search. It has no React in it. The SVG canvas renders straight from that model — the viewBox is plan.width × plan.height, the rectangles are the real object coordinates — so the picture and the tool output cannot drift apart, because they are the same numbers. The score is explainable on purpose. It starts at 100 and subtracts 22 per critical conflict, 10 per review conflict, 0.25 per centimetre below the 90 cm threshold, 2 per changed object, and 4 per lost seat. I wanted a number a person could argue with, not a black box — and it is labelled a planning heuristic, never a compliance score. Ranking is lexicographic, not weighted. Proposals sort by: route blockers → clear width met → clear-width deficit → other critical issues → review issues → capacity feasibility → capacity loss → number of changes → movement distance → route length. That ordering encodes a value judgement: capacity loss is ranked ahead of disruption. Lowering the minimum seat count to 22 makes a desk-removal option legal, but the 24-seat solution still ranks first. The agent is never nudged into quietly deleting a seat because you relaxed a constraint. Search is bounded and deterministic. Beam width 72, max depth 4, 1,500-state evaluation cap, duplicate-state elimination, and every candidate validated for locks, bounds, overlap and capacity before it is scored. It runs in about 2 ms. Verification is the deliverable. 76 Vitest unit and contract tests, 9 Chromium end-to-end workflows through a mock WebMCP host, and CI running typecheck, lint, tests, build and browser workflows on every push. Challenges I ran into The destination was cheating. The route has to reach the presentation wall, so my first audit treated the wall as non-obstacle geometry — which quietly exempted a 500 × 55 cm physical object from every clearance check. The fix was terminal-contact semantics: the wall is audited on every non-terminal segment, and only the final 45 cm (one corridor half-width) of a verified perpendicular contact is exempt. A parallel, penetrating, or misplaced final segment gets no exemption at all. Getting that right was most of a day. Two rounding paths, one measurement. Issues computed clear width as round(d × 2) while the metric tile computed round(d) × 2. For a clearance of 10.4 cm those give 21 and 20 — the issue card and the headline metric could disagree by a centimetre. In a tool whose entire pitch is "exact measurements," that is not a cosmetic bug. Now it rounds once. My audit trail was lying. This was the one that stung. The undo_plan_change and reject_staged_plan tools called handlers that hardcoded actor: 'human'. So an agent-initiated undo was recorded in the history as a human action — in the project whose central claim is human-in-the-loop provenance. No test caught it, because the tests called the session functions directly and never went through the tool path. The actor is now threaded explicitly, and there are tests for both routes. An accessibility tool with inaccessible text. I measured my own palette and eight muted greys failed WCAG AA at 9–12 px — the worst at 3.10:1 against 4.5:1 required. Fixing the colours was easy; making sure it stayed fixed was not. There is now a test that parses the JSX with the TypeScript compiler, resolves every text-[#…] literal against its nearest ancestor background, and fails below 4.5:1 — with icon-only exemptions listed explicitly at 3:1, and an assertion that every listed exemption is actually still in use, so stale ones cannot rot. Cancelling destroyed the human's work. When I added per-execution AbortSignal support, aborting a search cleared the staged proposal and every alternative, and logged it as a failure. So an agent cancelling mid-search would silently throw away the comparison a person was reading. A cancellation is now a genuine no-op on state, with its own 'cancelled' result in the audit trail. Cutting scope. ClearPath originally had a clinic and a café. They looked like three scenarios; they were one geometry engine wearing three skins. I deleted both. One honestly modelled classroom is stronger evidence than three demos that share coordinates. What I learned Structured beats plausible. The moment tools returned real coordinates instead of prose, the agent's answers became checkable — and several were wrong in ways a screenshot would have hidden. Exactness is what makes an agent auditable. "Human-in-the-loop" is a property you test, not a sentence you write. Mine was false in the audit log for days while the README described it correctly. If a safety boundary matters, there has to be a test that fails when it breaks. Schemas are not validation. Every tool declares additionalProperties: false and bounded lengths, and every tool also re-validates inside execute, because the schema is a hint to the model and the execute boundary is the actual trust boundary. Dynamic tool surfaces are the useful part of WebMCP. stage_route_proposal only exists after generation; apply_staged_plan and reject_staged_plan only exist while something is staged; undo_plan_change only exists once there is something to undo. The agent cannot attempt a nonsensical action because the action is not there — and proposal IDs are bound to a fingerprint of plan identity, geometry, locks, capacity and constraints, so a stale ID cannot stage or apply after anything changes underneath it. What's next Rotated-polygon collision (rotation is modelled but collisions are axis-aligned), importing real plans instead of one fixture, jurisdiction-specific rule packs instead of transparent defaults, and multi-user persistence. Honest limitations ClearPath is a planning aid, not accessibility certification, and no substitute for a qualified local review — thresholds vary by jurisdiction. It ships one deeply modelled scenario. The search is bounded and deterministic, not a general CAD optimiser. Collision checks are axis-aligned. State is local to the browser session. WebMCP itself is a draft AP

title: PagePatch
pitch: Turn any authenticated website into an agent-native CMS: AI stages structured edits and exact previews, while humans keep control of publishing.
about_excerpt: Turn any authenticated website into an agent-native CMS: AI stages structured edits and exact previews, while humans keep control of publishing. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Tired of Wordpress or traditional CMS solutions? why not just create your own solution via WebMCP! AI agents can draft useful website changes, but the last mile is often unsafe or incomplete. The agent edits source code, works through a separate CMS, previews an approximation, or receives credentials powerful enough to publish. Meanwhile, the real website already knows its users, permissions, content schemas, policies, and production rendering. PagePatch explores a simpler model: what if an authenticated website exposed exactly the reversible drafting capabilities an agent needs, while keeping every consequential decision under human control? What it does PagePatch is a WebMCP-powered fictional SaaS website with an authenticated author workspace. Once an author signs in, the site exposes twelve purpose-built tools that let an AI agent: discover editable structured regions and their current revision IDs; read field limits, audiences, and protected-content rules; create a persistent draft changeset; stage coordinated edits across the homepage, pricing page, and FAQ; inspect an image slot and prepare a secure replacement handoff; validate schemas, revision freshness, protected audiences, and cross-page policy consistency; and open a private preview rendered by the same components and responsive breakpoints as the production site. The agent never receives a publish tool. The live site remains unchanged until the author reviews the exact preview and chooses Approve & publish or Reject draft on the website. Publication is atomic and produces an immutable receipt. Restoring old content creates a new reviewable changeset instead of rewriting history. This makes WebMCP a strong fit for the problem: the agent handles interpretation, reconciliation, and reversible drafting, while the application retains authority over identity, policy, rendering, storage, and publication. How we built it The application registers WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() only for authenticated users with the application-owned author role. Every server operation independently rechecks the session, role, ownership, origin, content type, schema, state, and immutable revision. Dynamic tool visibility improves the agent experience, but it is never treated as the security boundary. Copy edits are stored as structured draft proposals pinned to immutable base revisions. Validation checks that protected audiences remain untouched and that a policy claim agrees across every affected page. A deterministic manifest locks a valid draft before preview and publication. The preview workspace renders the draft overlay through the same page components, content resolver, CSS, and responsive breakpoints used by the public site. This makes approval meaningful: the author reviews the real rendering rather than a separate approximation. For image replacement, PagePatch uses a short-lived authenticated upload handoff. The browser uploads directly to private Storage; the server verifies and decodes the file, rejects unsafe formats and dimensions, strips metadata, applies the registered crop, and emits deterministic WebP renditions. The agent reports the crop, resolution, format, and byte implications and must receive an explicit proceed-or-cancel decision before staging anything. Challenges we ran into The first real ChatGPT invocation used an execution shape that differed from the draft WebMCP example, so we adapted the bridge to support every observed shape while preserving cancellation and cleanup. Image transport was another important constraint. ChatGPT could understand an image pasted into the conversation but exposed no safe site-readable URL, path, attachment ID, or reference. Instead of inventing one or sending binary data through tool JSON, we built the same-site private upload handoff. Concurrency also required database-level guarantees. Draft edits, validation, publication, image decisions, and restoration use version checks, row locks, and state-specific transactions so simultaneous work fails explicitly instead of silently overwriting content. Accomplishments that we're proud of WebMCP is the product mechanism, not a decorative chat layer. Twelve authenticated tools cover the complete reversible author workflow. There is intentionally no publish, approve, reject, or restore tool. Exact previews use the production components and responsive layouts. Text and image changes can publish together in one atomic transaction. Publication, rejection, and restoration leave immutable audit history. Tool results stay within a strict serialized response budget. Automated tests cover authorization, RLS, conflicts, previews, image safety, responsive behavior, accessibility, security headers, and secret scanning. What we learned Tool discovery is useful for ergonomics, but server-side authorization must remain the source of truth. We also learned that exact previews are a trust and security feature, not merely presentation: when authors can inspect the real output and structured before-and-after differences, human approval becomes informed rather than ceremonial. Most importantly, strong agent experiences come from a clear division of responsibility. The agent is excellent at understanding intent and coordinating reversible work. The website should own permissions, policy, persistence, rendering, and commitments. What's next organization-scoped roles and multi-author review assignments; configurable structured-region registration for additional sites; multi-reviewer approval policies for higher-impact changes; configurable image focal points and signed media scanning; exportable audit receipts and post-approval deployment webhooks; and broader browser support as WebMCP availability expands. title: AAL (Agent Access Layer)
pitch: WebMCP gives agents tools. AAL adds identity, user-authorized permissions, spending limits, approvals, and verifiable receipts to WebMCP for consequential actions.
about_excerpt: WebMCP gives agents tools. AAL adds identity, user-authorized permissions, spending limits, approvals, and verifiable receipts to WebMCP for consequential actions. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP gives AI agents a much better way to interact with the web. Instead of looking at pixels, finding buttons, and simulating clicks, an agent can discover structured tools that a website exposes directly: search_products() add_to_cart() place_order() change_subscription() That felt like a major shift. But it also exposed a missing layer. If a website gives an agent place_order() , who says the agent is allowed to call it? WebMCP provides the interface between a website and an agent, but consequential actions introduce a different set of questions: Which user is the agent acting for? Which tools did that user authorize? How much can the agent spend? How long does that authority last? Which actions still require human approval? What happens if execution fails halfway through? Can we prove what was actually authorized and executed? We built AAL — Agent Access Layer to answer those questions. The simplest way we describe it is: WebMCP gives agents tools. AAL gives them permission to use them. What it does AAL adds a delegation and transaction layer around WebMCP. A user can connect an agent to a website and grant it explicit authority: which WebMCP tools it can call, under what limits, and which actions require additional approval. For a simple read, the agent can call the tool normally. For a consequential action, AAL turns the call into a transaction: Agent calls WebMCP tool ↓ Site prepares exact action ↓ AAL checks permissions + limits ↓ User or policy approves ↓ Site commits the action ↓ Signed receipt Under the hood, AAL focuses on four things: Delegation — explicit grants connect a user, a site, an agent session, a set of tools, and bounded permissions. Authorization — consequential WebMCP calls use a prepare → approve → commit flow instead of allowing page JavaScript to directly trigger effects. Accountability — grants, commitments, approvals, and outcomes are linked together with signed, verifiable receipts. Metering — agent activity can be measured using evidence tied to the authorized call, creating a path toward websites charging agents or agent platforms for usage. We also built an AAL SDK so this isn't limited to our demo. A developer building a WebMCP-powered site can integrate AAL into their existing tools and add delegation, permissions, approvals, limits, and receipts without rebuilding the protocol from scratch. The goal is for a developer to go from: WebMCP tool to: WebMCP tool + AAL policy = authorized agent capability For the demo, we pushed this all the way through a payment flow using WebMCP + AAL + x402 + Base Sepolia test USDC . The agent can construct a transaction, but it cannot approve its own consequential action. The user sees the exact payment terms, explicitly approves them, the designated wallet authorizes the payment, and the resulting execution can be reconciled into a verifiable receipt. How we built it We intentionally treated WebMCP as the tool transport , not the security boundary. AAL is built around three core pieces, packaged behind an SDK that WebMCP developers can integrate into their own sites. AAL SDK The SDK is the developer-facing layer. It gives WebMCP-powered sites a straightforward way to: register tools with AAL declare which tools are read-only or consequential define permissions and limits connect server-side prepare and commit handlers add agent delegation trigger approval when required handle revocation and session state return signed transaction receipts The goal was to hide as much protocol complexity as possible while keeping the important security boundaries intact. Developers should be able to keep building normal WebMCP tools while AAL handles the authorization lifecycle around them. WebMCP adapter A lightweight browser adapter detects WebMCP and exposes the site's tools to the agent. It handles the agent-facing interaction, consent UX, approvals, pending states, and receipt presentation. But it intentionally has very little authority. It cannot decide that an agent is authorized to spend money, mutate application state, or bypass a policy. Site transaction service The site's backend is the actual enforcement point. It: authenticates the site's user validates the WebMCP tool against a server-owned catalog verifies the agent's grant enforces tool and spending limits prepares the exact proposed effect reserves authorization capacity verifies required approval executes server-side handlers records the resulting state signs receipts One of our most important rules is: Page JavaScript never gets to decide that an agent is authorized to perform a consequential action. Grant Service The Grant Service handles explicit delegation. The user approves a grant covering a specific site, specific WebMCP tools, limits, expiration, and required forms of evidence. The site keeps the actual grant and enforcement logic server-side; the browser receives only the information necessary to drive the experience. We built the protocol around deterministic schemas, signatures, canonical hashes, idempotency keys, state machines, revocation, and conformance vectors so authorization decisions can be reproduced instead of depending on implementation-specific behavior. For the x402 demo, we added a separate trusted approval surface and a deliberately constrained testnet payment flow so we could test AAL against a real consequential action rather than just a toy API call. Challenges we ran into WebMCP exposes capability, not authority The first challenge was architectural. A WebMCP tool being available does not mean an agent should automatically be allowed to use it. We had to separate: "This tool exists" from: "This agent is authorized to use this tool, for this user, under these conditions." That distinction shaped the entire project. Making the protocol easy enough to actually integrate Designing a secure authorization protocol is one problem. Making it something a normal WebMCP developer would actually use is another. AAL has grants, commitments, proofs, approvals, receipts, revocation, limits, and recovery state. We didn't want every website developer to have to understand or implement all of that themselves. That is why the SDK became such an important part of the project. The challenge was finding the right abstraction: hide the protocol machinery without hiding the security model . A developer should mostly think about their tool, its effects, and the policy around it. AAL should handle the rest. Browser JavaScript is not trustworthy enough It would have been much easier to implement authorization in the page itself. But an XSS vulnerability, compromised dependency, or malicious page script could then alter tool descriptions, transaction terms, or approval flows. So consequential authorization had to move server-side. Exactly-once execution is mostly an illusion One of the hardest problems appeared after an action had been dispatched. Imagine an agent places an order. The merchant processes it, but the server crashes before receiving the response. Did it execute? Simply retrying could create two orders. Calling it failed could also be wrong. So AAL has an explicit unknown state. Instead of pretending every distributed action resolves cleanly, we use durable commitments, idempotency, outcome inspection, reconciliation, and receipt revisions to eventually determine what happened without blindly executing the action again. Authentication is not the same as approval Another major challenge was distinguishing: "The user is here." from: "The user approved these exact terms." For sensitive actions, especially payments, simply authenticating the user is insufficient. The approval has to be cryptographically connected to the actual transaction being executed. That forced us to model identity, agent-key possession, user authentication, trusted display, payment authorization, and execution evidence as separate signals instead of collapsing everything into one vague notion of "trust." Accomplishments that we're proud of We're proud that AAL is not just an architecture around one demo. We built the SDK so any WebMCP-powered website can start integrating the same authorization model into its own tools. That was an important milestone for us because the value of an authorization layer comes from being reusable across sites, agents, and use cases. We're also proud that AAL preserves the simplicity that makes WebMCP interesting. The developer still starts with: Expose a WebMCP tool. Then AAL adds the machinery necessary when that tool crosses from information into authority . We're especially proud of the end-to-end payment architecture. A single flow separates: the agent proposing an action, AAL determining whether it is permitted, the user approving the exact transaction, the wallet authorizing the transfer,

title: Terrain Leads
pitch: Terrain finds local businesses with weak digital presences, analyzes the opportunity, and turns leads into ready-to-build projects using AI.
about_excerpt: Terrain finds local businesses with weak digital presences, analyzes the opportunity, and turns leads into ready-to-build projects using AI. Like 3 Comment 3 Story Updates Thumbnail 2. Thumbnail 1. Terrain WebMCP Thumbnail Pipeline. Discovery Enrichment result The analysis Brief. Services. Inspiration Terrain started from a problem we kept seeing: local businesses often have outdated or missing digital experiences, while developers and agencies spend hours searching for prospects, researching them, and figuring out what they can actually offer. The idea was simple: what if you could find a business opportunity on a map and take it all the way to something ready to act on in one workflow? For this challenge, we pushed that further: what if an AI agent could actually use Terrain alongside you? What it does Terrain is a map-first prospecting and sales platform. Users can discover local businesses, inspect their digital presence, enrich leads, analyze competitors, generate briefs, choose services, and move opportunities through a visual pipeline. The goal is to move from: discovery → research → analysis → service → outreach → delivery How we built it Terrain is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, shadcn/ui, Supabase, and AI-powered workflows. Terrain was already an MCP server before this challenge, so AI clients could use its backend capabilities completely headlessly. With WebMCP, we added something different: frontend tools for the browser agent itself. The agent can read the map state, move and zoom the map, frame results, focus on businesses or leads, switch map views, and navigate different parts of the Terrain interface. Those frontend tools work alongside the same backend functionality Terrain already exposes. Challenges The biggest challenge was keeping the frontend synchronized with what the agent was doing in the backend. If an agent finds a business but the map never updates, the experience feels broken. We had to make sure agent actions, map state, discovered businesses, and visible UI all stayed connected without building a separate version of Terrain just for AI. What we learned Our biggest takeaway was that WebMCP becomes especially powerful when you expose frontend functionality, not just backend functions. MCP lets an agent use Terrain headlessly. WebMCP lets the browser agent actually operate the application with the user. Instead of relying only on screenshots and mouse clicks, the agent gets structured tools for navigating and manipulating the real interface. What's next We want to keep expanding Terrain's automation, agent workflows, bulk prospecting, outreach, and AI-powered services so a single developer or small agency can operate with much more leverage. title: Is It Taken?
pitch: When building software tools or libraries agentically you might start with just an idea and then need to come up with a name. Search 8 of the most popular package repositories for name availability.
about_excerpt:
When building software tools or libraries agentically you might start with just an idea and then need to come up with a name. Search 8 of the most popular package repositories for name availability.

 Inspiration 

 Coming up with package names can be a bit of a chore. There are so many long-dead and stale packages camping on the best names on platforms like npm. Scoping via organization helps but it can lead to confusion when there is too much similarity. That confusion can even extend to situations where a package exists in another language's registry. 

 What it does 

 "Is It Taken?" is a simple web app that allows users to search for a seed word. The web app then looks up synonyms via the Wordnik API and then checks the selected Registries for an existing package for the seed word and related words from Wordnik. Supported registries are: NPM, Maven, pkg.go.dev, Crates.io, PyPi, Packagist, Hex.pm, and RubyGems 

 The WebMCP implementation for this project has a couple modes. It can do the synonym lookup using the Wordnik API but it can also just inject it's own words and synonyms and check their availability. 

 How I built it 

 I did some simple discovery and planning using OpenSpec and turned the agent loose. Kepler was the main agent orchestrator. The architecture is an Astro site with Preact islands hosted on Netlify using server functions to fetch from most of the registries. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 Some of the registries have strict rate limiting and a couple others are strict about bot crawling. For those cases we needed to do Browser-based fetching as long as they supported CORS. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 The project was spun up within a day on stream and seeing the WebMCP tools get automated the next day was a delight. 

 What I learned 

 A tool like this is still subject to rate limiting that could be hit if it were used by many users at once. 

 What's next for Is It Taken? 

 I plan on creating a CLI tool and Skills that would allow users to get around a centralized server-based rate-limit issue.

title: Seating Repair
pitch: A WebMCP workspace for repairing constrained plans while keeping humans in control
about_excerpt: A WebMCP workspace for repairing constrained plans while keeping humans in control Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration A surprising number of everyday operational problems are really placement problems in disguise. You have a set of people, tasks, items, vehicles, or events, a limited number of places or resources, and a collection of rules that determine what can go where. We see this everywhere. Guests need to be assigned to tables. Patients need beds. Employees need shifts. Classes need rooms. Aircraft need gates. Jobs need machines. Inventory needs storage locations. In every case, the basic question is the same: how do you put the right thing in the right place while respecting all the constraints around it? Creating the first plan is only part of the challenge. The harder part often comes later, when reality changes after the plan has already been accepted. A guest suddenly needs an accessible table. Two people can no longer sit together. A VIP needs a specific position. A resource becomes unavailable. A manager makes a last-minute decision that should not be undone. At that point, the goal is not to throw everything away and optimize from scratch. It is to repair the existing plan while preserving as much of what already works as possible. Traditional optimization systems are good at solving structured problems, but people do not usually describe operational changes as formal constraints. They say things like "keep these two apart", "do not move this person", or "this group needs to stay together". An AI agent can help translate that kind of natural-language intent into structured constraints, but there is another problem: the agent may be working from an older version of the plan while a person is still editing the live page. That creates a very real failure mode. A person can make an important manual change, and the agent can later overwrite it simply because it is still acting on stale state. We wanted to explore a collaboration model where that cannot happen silently. We chose seating because it makes the larger idea easy to see. A guest represents an entity that needs to be assigned. A table represents a limited-capacity resource. "Together" and "apart" rules behave like clustering constraints. Accessibility and fixed-table rules represent eligibility and placement requirements. A locked guest represents a human decision that the agent is not allowed to override. Seating Repair is our way of exploring how WebMCP can bring these pieces together: natural-language agency, deterministic constraint solving, live application state, and direct human control, all operating on the same shared planning surface. What it does Seating Repair is a WebMCP application for solving and repairing constrained placement problems while a person and an agent are both working on the same live plan. The demo uses 12 fictional guests and three tables because that makes the idea easy to understand at a glance. But underneath the seating interface, the application is dealing with a more general planning problem: limited-capacity resources, people who must stay together or apart, fixed placements, eligibility requirements such as accessibility, decisions that a human has explicitly locked, and the need to keep as much of the existing plan unchanged as possible. Through WebMCP, a browser agent can read the exact current state of the board, understand the active constraints, add new hard constraints from a person's request, repair the plan, and then validate the result. The goal is not simply to press an "optimize" button and generate a completely new seating arrangement. In a real planning workflow, many existing decisions are already correct and should stay that way. A useful repair needs to preserve what still works, respect every hard constraint, treat human-locked placements as authoritative, change only what is necessary, and verify that the final result is actually valid. This becomes especially important when a person and an agent are working at the same time. If the agent reads the board and a person then moves or locks a guest, the agent is no longer allowed to write using the old version of the plan. That stale write is rejected with STATE_CHANGED. The agent has to read the page again and continue from the decision the person actually made instead of silently overwriting it. In the demo, this is easy to see: a person can move Grandma Rose to a different table and lock her there. The agent can then add another constraint, repair the remaining conflicts, and validate the board while leaving Grandma Rose exactly where the person placed her. Seating is the domain we chose to demonstrate the idea, but it is not the limit of the underlying pattern. The same kind of constrained allocation and repair appears in restaurant and event operations, protocol seating, workforce scheduling, room and resource allocation, patient-to-bed assignment, airport gate reassignment, and many other situations where a working plan has to adapt as constraints and human decisions change. The current build is intentionally focused on demonstrating that shared coordination model clearly. It is not meant to pretend that one seating demo is already a complete product for every one of those industries. Instead, it shows the core interaction pattern: an AI agent can help repair a constrained plan, while the live application remains the source of truth and human decisions remain in control. How we built it We built Seating Repair as a lightweight TypeScript app with Vite. Everything runs in the browser, with no backend and no separate database for the agent. The seating board that the person sees is the same state the WebMCP tools work with. We kept the WebMCP side intentionally simple and exposed only four tools. One reads the current seating state, one adds hard constraints, one repairs the plan, and one validates the result. That was enough to cover the full interaction we wanted to demonstrate without turning the project into a large collection of overlapping tools. We also did not want the language model itself to be responsible for deciding whether a seating plan is correct. The agent can understand a request such as "keep these two apart" or "do not move this guest", but the actual planning is handled by deterministic application code. The repair logic runs in the browser and searches for an arrangement that satisfies all of the current constraints. It checks table capacity, together and apart rules, fixed-table requirements, accessibility, and human locks. When there is more than one valid solution, it prefers one that changes as little of the current plan as possible. Human edits are treated as first-class state changes. A person can move a guest manually and lock that placement. Once a guest is locked, the agent cannot move them during a repair. There is no hidden tool option that lets the agent ignore the lock; the person has to unlock that guest first. One of the main things we wanted to get right was what happens when the human changes the board while the agent is working. Every change to the seating plan increments a revision number. When the agent tries to change the plan, it has to provide the revision it previously read. If the board has changed since then, the write is rejected with STATE_CHANGED. That means the agent cannot quietly apply an old plan over a newer human decision. It has to read the current board again and continue from there. Repairs are also atomic. The solver works on a snapshot first and only updates the live board after it has found a complete valid solution. If the constraints cannot be satisfied, the current plan stays as it was instead of being left in a partially changed state. The manual UI and the WebMCP tools share the same store, validation logic, and constraint model. We wanted there to be one source of truth rather than one version of the plan for the person and another version for the agent. For the demo, state is stored in browser localStorage, which keeps the project self-contained. We also added tests for the behaviors we considered most important: constraint validation, deterministic repairs, minimum-change solutions, human locks, unsatisfiable plans, stale revisions, invalid tool input, and WebMCP tool execution. The overall design is fairly simple on purpose: the agent handles natural-language intent, WebMCP gives it structured access to the live application, and normal deterministic code is still responsible for enforcing the rules and deciding whether the final plan is valid. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was not the seating solver itself. It was deciding how a person and an agent should safely work on the same plan without one silently undoing the other. At first, it is tempting to treat the agent like a normal automation flow: read the state, calculate a better arrangement, and write the result back. That works until the person changes something in the meantime. Once we started testing that interaction

title: Attendly
pitch: Attendly uses WebMCP helps guests discover and book free events, while enabling organisers to manage attendance, check in visitors, view live numbers, and generate emergency evacuation lists.
about_excerpt:
Attendly uses WebMCP helps guests discover and book free events, while enabling organisers to manage attendance, check in visitors, view live numbers, and generate emergency evacuation lists.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 This is built on another project of mine, which was originally written for my childrens PTA who were looking for a simple to use platform to help them keep track of ticket sales. The typical users are mums and time-strapped parents, and wanted something that reduces friction for them and the target audience. 

 I wanted to explore expanding on this using the new WebMCP to see if it was possible for a parent to quickly get tickets for upcoming events, without having to navigate through the site - by using natural language inside ChatGPT. 

 Taking this further, I'd expand it further by adding the ability to create events. 

 What it does 

 It uses natural conversation to discover relevant events for the user, allowing a parent, for example, to sign-up for upcoming events at a school without having to step through the site hierarchy. It provides everything they need to make an informed decision, and a confirmation record once registered. 

 For event organisers, it can provide quick feedback, i.e. 'Who is yet to arrive?' or following an evacuation 'Produce an evacuation report'. In what is becoming a familiar interface (ChatGPT). 

 How we built it 

 I used GPT 5.6 Sol to brainstorm a lightweight prototype of my existing application, and create Epics and user stories for the work which was kept in Linear. We then tackled each story in sequence, building out and pivoting as the demo became more fleshed out. 

 I used Fable 5.1 to pickup some edge cases where Sol was too quick to finish (i.e. it implemented a partial persistent storage), and independent agent analysis of each story and unit tests. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 GPT 5.6 Sol was quick to to a partial implementation, loosing context of the full scope of the build, and twice delivered partial features that I passed over to Fable 5.1 to complete. It also had a tendency to lean too heavily on the 'prototype' guidelines, and stamped this into the site. 

 I had some challenges understanding how to trigger the WebMCP standard, which didn't work in ChatGPT Chat mode - it needed to be in Work mode to load the Internal Browser tool and discover the exposed WebMCP on the site. Despite several prompts, the Chat could not even explain why it was unable to find it. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I am glad I took the time to play with WebMCP - this is my first ever challenge I've entered. I have spent the last several years working with LLMs and AI, building out a few projects - I am someone who learns by doing and I feel like I got some real value out of this which I can carry forward into my other projects. 

 What we learned 

 I learned how to implement WebMCP! I also learnt a few more tricks in how to prompt GPT 5.6 to keep it on track. 

 What's next for Attendly 

 This will eventually be implemented into the full Attendly product. The stories are in the backlog, but it's a big backlog.

title: Kitty
pitch: Everyone's AI agent adds their own items and allergies to one shared group order — Kitty tracks it live and splits the bill automatically, no manual collecting or spreadsheet math needed.
about_excerpt: Everyone's AI agent adds their own items and allergies to one shared group order — Kitty tracks it live and splits the bill automatically, no manual collecting or spreadsheet math needed. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Group orders always end the same way: one person becomes the unpaid dispatcher, allergies get missed, and the bill math takes longer than the meal did. We wanted agents to take over the boring parts — without losing what makes ordering together social. What it does Kitty is a shared order page where everyone's own AI agent adds their items and dietary restrictions straight into one live cart via WebMCP tools — no forms, no relaying your order through one exhausted human. The host locks the order in, and Kitty splits the bill automatically. How we built it Seven document.modelContext.registerTool() calls — browse_menu , add_item , remove_item , set_dietary_restriction , get_order_summary , split_bill , finalize_order — on a Next.js app on Vercel. Every mutating call is scoped server-side to the calling participant's identity, so an agent can only ever touch its own order. State lives in a lightweight session store, synced to every viewer with plain polling — no infrastructure we didn't need. Challenges we ran into Letting several independent agents write to one shared cart safely was the real problem. WebMCP's tool boundaries had to double as both a UX contract and a security boundary — otherwise a confused or malicious agent could overwrite someone else's order or invent a priced item that doesn't exist on the menu. Accomplishments that we're proud of Real multi-agent collaboration on one mutable session — not just one agent talking to one app — with guardrails (menu allow-lists, per-participant scoping, host-only finalize) tight enough we'd trust it with an actual office lunch order. What we learned WebMCP tools aren't just an API surface — they're a trust boundary. The moment more than one agent can touch the same state, "what should this tool refuse to do" matters as much as "what should it do." What's next for Kitty Itemized (not just equal) bill splitting, real restaurant menu imports, and letting a host's agent negotiate directly with a restaurant's own WebMCP tools once more storefronts expose them. Built With cloud firebase google in-memory-session-store react typescript web webmcp Try it out kitty-1003427733440.asia-south1.run.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by As a software architect with 16 years of experience, I led Kitty’s end-to-end architecture and technical execution. My contribution focused on turning the WebMCP concept into a secure, practical multi-agent ordering experience. I designed the system around seven purpose-built WebMCP tools for browsing the menu, adding and removing items, recording dietary restrictions, viewing the order, splitting the bill, and finalizing it. I treated every tool as both an application interface and a security boundary. I established the participant-scoped authorization model so each AI agent can modify only its owner’s items. I also designed host-only finalization, menu allow-list validation, participant tokens, and server-side allergy-conflict detection to prevent unauthorized or unsafe actions. To keep the hackathon implementation reliable and appropriately simple, I selected Next.js, React, and TypeScript, with lightweight REST endpoints and polling for live synchronization. I designed the in-memory session model and deployed the application to Google Cloud Run as a single-instance service, avoiding unnecessary infrastructure while preserving consistent shared state. Beyond architecture, I contributed to: - Product flow and interaction design - API and WebMCP tool contracts - Security and validation rules - Shared-order state management - Allergy and dietary-conflict detection - Automated bill splitting - Testing strategy and failure-case coverage - Cloud Run deployment architecture - Technical documentation and submission visuals support an actual group order. title: Zingposts
pitch: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust.
about_excerpt: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Browsing old cars, boats, campers, motorcycles, and machinery is fun. Managing the hunt is not. Good finds get lost across tabs, marketplace search misses obvious matches, alerts are rigid, research lives in scattered notes, and negotiations have no shared memory. A three-way trade is almost impossible to reason about cleanly. Zingposts starts from a different premise: the marketplace should be equally legible to people and their agents without embedding a model in the product. The site owns its native listings and structured deal workflow, while outside listings can be tracked as clearly labeled snapshots. What it does Zingposts is a complete peer-to-peer marketplace and durable workspace for interesting things. People can browse realistic native inventory, create and publish listings, upload photos, save finds, build boards, set alerts, keep research notebooks, message sellers, prepare offers, and create structured multi-party trade rooms. Outside finds can be tracked without confusing them with Zingposts-owned inventory. A connected outside agent receives a compact persistent core plus one focused pack drawn from 121 structured WebMCP tools. It can search with compound criteria, compare candidates, organize boards, tag and rank finds, record cited research and inspection risks, monitor price changes, draft communications and offers, calculate acquisition cost, propose trade scenarios, and coordinate the shared gallery, focus, or thumbnail canvas. The human uses the same structure through a canvas-first interface. Zingposts itself contains no LLM. The centerpiece is the shared canvas: an outside agent opens a durable session, places a shortlist, recommendation, or focused question beside the marketplace objects, and pauses only when human judgment matters. The person can inspect the exact listings and rationale, choose an option or add context, and return structured guidance. The agent reads that durable response on its next tool call and continues. This is turn-taking over shared marketplace objects, not a chatbot transcript. The loop now extends across visits. get_workspace_resume returns the last acknowledged checkpoint, everything that changed since, structured blockers, human responses, proposal status, and safe next actions. An agent can acknowledge the checkpoint only after processing it, so “come back later” is an explicit protocol rather than a hope that conversation context survived. For broad edits, the agent can prepare a sourced, versioned change set instead of making a trail of one-off mutations. Zingposts previews each proposed change in plain language, checks the expected object versions, and lets the person selectively accept only the changes they want. Agents cannot approve their own change sets. Completed deals can be recorded as private outcomes, and transparent aggregate patterns report counts, prices, and reasons without inventing a model-generated score. Either side can arrive first. A person can explore immediately in a prototype workspace, then replace a test email and verify the real address through Supabase only when work reaches the marketplace boundary. One Bring my agent click copies the canonical guide URL. Or an unauthenticated agent can inspect five setup-only tools and open a prototype handoff for the person. Once the person signs in, safe private tools appear automatically to an outside agent operating that browser document. Independent 12-hour revocable sessions remain available through one-use invites or codes for separate-browser or unattended work. The human remains in control. Publishing, enabling notifications, sending a message, submitting or responding to an offer, and inviting a trade participant stop at a visible confirmation gate. Every human and agent action is attributed, and reversible work can be undone. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, an agent has to infer intent from buttons and screen position. That is brittle for a marketplace with dozens of interdependent objects: listings, boards, research, alerts, conversations, offers, people, assets, and constraints. WebMCP gives Zingposts a stable collaboration language. “Find pre-1980 boats under $15,000, put the best four on a board, record the title risks, and draft a message to the strongest seller” becomes a sequence of typed, attributable actions. The human can watch the same state change, refine it directly, and approve the parts that cross a consequential boundary. That makes the product meaningfully better with an agent—not merely automatable. How we built it Zingposts uses React 19 and Next.js on Netlify. Supabase Auth provides verified human sessions, Supabase Postgres holds marketplace, identity, agent-session, and workflow state, and Supabase Storage holds listing photos. Versioned SQL migrations keep direct browser access locked behind row-level security. The browser client exposes 121 declarative tools through the WebMCP modelContext surface, but only five setup tools while signed out. After the person signs in, AbortSignal-managed registration keeps a compact persistent core plus one replaceable focused capability pack, so navigation never accumulates an oversized registry or silently unlocks business actions. get_agent_bootstrap returns setup guidance while signed out, then canonical browser-delegated identity, workspace, attention, active collaboration, capability index, and guide version after sign-in. activate_capability switches the focused pack without moving the person; open_for_human_review is optional. The action layer derives canonical human and agent identity on the server, prevents duplicate profiles, enforces ownership and state-transition enums, creates reviewable drafts, writes attributed activity, stores inverse operations for undo, supports idempotency keys and optimistic versions, returns stable deep links and WebMCP-native structured errors, and converts consequential operations into pending confirmations. Isolated QA runs register only their own artifacts, provide an exact cleanup preview, and require human approval before deletion. The marketplace is seeded with original project-owned imagery and realistic records so the full human-agent workflow is understandable immediately. WebMCP registration is document-scoped, while Zingposts durably stores connection profiles, scopes, alerts, boards, research, drafts, versions, and audit history. The public /for-agents guide and /api/agent-guide contract show agents how to reconnect safely without storing an invite, code, or stale catalog. Challenges The main design challenge was not adding more agent power; it was deciding where that power should stop. We separated preparation from commitment. Research, organization, comparison, and drafting can proceed quickly. Communication, publication, notifications, invitations, and financial commitments pause for the human. We also designed external-listing tracking so provenance stays honest. Zingposts can organize an outside find, but it never claims that its cached price, availability, or seller statements are authoritative. Accomplishments A coherent marketplace, not a WebMCP proof of concept 121 tools spanning authentication, onboarding, resumable work sessions, versioned proposals, outcomes, canvas views, discovery, organization, negotiation, and multi-party trade Agent-first and person-first onboarding with a five-tool setup surface before human sign-in Durable agent-to-human-to-agent turn-taking with a unified attention queue Explicit resume checkpoints and structured blockers for work that continues across agent runs Sourced, versioned change sets with semantic previews and selective human acceptance Private outcome recording with transparent, non-AI aggregate patterns Live agent activity, exact-payload approval, idempotency, dry runs, structured errors, and stable deep links No built-in AI or model dependency Supabase human authentication plus opaque invite URLs, code fallback, and single-use, expiring, revocable agent sessions—without password or session sharing Persistent bootstrap plus navigation-independent focused capability activation Structured errors, strict workflow transitions, optimistic concurrency, and namespaced QA cleanup Durable attribution, confirmations, and undo Native seller photo upload and publishing workflow Clear separation between owned listings and outside tracked snapshots Production build, automated API smoke tests, desktop browser testing, and mobile verification What we learned Human-agent collaboration works best when both sides operate on the same durable objects. A board is better than a chat-only list. A research notebook is better than an ephemeral summary. A pending confirmation is better than asking the model to remember which action is sensitive. We also learned to separate document-scoped WebMCP

video_transcript_excerpt: What if a marketplace did not contain its own AI? What if it simply gave people and any outside agent a beautiful shared place to work? title: PilotCircuits
pitch: Build it. See it. Understand it. An Arduino workbench for beginners, driven by an agent through the page's own WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: Build it. See it. Understand it. An Arduino workbench for beginners, driven by an agent through the page's own WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does## Inspiration Everyone who opens an Arduino kit hits the same wall in the first hour. The LED doesn't light. The wire is one hole off, or the resistor is in the wrong row, and the PDF that came with the kit can't tell you which. You take a photo, paste it into a chat, and the answer is a guess about a blurry picture. I wanted the agent to stop guessing. If the page that draws the breadboard already knows where every lead is, the agent should read that , not the pixels. WebMCP is exactly the missing piece: the page hands the agent a small set of tools, in the page's own vocabulary, and the agent works on the same build you're looking at. What it does PilotCircuits is a guided Arduino workbench for beginners. Six chapters, each adding one idea: a breathing lamp, a traffic light, a motion night-light, a plant guardian, a touchless soap dispenser, and a pre-built parking barrier as the capstone. You wire each one by hand on a simulated bench, dragging real-looking parts off a kit shelf into breadboard holes and header pins. An agent connected through WebMCP sees the same bench. On the workbench it can: explain_project — say what the chapter is for and what each part does inspect_build — compare your wiring against the sketch and list what's off show_correction — pan the camera to the lead at fault point_at — frame any part, pin or hole you ask about, without touching anything attach_lead — the one tool that changes the build: seat a lead, or pull it loose verify_current_step , navigate_build_step , run_functional_test — walk the steps and run the chapter's own checks Two things on screen tell you what the agent is doing. A ring on the bench shows where it is working, and a small LED-shaped coach in the corner shows what : reading, thinking, pointing, testing, and a happy face when the test passes. What's new here is the division of labour. You build. The agent checks the build against the plan, shows you the mistake on the board itself, and if you say "fix it", it moves the lead through the same code path your own drag would take. You can undo its move. Neither side is watching a screenshot of the other. It works as a normal web app without a WebMCP host, and it's fully localised in English and Turkish, tool descriptions and refusal messages included. How I built it Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind. The breadboard, Uno and component artwork is ported from Wokwi Elements (MIT). Deployed on Vercel at https://pilotcircuits.com . The WebMCP layer lives in src/lib/agent/webmcp.ts and a React hook around it. Tools are registered with navigator.modelContext inside an effect, per route, and torn down when the route changes: the library registers the search and open tools, the workbench registers the nine above, and nothing is offered on a page that can't act on it. When the build or the language changes, every tool re-registers with the new descriptions. Thirteen tool names in total. Every tool call goes through the same queue as the buttons in the UI, so an agent's attach_lead and a person's drag are literally the same operation, with one activity log and one undo stack. Every handler validates its own input and returns refusals as data the model can act on ("no finding has that id, the ids come from inspect_build"), not as thrown errors. The AbortSignal the host passes is honoured, so a cancelled call doesn't keep moving the bench after the agent walked away. The "Connected via WebMCP" badge only lights up when registerTool actually resolved, not when the API merely exists. 971 unit tests across 28 files cover the circuit model, the tool handlers, the step verification and the copy. Challenges I ran into For most of the build, no browser shipped WebMCP. The whole layer was written against the spec and a fake host. The first time it ran in a real host (Chrome with the WebMCP flags, driven by Playwright) was one day before the deadline, and that run changed things. Chrome passed my MCP-style result envelope straight to the model as text: 6,618 characters for 2,425 characters of payload, with isError reaching nobody. I switched every tool to return bare JSON. Chrome also doesn't validate arguments against inputSchema , so the handlers had to. ChatGPT's in-app browser is a split pane. Below 1120 px the bench has no room for a canvas, so a narrow window registers only the five tools that make sense without one. I couldn't measure the pane itself, so the README says it out loud. The bench itself was the other half of the work: pointer capture on drags, the view panning under a lead mid-carry, a cable router that turned hairpins on every stub. And the first draft of the mascot looked too much like someone else's mascot. It went in the bin, and the lamp took its place. Accomplishments that I'm proud of Watching ChatGPT desktop, connected over WebMCP, take a jumper I'd plugged in wrong on purpose, find both bad ends, move the cable, then build the remaining 18 connections of the traffic light off the shelf and pass the functional test. That's the demo video, and none of it is scripted on the page's side. Also: tool descriptions that tell the truth. attach_lead 's description says what it costs, because that string is the only channel that reaches the model. What I learned Measure against the real host. My reading of the spec was reasonable and wrong in three places, and each one was visible within minutes of running Chrome with the flag. A face that mirrors a 300 ms tool call is invisible. The coach holds each mood for at least 1.2 seconds, because it's a presentation for the person, not a debugger for the agent. And the description field of a tool is documentation for a reader who can't open the source. Write it like that. What's next for PilotCircuits A real board beside the simulated one, so the last step of a chapter is flashing the sketch to the Uno on your desk. More chapters past the capstone.
