title: AIAD (AI-Aided Design)
pitch: Computer-aided design is evolving. Agents can now review CAD/BIM designs with you: query, isolate, cut, annotate. And they see your viewport, so "what do we know about this door?" just works.
about_excerpt: Computer-aided design is evolving. Agents can now review CAD/BIM designs with you: query, isolate, cut, annotate. And they see your viewport, so "what do we know about this door?" just works. Like 1 Comment Story Updates From Computer-Aided Design to AI-Aided Design Inspiration CAD has been computer -aided for fifty years, and the computer's role hasn't changed much. Every question about a design still gets answered by a human clicking through it, and every problem found that way gets typed into a form somewhere away from the model. I've spent years building the browser viewer that does the clicking-through. WebMCP made me wonder what happens when the viewer stops being a display and becomes a set of tools an agent can use. Not AI that generates a design, but AI that can review one. What it does A BIM design review app: a Revit model in the Autodesk Platform Services Viewer, with the viewer and the review's issue list exposed to an agent as WebMCP tools. You walk the building in first person, select something, and talk. The agent searches design metadata, browses the model hierarchy, isolates and frames parts, colors objects by any property, etc. Then it drafts an issue against it, revises the draft while you watch, and submits when you say so. show-issue puts you back inside the model at the reporter's eye position, with the viewer state they had. It reads the current selection and camera every turn, so "what is this door?" resolves without either of us naming anything. How I built it APS Viewer loads and renders the translated Revit model, and provides the first-person walkthrough. WebMCP registers several tools straight from the page, with return values shaped for a token budget rather than for a database client. The form is the draft. draft-issue writes into the same form you can type into. submit-issue takes no arguments at all. The only thing that can be filed is what's on screen. Tools register conditionally on viewer state : none until geometry has loaded, and all ten dropped before a different design loads. A property query against a half-loaded model doesn't give you a degraded answer, it gives you a confident wrong one. Nothing leaves the browser. Issues go to IndexedDB. "The north stair doesn't meet code" next to a client's project name is a professional judgement about someone else's building, and a hackathon demo has no user auth to protect it with. What I learned The interesting work wasn't wiring up tools, it was deciding what a tool should say back. A property query on a real model returns thousands of rows, which is useless to an agent. Returning counts, outliers and a category breakdown is what turns guessing into answering. My favourite question in the demo, "how many doors have no fire rating set?", is one no amount of looking at the screen can answer, and it costs about twenty tokens. The best tool I wrote was the one I deleted. I built a screenshot tool so the agent could check its own camera moves. It worked, and then I confirmed the host reads the viewport directly without being asked. A viewpoint beats a picture anyway. Half the problems worth reporting are only visible because a floor was isolated or the model was cut at mid-height. Store the camera alone and the reviewer arrives at the right coordinates staring at an opaque wall, which is worse than not navigating at all, because it makes the issue look wrong. Challenges Shared state. Two actors driving one camera needs a clear owner. Every agent move is an animated flight rather than a cut, because a cut drops you somewhere else in the building with nothing to say how the two places relate. Trust. If submit-issue accepted overrides, the review step would be a formality. The agent says "I set it to high and submitted it" and you have no way to check. Forcing every edit back through the on-screen form is what makes "looks good, submit" mean something. Scale. Engineering models have hundreds of thousands of objects. Every list is capped and carries its true total, and color-coding paints recursively, so 5,000 doors cost one id. Deixis. Making "this" work meant treating the viewport as context the agent always has, rather than something it asks about. title: svgent Agent Stage
pitch: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video.
about_excerpt: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent Stage: two showcase scripts rendered by svgent, a terminal and an app Inspiration svgent is a client-only studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. A script describes a chat window or a terminal, with typing, thinking, tool runs, approvals and choices, and the studio renders it to SVG, PNG, GIF and MP4. People use it for READMEs, docs, talks and posts, where a recording of a real session would leak secrets and could not be re-shot or translated. Before this, the studio's AI assist was copy and paste: copy a prompt into a chat, paste the JSON back. WebMCP replaces that with tool calls on the page. The page can also answer with facts a language model cannot see: how long a page runs, when each message lands, what the frame looks like at eleven seconds. The agent works on the stage itself, not on a guess about it. What it does Agent Stage is the studio with WebMCP site tools. The agent in ChatGPT's built-in browser writes the script, sets the surface, look, camera and pages, measures the result, looks at a frame, proposes rewrites, and asks to export. The person keeps the decisions: rewrites and exports wait on a card, every string the script puts on the stage is listed, and each change can be undone. load_script validates a script and previews it at once. direct_camera turns on a deterministic follow camera. inspect_timeline returns per-message timing and a review. snapshot_frame returns a PNG of any moment. fit_duration lands a page on an exact length and reports what it changed. propose_patch puts rewrites on a card. approve_proposal exists only while a proposal is pending and waits for the person's click. export asks first. The rail shows every call. The "Every word on the stage" list holds every string the script puts on the stage, including what a collapse or a page turn hides. The tool descriptions tell the agent to treat what it knows from the conversation as private and to use stand-ins for real names, unless the person relaxes that on the page or in the chat. Credentials never pass. A loaded script keeps only the fields that render. Looks, fonts, images and camera go through their own tools. Live: https://agent.svgent.zakideee.dev/ Code: https://github.com/zakideee/svgent (the page is apps/webmcp/ ) How we built it 13 tools on document.modelContext , with navigator.modelContext as the fallback, registered with an AbortSignal for teardown. approve_proposal is registered only while a proposal is pending. Results are plain objects plus an MCP-style content array (text, and an image part for frames). The studio package gained a small imperative handle: read, replace and patch the project, seek, play, export, render a frame, spotlight a message. An agent's edit goes through the same state the person's controls use, so undo, autosave, validation and preview all see it. Text layout and rasterization run in WASM (boundsvg) in the browser. The animated SVG is CSS keyframes with no JavaScript. There is no server; nothing leaves the tab except the files the person downloads. The submission is apps/webmcp/ : the WebMCP tools, the agent rail, the privacy default, the showcase scripts and the share card, plus the studio handle ( StudioHandle , chrome , renderFrame , spotlight ) and one preview aspect-ratio fix. The studio, scene and render packages predate the challenge. Challenges we ran into ChatGPT's browser exposes document.modelContext , Chromium exposes navigator.modelContext , and the API can appear after the page has loaded. Registration prefers the document, polls for a late API, and reports the outcome in the rail. A dynamic tool ( approve_proposal ) that unregisters itself while a call is in flight fails that call. It now stays registered for a short grace period after the proposal resolves. A script an agent writes from a conversation can carry real names, paths, hosts and keys from that conversation. The privacy default, the script allowlist and the "every word" list exist for that. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole loop runs in the ChatGPT desktop app (built-in browser, GPT-5.6 Sol) and in Chromium with WebMCP enabled, and the demo video is a recording of it. The agent edits through the same state as the person's controls, so undo, autosave, validation and preview treat both alike. Four of the showcase scripts are problems agent-app users have: a clip for the team channel without the secrets; a reproduction of a decline that was missed, when recording is not allowed; three slides that walk a colleague through choices and approvals; a README hero for your own MCP server. What we learned A page can hand an agent facts it cannot infer (timing, frames, what would render), and that is worth more than letting the agent guess well. Approval and visibility have to be part of the tools, not a note in a prompt. What's next for svgent Agent Stage A deny list of the person's own words (names, hosts, projects) checked on the page, next to the pattern-based hints. The same tools on the other surfaces the studio renders, and on the CLI for headless use. The demo video was recorded in the ChatGPT desktop app. Waits are sped up where marked. The narration is a synthetic voice. title: Known Good WebMCP Verifier
pitch: Every other WebMCP checker tells you pass or fail. This one tells you where you stand in 14,351 probed sites, admits the 1,224 it couldn't ask — and is itself callable as a WebMCP tool.
about_excerpt: Every other WebMCP checker tells you pass or fail. This one tells you where you stand in 14,351 probed sites, admits the 1,224 it couldn't ask — and is itself callable as a WebMCP tool. Like Comment Story Updates "What matched" panel showing the actual JavaScript from the checked page Inspiration We already run an index of 14,351 sites whose agent-facing capabilities are probe-verified and dated. When we turned that machinery on WebMCP, the finding was awkward: registered tools round to zero outside demos and the checker sites themselves. There were more tools for checking WebMCP than there were sites using it. So the missing thing was never another checker. It was a denominator . Nobody could tell a site what its result meant, because nobody had a population to compare it against. Then a bug decided the rest of the product. Our first detector reported a clean no tools found for a page whose script robots.txt had disallowed us from reading. It wasn't a no. It was a question we weren't allowed to ask, and reporting it as a no is the same error as counting a locked door as an empty room. Across the index that turned out to be 1,224 hosts . Every checker we could find reports those as failures. That distinction became the product. What it does Give it a hostname. It fetches the page, then opens it in a real browser, and reports three things a checker normally collapses into one: whether the site declares WebMCP in its source, whether it actually registers tools when the page executes, and — the state that matters — whether we were allowed to ask at all. Then it does the thing no other checker can: it places the answer. 647 sites in our index carry the code, 580 register something at runtime, and 997 distinct tool names have been observed across them. If you're deciding which tools to expose, the distribution is the answer — search_site on 122 sites, fetch_as_markdown on 105, search_content on 28, get_contact_info on 18, get_pricing and search_products on 17 each. Measured and dated, not guessed. Why WebMCP is the right shape for this . What anyone wants from this page is one action with one parameter: check this host. That's a tool call, not a document. An agent forced to fetch our HTML, locate the form, synthesise a POST and parse a verdict out of the markup is doing four fragile things to accomplish one simple one — and all four break the next time we change the layout. So the page declares its own WebMCP tools. An agent calls it rather than reading it. The checker is an instance of the thing it checks. What that unlocks . An agent can audit fifty hosts in a loop with no HTML parsing and no brittle selectors. More interesting is the reverse direction: "does this host expose tools I can call, and were they observed running or merely declared?" is a question an agent should ask before it interacts with an unfamiliar site. Declared-versus-verified is exactly the distinction an autonomous agent needs and rarely has. This turns it into one call, with a date attached. And a boundary that matters more as agents get more capable: we list tools, we never invoke them . Enumerating a stranger's tools is safe. Executing one could place an order, send a message, or spend someone's money. How we built it Two layers, mapping onto the verification tiers we already run. Declared — a static fetch matching navigator.modelContext, document.modelContext, provideContext and registerTool. It matches both namespaces, because the spec renamed one mid-origin-trial and a site written against the earlier draft still counts. And it matches a call, not a mention — an article explaining WebMCP doesn't get scored as a site using it. Registered — headless enumeration in a real browser via Cloudflare Browser Rendering, the tools/list equivalent. This is what separates a site that ships the code from a site where the code actually runs. 647 carry it; 580 register something. It runs on Cloudflare Workers with D1 behind it. The page's own tools are declared with the declarative form attributes — toolname, tooldescription, toolparamdescription — so this is a WebMCP surface, not a page about WebMCP. Consent is enforced before any fetch , because the tool probes third-party hosts on demand: robots.txt read before the resource request; ai-input=no treated as an absolute stop, with the host reported as excluded rather than as failing; the user-agent KnownGood-Verifier never disguised; Retry-After honoured. And running a check has zero effect on ranking in our index — listings there are earned by probe and never sold. Challenges we ran into Cloudflare Browser Rendering caps at two concurrent browsers and two new per minute, with a 60-second inactivity kill — a different problem at index scale than at demo scale. The detector took two rewrites. The first version matched modelContext inside comments, and fixing that surfaced the worse case: WebMCP discussed in HTML body prose. Separating a call from a mention is most of the work in a detector like this, and neither failure was obvious until we looked at what had matched. And the spec renamed navigator.modelContext to document.modelContext mid-origin-trial, so anything matching a single namespace silently under-counts. We match both. Accomplishments that we're proud of We shipped the state that makes our own number smaller. Adding "could not ask" means 1,224 hosts don't count toward anything, where every checker we found reports them as failures. It's the right number and it cost us the bigger one. The checker passes its own check. Run it against https://knowngood.sh/verify/webmcp and it comes back registered, with its tools enumerated. We didn't want to ship a tool telling sites to do something we hadn't done. The population produced a finding nobody else could. Treating each site's tool signature as a fingerprint puts 39.5% of the 580 registering sites in a cluster with at least one other site, and the largest single cluster is 18.1%. Most WebMCP "adoption" is one plugin — and you can only see that from a denominator. Every figure carries the population and date it was measured against. No number on the page floats free of what it was measured over. What we learned A checker that cannot distinguish "no" from "couldn't ask" is worse than no checker at all for the sites it mislabels — it manufactures a false negative and presents it with the same confidence as a real one. And adoption numbers in a young standard are mostly plugin numbers. Without the tool-signature clustering we would have reported 580 independent implementations. The truth is closer to a handful of implementations installed many times, and only a population makes that visible. What's next for Known Good WebMCP Verifier Declarative detection. The checker sees the imperative API but not toolname / tooldescription on form controls — the half of the standard a browser-side audit is most likely to score, and a real gap. When it lands, the attribute route will report as declared and never as registered . Attributes prove intent; only execution proves registration. Conflating the two is exactly the error this tool exists to avoid, and we'd rather ship the gap honestly than close it dishonestly. title: Weave
pitch: The visual website builder where humans and AI agents collaboratively create, edit, validate, and publish agent-ready websites through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: The visual website builder where humans and AI agents collaboratively create, edit, validate, and publish agent-ready websites through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates demo vedio : https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1OA56ZB6VfMFG1dIzqcJiOLojGptgHV85?usp=sharing Inspiration The web was built for humans, but the next generation of the web will also be used by AI agents. We were inspired by a simple question: What if an AI agent could work inside the same visual workspace as a human, instead of trying to control a website by guessing clicks, reading screenshots, or manipulating the DOM? Existing AI website builders mostly follow a prompt → generate → review workflow. We wanted something more collaborative. That led us to WEAVE : a visual website editor where humans and AI agents can work on the same live website together. Humans provide creative direction and visual judgment, while agents handle structured editing and repetitive work through WebMCP. Our goal was to explore what an agent-native creative tool could look like. What it does WEAVE is a collaborative, agent-native website builder. A human can visually create and edit a website using the canvas, while an AI agent can understand the same project and make changes through structured WebMCP tools. Instead of asking an agent to "click this button" or figure out a website from screenshots, WEAVE exposes meaningful capabilities such as: weave_get_context — understand the current project, page, sections, elements, and selection weave_get_selection — understand the element currently selected by the human weave_add_section — add a new website section weave_update_element — modify content or properties of an element weave_move_element — reorganize elements weave_delete_element — remove elements weave_publish_site — request publication of the website This allows an agent to perform workflows such as: "Add a pricing section below the testimonials, change the hero headline, and move the CTA above the footer." The agent first reads the structured state of the editor, chooses the appropriate WebMCP tools, and performs the requested mutations. Most importantly, human and agent edits go through the same validated mutation pipeline , so the agent is not given a separate backdoor into the editor. For high-consequence actions such as publishing, WEAVE keeps the human in control. The agent can request publication, but the final action requires human approval. How we built it WEAVE is built around a structured representation of the visual editor. Instead of exposing the DOM or screenshots to the agent, we maintain a semantic CanvasNode model representing the pages, sections, elements, content, and relationships inside the project. We then expose this model and the editor's capabilities through WebMCP. The architecture is roughly: AI Agent → WebMCP → WEAVE tools → validation → mutation queue → editor/source → live canvas The WebMCP layer registers WEAVE's tools through the browser's model context interface when available. For read operations, the agent can request a bounded snapshot of the current editor state. For write operations, tool inputs are validated before being passed into the existing mutation system. This gives us one important property: Human edits and agent edits use the same underlying mutation pipeline. We also maintain a context version so that the agent can detect when the editor has changed and retrieve fresh context rather than blindly acting on stale information. The project is built with a TypeScript/React-based web stack and integrates WebMCP directly into the browser application. Challenges we ran into Making agent actions reliable We did not want the agent to manipulate the UI through arbitrary clicks or DOM operations. We needed a structured representation that an agent could understand reliably. This led us to build the CanvasNode representation and expose semantic operations instead of low-level browser actions. Keeping human and agent edits consistent A major challenge was ensuring that an agent edit behaved exactly like a human edit. We solved this by routing agent mutations through the same validated mutation queue and editor pipeline rather than creating a separate agent-only editing path. Handling stale context A human can modify the canvas while an agent is reasoning about a previous state. To address this, WEAVE tracks a contextVersion and allows the agent to retrieve the latest structured context before performing subsequent operations. Safety and human control Giving an agent the ability to modify a website also creates the possibility of unintended destructive actions. We therefore separated read, write, destructive, and high-consequence capabilities and kept publication behind an explicit human approval step. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are most proud that WebMCP is not just an additional feature in WEAVE — it is part of the core interaction model. We built a system where: Agents can understand a structured visual website rather than relying on screenshots. Agents can perform meaningful website operations through typed WebMCP tools. Human and agent changes use the same mutation pipeline. The agent can react to the human's current selection and project state. Stale context can be detected and refreshed. Destructive and high-consequence operations are handled with additional safety. Publishing remains under human control. WebMCP activity can be observed as part of the editor workflow. We are also proud of turning a traditional visual website editor into something that can be treated as an agent-operable creative workspace . What we learned We learned that making a website "AI-enabled" is very different from making it agent-native . An agent does not necessarily need more UI access. It needs better capabilities and context . Instead of exposing hundreds of low-level browser interactions, a small set of well-designed semantic tools can give an agent much more reliable control. We also learned that human-agent collaboration works best when both sides share the same source of truth. The human should not have to work around the agent, and the agent should not need to simulate a human. WebMCP gave us a way to experiment with this model directly inside the web application. What's next for WEAVE Our next goal is to make WEAVE a broader platform for agent-native websites and creative applications . We want to explore: More powerful agent workflows for complete website creation Better multi-step planning and execution Richer structured context for complex projects More granular human approval and collaboration controls Version history and agent action rollback Multiple specialized agents working on different parts of a project Exporting websites with their capabilities and agent-facing metadata Making published WEAVE websites themselves more discoverable and usable by agents Ultimately, we want WEAVE to explore a future where websites are not just pages that agents can read, but interactive environments with structured capabilities that agents can understand and use alongside humans. title: StockPilot
pitch: StockPilot is an agent-native inventory management app where AI agent doesn't just read your data, it proposes actions, files them for approval, and you decide with a single click.
about_excerpt: StockPilot is an agent-native inventory management app where AI agent doesn't just read your data, it proposes actions, files them for approval, and you decide with a single click. Like Comment Story Updates StockPilot with WebMCP StockPilot Why WebMCP Is a Strong Fit Inventory management is fundamentally a shared-state problem . The dashboard shows data, but analyzing it requires cross-referencing products, suppliers, sales velocity, and profit margins — work that takes 30-60 minutes manually. WebMCP solves this by letting an AI agent operate on the same data, through the same logic, as the UI — not a copy, not a mirror, the identical code path. The agent doesn't just read data. It proposes actions (replenishment plans, purchase orders), but the human retains control over consequential decisions. This is only possible because WebMCP tools are registered on document.modelContext — they execute in the browser, against the same database, with the same server-side validation as the dashboard. How It Creates a Better User Experience Before WebMCP: User opens dashboard → sees health score, at-risk products, open POs User manually clicks each product → checks velocity → mental math on profit User opens spreadsheet → calculates which products are worth restocking User creates POs one by one, copying supplier data manually Time: 30-60 minutes for a weekly inventory review With WebMCP Agent: User types: "Protect my inventory with a $3,000 budget" Agent analyzes all products in one call → risk levels, velocity, profitability Agent proposes a budget-aware replenishment plan → grouped by supplier with cost subtotals User clicks Approve → POs are created → stock is received Time: 2 minutes for the same review The agent auto-navigates to relevant pages after each action. The Agent Activity Panel shows every tool call in real-time. The human always knows what the agent is doing. What People and Agents Can Do Together That Was Difficult or Impossible Before Cross-Product Profitability Analysis : "Which products will make me $1,000 profit this month?" — impossible to answer manually without cross-referencing sales velocity, profit margins, and inventory levels across all products. The agent calls get_profitability_analysis once and returns sorted projections. Budget-Aware Replenishment : "Replenish my inventory with a $3,000 budget" — the agent prioritizes by urgency (critical → warning → watch), fits items within budget, and returns what fits vs. what's rejected. Manual equivalent: 2+ hours of spreadsheet work. Emergency Impact Simulation : "What if my electronics supplier delays 10 days?" — instant analysis of which products stock out, days until stockout, alternate suppliers available, total revenue at risk. Manual equivalent: calling each supplier, checking lead times, calculating impact. Agent Proposes → Human Approves : The agent can't unilaterally place orders. It files pending actions with reasoning and cost estimates. The human approves or rejects via the Agent Actions queue. Server enforces the approval gate — the agent can't bypass it. Real-Time Visibility : The Agent Activity Panel shows every tool call as it happens. The human watches the agent work, sees the reasoning, and can intervene at any point. How WebMCP Was Implemented Architecture : Shared domain logic in inventory.server.ts (~2,200 lines) is called by two entry points: UI : TanStack Start server functions via inventory.functions.ts WebMCP : 52 tools registered via document.modelContext.registerTool() in tools.ts Tool Design : Each tool has: 4 annotations ( readOnlyHint , destructiveHint , idempotentHint , openWorldHint ) Zod → JSON Schema input validation (auto-generated, no manual drift) Structured error codes ( NOT_FOUND , CONFLICT , PRECONDITION_FAILED , INVALID_INPUT ) Audit trail logging to agent_tool_calls table Collaboration Model : 24 consequential tools are marked with agent hints ("only call after human approval") Server-side enforcement: PO state machine ( draft → approved → received ), decidedBy derived from session Agent Activity Panel: real-time visibility into every tool call Auto-navigation: 9 tools navigate to relevant pages after execution Deployment : Cloudflare Workers with D1 (SQLite) database. Live at https://stockpilot.aakas.workers.dev Tech Stack : TanStack Start, React 19, Tailwind CSS 4, Drizzle ORM, Cloudflare D1, TypeScript 5.7 Built With cloudflare react tailwind tanstack Try it out stockpilot.aakas.workers.dev github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Aakash Shakya Like Share this project: Updates Aakash Shakya started this project — Sep 02, 2026 06:57 AM EDT

title: Stapler
pitch: An AI agent preps your documents right in your browser via WebMCP — it finds the right pages itself, merges and downloads. Your files never leave your device.
about_excerpt: An AI agent preps your documents right in your browser via WebMCP — it finds the right pages itself, merges and downloads. Your files never leave your device. Like 4 Comment 1 Story Updates Inspiration Every visa application, rental application, or insurance claim ends the same way: you sit with a pile of PDFs, hunting for the four pages of a bank statement that actually prove your salary, extracting them, merging everything in the right order, naming the file properly. Today you have two options — upload sensitive documents like your passport and bank statement to a cloud AI, or do every click yourself in a dumb local PDF tool. WebMCP dissolves that trade-off, and Stapler is built on exactly that: document prep is a workflow problem, and workflows are what agents chaining structured tools are good at. What it does Stapler is a local document workspace whose tools an AI agent can operate. You say what you need: "I'm applying for a visa. I need one PDF with my passport, the bank statement pages that prove my regular salary, and my application form. Name the file after the applicant and its purpose, and download it." The agent lists the documents, reads a 12-page bank statement page by page, finds the salary pages (4–7) on its own — it even reads the visa form's supporting-documents checklist first — extracts them, merges passport + salary pages + form, and downloads a packet named after the applicant, whose name it read off the passport. You never typed a page number or a name. And because every operation executes client-side, no document ever leaves the browser tab — there is no backend to upload to; the privacy isn't a policy promise, it's the architecture. This is a person and an agent doing something together that was impossible before: previously an agent could either talk about your documents (after you uploaded them to a server) or click through a UI blindly. Now it invokes structured, deterministic operations inside your own tab, on files that never leave your device — while you supervise through a live Operations log, click any document to preview it, and undo anything the agent got wrong. Try it yourself Open https://stapler-equ.pages.dev in the ChatGPT desktop app's browser (Cmd+Shift+B; accept "Continue in Work" if offered) — or in Chrome with Google's Model Context Tool Inspector extension. Click Load sample documents (fictional data, generated in-browser). Ask for the visa packet in your own words — or use the prompt above. Watch the Operations log as the agent works. Or drop your own PDFs: nothing is uploaded anywhere. How we built it React + Vite + TypeScript, zero backend. Seven tools — list_documents , inspect_document , extract_pages , merge_documents , rename_document , export_document , undo — are registered via document.modelContext.registerTool with narrow JSON schemas ( additionalProperties: false ), plain serializable results, and AbortController cleanup. The registrations are live: whenever the workspace changes, the schemas are regenerated — every document parameter becomes an enum of the currently loaded filenames, so the agent can't reference a file that isn't there. Document tools appear once files are loaded, and merge_documents registers only when at least two documents exist. One subtlety: the store emits changes from inside tool execute() calls, so re-registering immediately would tear down the very tool still delivering its result — re-registration is deferred a tick instead. pdf-lib performs the operations; pdf.js extracts per-page text for inspect_document , which is what lets the agent find content instead of being told page numbers. The sample documents (fictional passport, 12-page bank statement, visa form) are generated in-browser by pdf-lib — the repo ships no binaries and demo data never exists outside the tab. Deployed on Cloudflare Pages with a first-party Chrome origin-trial token, so it runs on stock Chrome 149+ with no flags. Challenges we ran into The real agent runs found bugs no manual test did: Truncation hid the evidence. inspect_document capped page text at 500 chars — and the salary lines started at char 441+. The agent, seeing cut-off text, guessed pages 3–7 (wrong). Raising the cap and adding a smoke-test guard fixed it. Ambiguous data misleads honest agents. A "FREELANCE INVOICE" credit on the January page made pages 3–7 a defensible answer. The demo premise needs exactly one right answer, so the sample data is now guarded by a regex in the smoke test. Return-shape spelunking. Early code returned MCP-style {content:[...]} envelopes; the WebMCP spec, Chrome docs, and TypeScript types all agree tools return plain serializable values. Agent surfaces behave differently. Plain ChatGPT chat asks you to upload files; the unlock is accepting its "Continue in Work" handoff, where the agent actually drives the page's tools. Accomplishments that we're proud of The hero workflow is verified end-to-end on both judge surfaces: ChatGPT's in-app browser (via Work mode) and Chrome with Google's Model Context Tool Inspector extension. In every verified run the agent chose pages 4–7 unprompted and explained why. The contrast test is just as telling: the same request to an agent without page tools produced a confidently hallucinated "visa packet" that never touched the real files. It also works on documents it has never seen: we dropped in three unrelated PDFs (an ID card, an employment letter, six months of payslips) and asked for a rental-application packet with only the April–June payslips — the agent picked payslip pages 4–6 by itself and named the file after the applicant. And the whole thing is honest engineering — a Node smoke test guards the demo's integrity (salary credits on exactly pages 4–7, every page under the inspect limit), so the wow moment can't silently rot. What we learned Tool descriptions are UX for agents — the agent reads them the way users read buttons. Real agent runs are the only test that matters: every demo-breaking bug was found by an agent, not by a human. And keeping humans in the loop (live log, preview, undo) is what turns "an agent did something to my files" into something you can trust. What's next for Stapler More operations (split, rotate, delete, compress), OCR so scanned documents can be inspected too, and per-document page-range bounds in the schemas themselves. title: CoRep
pitch: CoRep is a local-first training log that publishes its entire feature set as 31 WebMCP tools. Your AI coach doesn't advise from outside the app — it operates the same plan you do. Every change signed.
about_excerpt: CoRep is a local-first training log that publishes its entire feature set as 31 WebMCP tools. Your AI coach doesn't advise from outside the app — it operates the same plan you do. Every change signed. Like Comment Story Updates CoRep You and your AI agent build the plan together! plan page Edit Logging an exercise Timer Badges! Mobile view Every change is logged Mobile friendly Bring it to the gym Skip or add time at any time The gap I already had an AI fitness coach. It worked like everyone's does: I'd describe my training week to a chat window, it would give me thoughtful advice, and then I would switch to a different app and type that advice in by hand. The advice was good. The arrangement was absurd. My coach could reason about my knee but couldn't see that I'd already dropped the weight on Tuesday. I was the integration layer — a human clipboard between two systems that both wanted the same data. I'd actually tried to fix this before. The app CoRep grew out of had an MCP server bolted onto its Python backend, so my coach could read the database and write to it. It helped, and it also taught me why it wasn't enough: the agent was talking to my database , not to my app . It could change a number, but it couldn't put that number in front of me. I'd find out what it had done later, if I happened to look. WebMCP inverts that, and the inversion is the whole project. What it does CoRep is a training log with no server and no account — every user's data lives in their own browser. It publishes its entire feature set as 31 WebMCP tools , so an agent on the page operates the same application you do. Not a copy of your plan. Not a screenshot. When the agent raises a weight, it calls the same function your own tap on "Edit" calls, against the same data, and you watch the result land. Three things fall out of that, and they're the parts I'd point a judge at: Every change is signed Writes record who made them and why. The plan view shows both parties in one timeline: Coach 10→15 lbs · shoulders felt strong, small bump You 15→25 lbs · Edited in the plan editor Neither of us is the source of truth. This is the single feature I'd keep if I had to throw the rest away. It's what makes it safe to let an agent act rather than only suggest — you can always see what it did, why it thought so, and overrule it. The nice accident: the app I forked already had an edited_by field and a per-field edit history, built for that old server-side coach. I'd designed the substrate for this without knowing it. Turning it into a shared, two-party document was mostly a matter of letting the second party in. The agent moves the interface, not just the data Four tools exist purely to drive the UI: fitness_navigate , fitness_start_session , fitness_open_plan_editor , fitness_highlight_exercise . So when the agent changes an exercise, the app switches to the plan tab, scrolls to that exercise, and flashes it. When you say you're ready to train, it opens the guided session flow and you're looking at set one. The agent can say "this one" and have you actually be looking at the thing. fitness_open_plan_editor is my favourite of the four because it runs the other direction: it's the agent handing the decision back , opening a blank editor instead of making a choice that isn't its to make. Destructive actions stop and ask delete_plan , delete_exercise and delete_workout don't delete anything. They park the tool call and render a confirmation card in the app showing exactly what's about to go. You tap; the agent is told what you chose. Declining is a normal outcome it handles, and an unanswered prompt counts as "no" after a minute. I built this in the app's own UI rather than leaning on the spec's requestUserInteraction() , partly because that surface is still in flux, and partly because doing it myself meant the confirmation could name the specific plan and its phase count instead of being a generic browser prompt. Why WebMCP is the right primitive here Coaching is a case where an agent and a person genuinely need to co-own one artifact. A training plan is a living document. It changes because your knee hurt on Tuesday, because the gym was out of 25s, because a set that was brutal last month is easy now. Some of those edits you want to make yourself in three seconds. Some you want to talk through. Both kinds have to land in the same place or the plan stops being true. Every other arrangement I tried forces a choice: either the agent owns the plan and you file requests with it, or you own the plan and the agent narrates from outside. WebMCP is the first primitive that let me refuse the choice. What's newly possible: not "an AI that writes you a workout" — that's been available for years and it isn't interesting. It's a plan with two editors and one history , where the reasoning behind every change is attached to the change and visible to both parties. That's a different relationship, and it's one the browser had no way to express until tools could live in the page. How I built it Vite + React + TypeScript + CSS Modules. No backend, no state library, no router. Dependencies: React, Lucide icons, and the WebMCP polyfill. Porting a backend into the browser The original was FastAPI + SQLAlchemy + SQLite. Making it multi-user meant making it zero -user: no server at all, one versioned JSON document in localStorage . The domain layer ported over almost mechanically, because it had been written framework-free — rules.py , badges.py and service.py became rules.ts , badges.ts and store.ts . The Python test suite came with it. src/lib/__tests__/ holds 33 tests carried over from pytest, and having a known-green oracle was worth more than the time it cost, because of this: Python's date.weekday() is Monday=0. JavaScript's getDay() is Sunday=0. The schedule lookup tables were indexed the Python way. Get this wrong and every streak, completion rate and calendar cell silently shifts by one day — nothing crashes, the numbers are just quietly false. The ported tests caught it on the first run. I'd have shipped it otherwise. One choke point makes everything live The load-bearing decision: db.write() is the only way anything in the app changes, and it notifies subscribers. Every data hook subscribes. That's the entire mechanism behind the demo. An agent calls log_workout , and the streak, the calendar, the stat tiles and the badge wall all update instantly — no polling, no refresh, and no separate code path for agent-driven changes. Agent writes and human writes are indistinguishable to the UI, which is exactly the property I wanted. Registering 31 tools Worth passing on to anyone else building this: register your tools in parallel. My first version awaited each registerTool() in a loop. It took several seconds to get through the set, because the implementation flushes the tool list between calls. An agent connecting during that window would see a partial toolset — some tools present, some missing, no error anywhere. I only noticed because I queried getTools() while debugging and got 11 back instead of 31. Promise.allSettled over the whole array lets the flushes coalesce. Same 31 tools, 3 milliseconds . I also hit the spec moving underneath me: the W3C draft relocated the getter from Navigator to Document in May 2026. The app reads whichever exists: const mc = document.modelContext ?? navigator.modelContext Tool descriptions are written for an agent audience, not a changelog. They state units (pounds, centimetres, seconds), name which tool to call first to get an id, and give judgement guidance — update_exercise asks for a reason phrased for the user , because that text is what shows up next to their exercise. The hardest constraint was the one nobody grades directly I decided early that CoRep had to be completely usable with no agent connected. The agent should be an amplifier, never a dependency. This turned out to be the biggest chunk of work in the whole project, for a reason I didn't see coming: in the original app, plans could only be created by the AI. Plan creation existed solely as an MCP tool. There was no UI for it, because there had never needed to be one — I was the only user and I had the coach. So "works without an agent" meant building the feature an agent-only app never needed: a full manual plan editor. Phases, exercises, reordering, weekday scheduling, the lot. I'm glad the constraint forced it. An app that collapses when the agent disconnects isn't demonstrating collaboration, it's demonstrating dependence. And the editor made the attribution feature real — before it, every edit in the history said "Coach", and there was nothing to contrast against. The agent indicator says all this out loud, too. With no WebMCP available it reads: "WebMCP is not available in this browser, so no agent can connect. Everything in the app still works."  Every agent either just talks, or does things you can’t see and can’t stop. We wanted one that does real work in the open and leaves every decision that costs money to you. 

 What it does 

 You type a goal. Cardea plans it, runs the steps in parallel in real browsers you can watch, and comes back with real prices. Anything that spends, sends, or signs stops and asks you. ChatGPT can drive the whole thing through 13 WebMCP tools. 

 How we built it 

 Next.js on Vercel. Supabase for an append-only mission log. Inngest for durable runs that pause on approval and resume. Cloudflare for real headless Chrome streamed onto the canvas. GPT-5.6 for planning. Shopify’s agent protocol for real carts. 890 tests. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Big retailers served bot walls, so we made Cardea say “this site blocked me” instead of inventing prices. We built an enforced approval gate, it broke in the real ChatGPT browser, and we pulled it the same hour. ChatGPT preferred its own browser over ours until our tool descriptions said when to use them. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 It runs end to end on real websites and ends on a real cart. It admits what it couldn’t verify. We tested the tools in ChatGPT itself, not just our own harness. 

 What we learned 

 Test where you’ll be judged. Measure before you fix. The agent and the human have to see the same thing, or it’s theater.

 Enforce approvals in the browser, carts from any store, more connected apps, and a real mobile view.

title: GotPaid Agent Desk
pitch: An invoice-reconciliation dashboard humans and AI agents use together — agents query receivables, point at rows in your view, and draft chaser letters you review, via 8 WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: An invoice-reconciliation dashboard humans and AI agents use together — agents query receivables, point at rows in your view, and draft chaser letters you review, via 8 WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates GotPaid dashboard — 8 WebMCP tools registered via document.modelContext.registerTool Agent calls a tool live — the human sees exactly what their agent just did Inspiration I run a Thai agri-export company that invoices Chinese buyers in USD/CNY. Every month a deposit lands with the wrong amount and a useless reference — "INWARD REMIT REF 88213" — and I have to guess which invoice it was, work out how much the bank silently skimmed, and remember which client always pays like this. I already built GotPaid to fix that. For this challenge, I asked a narrower question: reconciliation questions ("which buyer is slipping?", "why did this deposit match that invoice?") only really make sense pointed at a real row on a real screen — so what if the agent helping me could act inside the dashboard I'm already looking at, instead of just answering in a disconnected chat window? What it does GotPaid reconciles cross-border invoice payments against messy bank deposits — tolerant of hidden fees, batched payments, and split payments — learns each buyer's payment behavior over time, and surfaces what's still unpaid. The WebMCP layer adds 8 tools so a human and an AI agent can work the same dashboard together: the agent reads structured data (no screen-scraping — an embedded JSON island), switches tabs and flashes the exact row it's talking about in the human's own view, and drafts a chaser letter that opens on screen for review. Nothing is ever sent automatically — the agent proposes, the human decides, both looking at the same thing. That's the gap WebMCP closes: before, an agent could only describe what's on screen; now it can point at it. How we built it Python renders a static dashboard ( dashboard.py ) with all data baked into an embedded JSON script tag. On top of that, 8 tools are registered via document.modelContext.registerTool() : 5 read-only ( list_companies , list_unpaid_invoices , get_buyer_profile , explain_match , get_dashboard_totals ) and 3 UI-action tools ( show_company , highlight_invoice , draft_chaser_letter ) that manipulate the DOM the human is looking at. Every tool call is echoed to an on-page "Agent activity" log so the human always sees what their agent just did. Deployed static on Cloudflare Pages — no server, no build step. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is brand new — Chrome support is flag-gated ( chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing ), so I had to design a graceful fallback banner rather than assume every judge has it enabled. I also had to resist just exposing raw data dumps as tools; the ones that ended up mattering most act in the human's view (highlight, draft) rather than just answering questions in text. Accomplishments that we're proud of A working execute implementation behind every tool — not stubs — verified end-to-end (filtering, cross-company lookups, a chaser letter that actually reflects a buyer's real payment history) before ever opening Chrome's WebMCP flag. And keeping the human-in-the-loop boundary hard: the letter tool drafts and opens for review, it never sends. What we learned A "reasonable-sounding" tool surface (just dump every field as a tool) is worse than a smaller set of tools that do something in the human's view. Also: sponsor sandboxes don't always match their public docs — worth verifying the live account rather than trusting documentation alone when they disagree. What's next for GotPaid Agent Desk GotPaid already plugs into my company's deployed durian-export platform (2 awards at the Nanning ASEAN summit). This WebMCP layer is the template for making the rest of that platform agent-native — inventory, grading, logistics — all queryable and actionable by an agent working alongside the person actually running the business. Claude (via Claude Code) was my engineering execution partner throughout, including debugging the Chrome flag / managed-browser activation issue live. title: Dish Decider
pitch: Everyone’s AI has a seat at the table. DishDecider lets agents coordinate on one shared plan, catch conflicts, and make smarter choices together—with WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
Everyone’s AI has a seat at the table. DishDecider lets agents coordinate on one shared plan, catch conflicts, and make smarter choices together—with WebMCP.

 Architectural Diagram 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Inspiration 

 Every group event has the same failure mode: five people bring chips, nobody brings a main course, and somebody blows the budget — and nobody notices until it is already awkward to fix. That is not really a communication problem; it is a coordination problem . Group chats and shared spreadsheets still rely on someone manually cross-checking everyone's plans. 

 WebMCP made us wonder: what if every participant's own AI agent could act on the same live shared plan instead of every assistant working in isolation? Agents could understand what each person wants, see what has already been claimed, and catch conflicts before they are committed. That is the idea behind DishDecider. 

 What it does 

 DishDecider is a shared event planner. One person creates an event with a budget cap; anyone with the link can join with just a name and dietary restrictions — no account required. 

 Participants can claim dishes manually or simply tell their agent what they want in natural language, such as "I'm broke this week" or "I want to impress but only have 20 minutes." The agent turns that request into structured constraints and recommends a specific dish. 

 The core feature is shared-state conflict resolution . If a proposed dish duplicates an existing choice, violates a participant's dietary restriction, or pushes the group over budget, the system detects the conflict, explains why in plain language, and suggests an alternative. Every action is visible in the shared event and recorded in an activity log. After the event, a recap shows computed metrics such as total spending, conflicts resolved, and suggestion acceptance rate. 

 How we built it 

 We built four WebMCP tools, registered through document.modelContext.registerTool : 

 
 interpret_intent — converts open-ended requests into structured constraints 
 suggest_item — recommends an item using those constraints and the current event state 
 resolve_conflict — validates a proposal against live shared state and identifies conflicts 
 explain_tradeoff — compares valid alternatives and explains the reasoning 
 

 All four route through a consolidated reasoning endpoint backed by an LLM, with Zod-validated structured output and a deterministic fallback so the application remains functional if a model call fails. 

 Event state is stored in Supabase , with realtime subscriptions so every participant sees updates without refreshing. The application is deployed on Vercel . 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Our biggest challenge was proving that WebMCP itself actually worked . It is easy to write registerTool calls and assume they are working; it is much harder to verify that a browser-native agent can actually discover them. 

 We tested this directly in Chrome Canary with WebMCP enabled. document.modelContext returned a live ModelContext object, and document.modelContext.getTools() resolved with all four tools and their definitions. That was the point where the project went from "this should work" to "we can prove it works." 

 We also hit a frustrating deployment issue when our LLM provider deprecated the model we were using. The actual fix was small, but a stale deployment initially kept serving old code, making the problem much harder to diagnose. It taught us to verify the actual deployed commit and runtime behavior , rather than assuming a successful push means the newest code is live. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud that DishDecider is not just a UI calling an AI API — it is a genuinely agent-native page with a browser-discoverable WebMCP tool registry . 

 We also got real multi-participant conflict resolution working across separate sessions: two participants, two agents, one shared event, and a genuine conflict detected and resolved with a specific explanation. The result is visible to both participants in real time rather than being a scripted demo. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that "does it work?" and "did we verify it works?" are very different questions. With an experimental standard like WebMCP, assumptions can easily look correct until you test the actual browser behavior. 

 We also learned that building an agentic application is not just about getting an LLM to produce a good answer. The interesting engineering problem is connecting that reasoning to structured tools, shared state, validation, and observable actions . 

 What's next for DishDecider 

 The underlying pattern is not specific to potlucks. Multiple people independently contributing to a shared, constraint-aware plan could also apply to roommate expense management, group trip planning, or gift coordination . 

 Longer term, we would like to test DishDecider with a real external WebMCP-aware agent completing the workflow through natural conversation. That would take the project from proving that our tools are technically discoverable to proving the full agent → tool → shared state → resolution loop end-to-end with an independent agent.

 Inspiration 

 As a former design and technology studio co-founder, my first thought when I saw WebMCP was: "Web developers are about to get paid a lot." But I realized getting millions of businesses to rebuild or adapt their websites for AI agents would take years. That made me think about Google Business Profiles. A simple way for businesses to get visibility on the web. Same for Agents. It shouldnt take years for businesses to adapt to agents. 

 What it does 

 Agentprofiles gives businesses an identity built for AI agents. Each profile exposes information about the business, its capabilities, and the actions an agent can perform through WebMCP. An agent can discover a business, understand what it offers, and interact with supported actions. 

 But it doesn't just stop at businesses. People can create events and happenings that ChatGPT can find/recommend to a user, giving a clear overview for users on whats happening around them. This could be dragged even further by enabling restaurants to add deals so users can find 2 for 1 or other deals straight from the agent. 

 How we built it 

 We built Agentprofiles around WebMCP as the interaction layer between AI agents and businesses. Businesses create a structured profile containing their identity and available actions, which agents can discover and use when completing tasks on behalf of users. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was figuring out what an "identity" for a business should contain when designed for agents. We had to separate information meant to describe the business from capabilities that agents should be able to invoke directly. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We built a working concept for turning businesses into discoverable and actionable entities for AI agents. Instead of requiring an agent to understand an entire website (often outdated info), Agentprofiles gives it a structured representation of who the business is and what it can do/offer. 

 I think this would be the fastest way for businesses to start getting into AI. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP changes how websites can be designed for agents. The interesting part is not only exposing individual actions, but creating a structured layer around those actions so agents can understand which businesses and capabilities are available to them. 

 What's next for Agentprofile 

 I would love to see OpenAI take this concept further and create Agent Profiles, similar to Google Business Profiles. Businesses could provide their information, services, and WebMCP actions once, giving AI agents a standardized way to discover, understand, and interact with them.

title: Potter's Wheel
pitch: Connect research papers, experiment tracking, and your AI agent in one loop. Runs become evidence, and the agent can verify, add to, or update the paper via WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Connect research papers, experiment tracking, and your AI agent in one loop. Runs become evidence, and the agent can verify, add to, or update the paper via WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Why Web Inspiration Software has dependency graphs, diffs, and CI. Research papers still copy results by hand. A run changes. A configuration changes. A new figure replaces the old one. But the manuscript often stays frozen until someone notices the mismatch manually. Potter's Wheel keeps the paper connected to the research that produced it. What it does Potter's Wheel is a provenance-aware research dependency system built around one continuous lifecycle: Experiments → Evidence → Paper Experiments are first-class objects with planned/running/completed/failed/superseded states, methods, parameters, scalar metrics, metric histories, datasets, artifacts, notes, source commits, timestamps, and run-to-run supersession. Results can be published as typed evidence and linked directly to the manuscript objects that depend on them: claims, methods, tables, and figures . The trace is bidirectional: run → evidence → paper, and paper → evidence → run. When newer evidence replaces older evidence, Potter's Wheel can mark downstream manuscript objects stale and generate a reviewable Research Diff instead of silently rewriting the paper. Three signature experiences make that visible: Research X-Ray turns the manuscript into an integrity map, highlighting verified, stale, contradicted, unlinked, and review-required objects directly in the editor. Verify This deterministically checks a selected quantitative claim against its linked evidence, including percentages, decimals, grouped numbers, and scientific notation, while surfacing ambiguous or conflicting evidence for review instead of guessing. Research Diff shows Git-like drift between the current research and the manuscript across results, methods/configs, tables, figures, and artifact identity. Corrections are staged visibly and require researcher acceptance. The demo deliberately contains multiple kinds of drift: a paper that says 18.2% while the current experiment says 16.8% , a learning-rate mismatch, a stale table, and a stale figure. Potter's Wheel also includes an agent-side experiment sync workflow: when a research agent starts, evaluates, or finishes a run, it can synchronize the visible Experiments and Evidence workspaces through WebMCP—recording parameters, metric history, artifacts, run status, evidence, and manuscript links without scraping or clicking the UI. Why WebMCP Potter's Wheel is fully usable without AI. A researcher can record and compare runs, publish evidence, write the paper, inspect provenance, verify claims, review diffs, and accept or reject changes manually. WebMCP adds a second native control surface for the user's existing research agent. The application currently registers 37 WebMCP tools spanning live manuscript context, selections, claims, figures, tables, provenance, integrity state, experiment reads/comparison, run creation and updates, metric logging, parameter logging, artifacts, run status and supersession, evidence publishing, evidence linking, verification, navigation, comments, and reviewable corrections. That matters because the user's agent may already know the repository, experiment history, code paths, and research decisions, while Potter's Wheel knows the exact manuscript, selection, evidence graph, and integrity state currently open in the browser. WebMCP lets those two contexts meet in the same live workspace. The agent can maintain runs, publish and compare evidence, verify claims, navigate stale dependencies, add comments, and stage corrections. It cannot accept its own manuscript rewrite. Final authority stays with the researcher. How we built it Potter's Wheel builds on Antmicro's Apache-2.0 licensed MyST Editor for the scientific editing foundation. For this challenge, we added the experiment/evidence lifecycle workspace, provenance graph, typed evidence model, Research Integrity panel, Research X-Ray, deterministic quantitative verification, evidence-driven Research Diff, supersession logic, a reproducible research fixture, agent experiment-sync workflow, and the 37-tool WebMCP surface. WebMCP tools operate on the same state visible to the human, use explicit input schemas, distinguish read-only from state-changing actions, mark researcher-authored content as untrusted input, return structured failures for stale or invalid context, and unregister with the editor lifecycle. The browser suite currently passes 112/112 Playwright tests , covering the research workspace, provenance/integrity flows, WebMCP registration and actions, experiment lifecycle, evidence publishing, manuscript linking, stale-context guards, and review-only writes. No account, model API key, or backend is required to run the deterministic judge demo. Challenges The hardest problem was not making the agent powerful; it was making it powerful without making it authoritative . Research facts need stronger guarantees than generated prose. We therefore keep experiments, evidence, verification state, and manuscript dependencies structured and inspectable. Agent conclusions do not directly rewrite the paper. Changes are staged into the same review surface the researcher uses. A second challenge was treating WebMCP as a real application interface rather than a demo wrapper. The tool surface needed stale-state protection, evidence gating, structured failures, safe navigation, lifecycle cleanup, and shared UI/tool state while the WebMCP API itself is still evolving. What we learned The most interesting part of the agent-native web is not adding chat to an application. It is letting a user's existing agent enter a specialized tool with a first-class semantic control surface, bringing the context it already has while operating the exact same state as the human. For research, that creates a new possibility: the agent that helped run the work can help keep the paper honest about the work. What's next The next step is turning Potter's Wheel from a self-contained research workspace into a professional research-integrity layer across the existing stack: adapters for MLflow, Weights & Biases, DVC, and other experiment trackers persistent multi-user provenance and collaboration typed live evidence bindings inside manuscripts a full provenance/dependency graph explorer Research CI checks for stale or unsupported manuscript claims immutable submission snapshots that freeze the exact runs, evidence, commits, datasets, figures, and manuscript version behind a paper deeper Git/Overleaf-style interoperability The long-term goal is simple: research artifacts should evolve without the paper silently drifting away from them. title: ClaimGate
pitch: Agent-assisted lost-property search with private proof and human release decisions.
about_excerpt: Agent-assisted lost-property search with private proof and human release decisions. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP exposes privacy-safe candidate matching while private proof stays manual. Staff reviews aggregate eligibility and a redacted timeline, never evidence values. Atomic handoff completes the claim, returns the item, and resolves the report. ClaimGate — privacy-first lost-property claims with human release decisions. Problem Lost-property desks need enough public detail to find a likely item without publishing the details that prove ownership. Giving every field to an Agent would turn private proof into searchable material. ClaimGate separates public matching from private proof. The Agent handles structured preparation and safe reads. People publish, submit evidence, decide the claim, issue the pickup credential, and complete the release. Why WebMCP This workflow changes as the claim moves from draft to match, review, pickup, and collection. WebMCP lets the page expose the few actions that are valid now, with typed inputs and bounded results. The Agent does not have to infer controls from page layout, and sensitive actions can stay absent from the tool set. Better experience A Claimant can describe a loss once, let the Agent structure the public fields, and receive explainable candidates without copying data between screens. Staff gets a short queue and a redacted summary. Each person sees the next action in the same claim instead of reconstructing context after every role change. Before and after Before ClaimGate, the demo journey is a sequence of manual forms and page searches, with a risk of mixing public clues and ownership proof. With ClaimGate, the Agent prepares, searches, and summarizes through explicit tools while the UI reserves publication, proof, judgment, credential transfer, and handoff for visible human controls. What it does A Claimant starts a fresh two-hour instance with fictional Northbridge Campus inventory. The Agent can create or update a lost-report draft, list reports, find up to three candidates, and stage one candidate. Results contain broad fields, confidence bands, and public reasons, not internal inventory IDs. The Claimant publishes and submits masked evidence manually. Two correct slots are sufficient even if a third submitted slot is wrong. The browser receives only aggregate eligibility, insufficiency, or the third-attempt LOCKED state. Staff reads a bounded queue and redacted review summary, then decides manually. After approval, the Agent can read pickup instructions. The Claimant manually generates and copies a ten-minute, one-time credential, then Staff pastes it into the handoff form. One transaction marks the claim collected, item returned, and report resolved. The normal web flow also works without WebMCP. How implemented ClaimGate is one Next.js 16 application with separate report, matching, evidence, claim, authorization, audit, and WebMCP modules. SQLite scopes every record to a demo instance. Signed HttpOnly sessions and server routes enforce role, ownership, state, version, CSRF, origin, idempotency, and rate limits. The browser uses native document.modelContext.registerTool() . A page and state registry selects nine tools, and an AbortController removes the previous generation on navigation or state change. Tool visibility assists selection; the server remains authoritative. The tools are create_lost_report_draft , update_lost_report_draft , list_my_reports , find_candidate_matches , stage_claim_candidate , get_claim_status , get_pickup_instructions , list_pending_claims , and get_claim_review_summary . Publishing, evidence, decisions, pass issue or reissue, role switching, and handoff have no WebMCP tool. Matching uses fixed category, time, area, color, and tag rules. Runtime evidence comparison uses salted HMAC digests and a fixed three-slot shape. The public repository contains the readable fictional seed answers so judges can run the demo; the privacy boundary covers runtime clients, pages, APIs, WebMCP, logs, and stored raw evidence, not repository readers. Only a successful issue or reissue response returns the full pickup credential. The current Claimant page keeps it in memory and can reveal, mask, or copy it. Navigation or refresh clears it and cannot recover it. The server stores only a digest, and reissue invalidates the previous generation. Challenges we ran into State-aware tool lifecycle: Chrome 151 can briefly change membership while registrations are replaced. A serialized generation manager and server state checks make stale calls fail safely. Runtime privacy evidence: We separated public DTOs from private transports, signed opaque candidate handles, bounded outputs, and scanned tool results, HTML, logs, storage, history, and public build assets. Visible cross-role continuity: Claimant and Staff must resume the same authorized claim without hidden navigation. Contextual role switching and a 14-scenario visible Playwright suite cover that path. Accomplishments that we're proud of The complete report, match, proof, review, pickup, and handoff flow works in the normal UI and the WebMCP-assisted path. Nine tools appear only in valid page and state scopes; human-only actions stay absent. A clean production build completed three independent native Chrome 151 runs. Each used fresh SQLite state, exercised all nine tools, completed the manual transitions, and ended with Home tools [] . All 14 visible Playwright E2E scenarios passed after commit 04c618d added contextual cross-role claim navigation. The release path isolates its runtime, data, processes, ingress, and Nginx resources from unrelated services. These are implementation and test results, not claims of awards, adoption, users, or judging outcome. What we learned Tool discovery improves planning but is not authorization. Runtime privacy needs separate data paths, not hidden UI fields. Human control is clearest when a sensitive transition has no tool at all. Stateful WebMCP also needs navigation, stale-version, delayed-completion, and teardown tests, not only a happy path. What's next A production pilot would need institutional identity, enrolled Staff, accessibility and abuse review, retention policy, backup and recovery, and a database architecture for multiple application instances. Configurable matching and evidence policies should preserve the same public-match, private-proof, and human-release boundaries.
