Both blocked wells were avoided. And two violations became zero. The receipt matches the interface. The release passed 136 automated tests and five out of five fresh site tools trials.

title: NWA Growth Signal
pitch: A source-backed municipal planning desk where people and browser agents share filing-level evidence, with human review before anything leaves the page.
about_excerpt: A source-backed municipal planning desk where people and browser agents share filing-level evidence, with human review before anything leaves the page. Like Comment Story Updates Four real WebMCP calls completed in one visible workflow: search, list changes, inspect, and stage. The brief remains human-review-required. One parcel, two filings: VAR26-0397 Withdrawn and RZ26-00511 Recommended, kept distinct with their official sources. A three-filing brief staged for human review. Nothing is published or sent. The signal desk: the same dated municipal record for people and browser agents. Inspiration An agenda-wording-only heuristic could determine just 3 of 23 real planning outcomes, and 2 of those 3 were wrong: the wording implied approval for requests that were actually tabled. This week, Rogers changed an existing 8/18/26 outcome row in place from Tabled to 9/1 to Recommended to City Council , with no separate September 1 row. That is the kind of quiet procedural change that can burn land and development teams, lenders and title professionals, local journalists, and public-interest planners in Northwest Arkansas. Municipal records are public, but the procedural truth is scattered across agendas, minutes, outcome tables, hearing pages, and companion filings. One parcel can have several filings with different statuses. NWA Growth Signal gives a person and a browser agent a dated, filing-level planning evidence desk for Bentonville and Rogers, Arkansas. Adjacent products serve related jobs. CivicPlus provides agenda and meeting management. Regrid provides a parcel and property map. PermitFlow provides permitting workflow. NWA Growth Signal focuses on the evidence handoff between a researcher and an agent as official planning records change. What it does Why is this a strong fit for WebMCP? The research task has four distinct steps, each with a clear contract. search_planning_cases filters 5 verified records by municipality, procedural status, residential relevance, and pending government action. list_status_changes returns the filings whose verified status moved since the previous check, with the official source on both dates. inspect_case_record returns one filing-level record with its context and official sources. stage_source_backed_brief places 1 to 5 selected records into the visible briefing workspace. The agent receives typed results from the same dated data the person sees instead of inferring status from page wording or clicking by coordinates. How does it create a better experience? One prompt can drive the whole flow: “Find residential Bentonville and Rogers cases still awaiting procedural action. List which filings changed status since the previous verification, inspect their official evidence, and stage a three-item brief without representing any recommendation as final approval.” The fixed demo script takes 10 direct human control activations or 4 agent tool calls. Each real handler call adds an on-page receipt, so the person can see search, list changes, inspect, and stage start and then succeed or fail in order. What can people and agents now do together? The person states the research intent and keeps editorial judgment. The agent searches, inspects the filing-level evidence, and stages the brief. The person can check every selected filing and source before using it. The staging tool cannot publish, send, or persist a brief, and only a human control can record review. How did we implement WebMCP? The page registers all 4 tools atomically with document.modelContext.registerTool after the record set loads and supports AbortSignal . Handler inputs are validated. The 3 read tools carry readOnlyHint annotations. Search, inspection, staging, the ordinary browser interface, and the receipt row all use the same deterministic record operations, so the agent and person work from one application state. Every filing also carries a status_history : its August 25 and September 2 statuses, the official source checked on each date, and a note where the record moved or went silent. The tools return it through their existing outputs, and the page shows the same line beside each filing, so an agent inspecting RZ26-00419 sees Tabled on August 25 and Recommended on September 2 with the same outcome-table URL for both, not a single current label. A fourth tool, list_status_changes , landed after the first demo video was recorded; the current video shows it in the same run. It reads that same status_history and returns the filings whose verified status moved between the previous check and the current one: RZ26-00419 (Tabled to Recommended) and RZ26-00511 (Scheduled to Recommended), each with the official source checked on both dates. With changed_only set to false it also lists the six unchanged filings and their notes, such as FP26-0005 absent from the reissued agenda. It is read-only, registered atomically with the other three, and writes the same on-page receipt: 2 filings changed since 2026-08-25. What changed during the challenge The project was created during the challenge. Its first commit was 85c27f7 on August 26, 2026. In the 8 days since the first snapshot, the official record moved 4 times across just 5 tracked records: Rogers RZ26-00511 , Poplar Street Paired Homes at 408 E. Poplar, moved from Scheduled to a 9/1/26 outcome of Recommended to City Council . Its companion filing on the same parcel, VAR26-0397 , still reads Withdrawn by applicant . The split-filing result is now Withdrawn plus Recommended, and council action is still pending. Rogers RZ26-00419 , 209 W. Locust, changed inside the same 8/18/26 row. On August 25 it read Tabled to 9/1 ; on September 2 it reads Recommended to City Council . The table publishes no separate September 1 row. Bentonville FP26-0005 , Brier Hill Phase II final plat, appeared on the September 1 agenda published August 25 as CivicClerk file 9108 . The city reissued that agenda as file 9133 without the filing. The current CivicClerk event record now points to agenda file 9143 ; the tracked filing contents are unchanged, and FP26-0005 remains omitted. No reason, outcome, or new date is published, so the product keeps the filing visible with its last published status and states what changed. Rogers RZ26-00345 , 6253 S. Mt Hebron Rd, disappeared from the outcome table. No City Council action appears in the official sources reviewed, so the product retains the last recorded status, Recommended, and says the row is gone. Bentonville RZ26-0041 , FP26-0003 , and FP26-0004 were heard September 1 according to the agenda. Minutes are not yet published, so the product represents no outcome for them. We also tested the approach on a held-out historical study: 23 real Rogers requests, 26 procedural events, 6 meetings in 2025, and 12 official agenda and minutes documents. NWA Growth Signal preserved 26/26 exact statuses through both inspection and staging. Expected source pairs were present in 26/26 record-wide outputs. All 23/23 same-meeting agenda and minutes pairs were present, and 3 multi-meeting lifecycles stayed intact. The request wording left 20 of 23 outcomes unknowable; as the opening example shows, it also gave the wrong answer for 2 of the 3 outcomes it appeared to reveal. How we built it NWA Growth Signal is a dependency-free static HTML, CSS, and JavaScript site deployed on Cloudflare Pages. A dated JSON snapshot holds the editorial sample. Shared JavaScript owns deterministic filtering, record inspection, brief staging, freshness checks, and receipts. The WebMCP adapter and the ordinary browser interface call those same operations. The release has 99 passing dependency-free tests, a deterministic benchmark, and a fail-closed freshness gate. The current video and public main both reflect the 99-test release. The team used Codex and Claude Code for implementation, review, testing, and submission work; Hyperagent for municipal research and editorial work; and Google Gemini for the approved demo narration. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was preserving truth at the filing level while the official record kept moving. A parcel summary would hide the difference between a withdrawn variance and a rezoning recommended to City Council. We carried each filing, status, source, and date through the data, tools, interface, benchmark, and demo. The other hard boundary was useful agent action without an unsafe side effect. Staging had to be visible and valuable while leaving review and any later use of the brief with the person. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete public planning desk with 4 native WebMCP tools over 5 verified records. One browser request that searches, inspects, and stages a source-backed brief, with a live receipt for every handler call. 99 passing tests, all 4 tools exercised, input validation, atomic registration, cancellation support, and a fail-closed freshness gate. title: Proof Gate
pitch: Accountable intelligence for the open web: humans and agents build, challenge, and verify the same evidence-backed case.
about_excerpt:
Accountable intelligence for the open web: humans and agents build, challenge, and verify the same evidence-backed case.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Proof Gate 

 Most competitors build intelligent agents. Proof Gate builds accountable intelligence. 

 Proof Gate is a WebMCP-native evidence workspace where a human and a browsing agent build the same versioned case together. 

 The contradiction is simple: web agents can often click and act, but they struggle to preserve shared state, provenance, uncertainty, and decision lineage across a real workflow. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Claim evaluation is stateful. A case contains a claim revision, decision context, evidence records, provenance, conflicts, a deterministic verdict, and an audit lineage. Without a structured application interface, a browsing model has to infer that state from DOM controls and maintain a separate copy. 

 Proof Gate exposes six narrow tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) : 

 
 read the current case 
 set or revise the claim 
 add evidence 
 identify conflicts 
 evaluate the current claim revision 
 export the versioned record 
 

 The human and the agent operate on the same application state. The agent does not maintain a hidden parallel case, and the human does not have to trust a black-box conclusion. 

 Distillation Protocol: the governance boundary 

 Proof Gate applies a two-way Distillation Protocol at the boundary between the web and the governed case. 

 Inbound: raw user input, tool output, and external observations are converted into structured evidence with provenance, revision binding, uncertainty labels, and explicit source roles before they enter the case. 

 Outbound: internal evaluations and proposed actions are converted into scoped, inspectable outputs. Evidence-derived content is marked as untrusted, and no raw external statement becomes authority merely because an API, tool, user, or model asserted it. 

 This prevents four common failures: 

 
 prompt or content injection becoming governance state 
 API responses being mistaken for independently verified reality 
 AI conclusions being silently promoted to facts 
 stale or contradictory evidence being overwritten instead of preserved 
 

 The anti-magic rule is: I do not know yet, and here is exactly what evidence would resolve it. 

 Global Compass signature 

 Proof Gate follows the Global Compass design philosophy: 

 SEE REALITY → PRESERVE EVIDENCE → UNDERSTAND RELATIONSHIPS → SEPARATE CAPABILITY FROM AUTHORITY → VERIFY WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED → LEARN WITHOUT REWRITING HISTORY 

 In this application that means: 

 
 evidence is bound to explicit claim revisions 
 duplicate source families do not manufacture independence 
 context records do not inflate support or refutation confidence 
 unknown dates remain unknown and future dates are rejected 
 contradictory evidence stays visible instead of being silently overwritten 
 only HTTP/HTTPS evidence URLs are accepted 
 evidence-derived WebMCP outputs are marked as untrusted content 
 conflicts are aggregated and the evidence ledger is bounded 
 the evaluator does not claim to independently establish truth 
 

 Better human + agent collaboration 

 Before WebMCP, an agent interacting with a case workspace has to reverse-engineer controls and reconstruct application state from the page. With WebMCP, the application exposes the actual operations and schemas directly. 

 The division of labor is explicit: 

 Human: frames the claim, inspects evidence, corrects context, challenges conclusions, and retains authority over meaningful decisions. 

 Agent: structures evidence, detects conflicts, evaluates the current revision, and prepares an export. 

 Application: deterministically enforces revision boundaries, validates inputs, and preserves the lineage both sides can inspect. 

 The agent can therefore be useful without becoming an unaccountable source of truth. 

 Reality Triangle 

 Proof Gate distinguishes three states instead of collapsing them: 

 
 Intended: what the claim or decision asks us to establish 
 Reported: what a source, tool, or provider says happened 
 Observed: what the accumulated evidence actually supports 
 

 Success is not established merely because a tool returned success or a model produced a confident answer. 

 Implementation 

 The WebMCP layer calls the same pure JavaScript evidence engine used by the visible human UI. Tool calls and UI actions mutate the same state. Where supported, the application also checks getTools() enumeration after registration. 

 The evaluator is deliberately modest. Thresholds and source-family grouping are transparent demo heuristics rather than claims of calibrated universal truth. 

 Scope 

 Proof Gate is deliberately one focused web application, not an AI backend disguised as a hackathon entry. The demonstration is shared application state: explicit schemas for the agent, visible and revisable evidence for the human, deterministic evaluation, a governed boundary, and a versioned record they can inspect together. 

 Accountable intelligence, not merely intelligent agents.

title: Vast
pitch: A real-time collaborative canvas that gives AI agents the same tools a human uses not screenshots, not clicks, the actual API.
about_excerpt: A real-time collaborative canvas that gives AI agents the same tools a human uses not screenshots, not clicks, the actual API. Like Comment Story Updates vast Inspiration Every "AI edits your app" demo we'd seen worked the same way: an LLM either writes DOM-manipulation code and hopes it doesn't break something, or a browser-automation layer clicks around pretending to be a mouse. Neither one actually knows what a "connector" or a "frame" means in the app it's touching it's reverse-engineering intent from pixels. We'd already built Vast as a from-scratch realtime canvas rooms, shapes, live cursors, a shared undo stack as its own project, no AI involved. When WebMCP landed, the fit was obvious: Vast is already multiplayer. Every edit already goes through a typed, named function (create_element, align_elements, undo_action) over the same Socket.IO connection every guest uses. Making an agent a participant didn't mean bolting on a special "AI mode" it meant registering those exact functions as tools and letting an agent join the room like any other guest. What it does How we built it The base —Vite/React/TypeScript/Canvas2D client, Node/Express/Socket.IO server in a layered architecture, Postgres for shape state and an event log came together first, over about five days, ~14,000 lines. WebMCP went in afterward in a single focused push, under one rule: no separate agent path. Every tool calls the exact same socket events a human edit fires. Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of One code path, not two an agent literally cannot do anything the UI itself couldn't. Undo/redo that's genuinely shared between human and agent, cascades and all. A believable peer, not a gimmick the agent gets a name, color, and cursor because the server has no privileged notion of "human" to begin with. Real, deployable output via export_html, not just a screenshot of a session. Native-first: proving out where WebMCP is headed, not propping up an API that doesn't exist yet. What we learned What's next for Vast More tools under the same rule grouping, z-order, true component instances. Multi-agent rooms, to stress-test the undo stack with more than one agent peer at once. Giving the agent read access to why something was drawn (nearby notes, replay history), not just current state. Scoped tool permissions once the server has real auth, without breaking the no-separate-path guarantee. Following WebMCP beyond Chrome as other runtimes adopt document.modelContext. title: WebMCP Guard
pitch: WebMCP Guard is a security control plane between your app's WebMCP tools and the agent, providing data protection and other security policies for agents accessing data through your WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: WebMCP Guard is a security control plane between your app's WebMCP tools and the agent, providing data protection and other security policies for agents accessing data through your WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Organizations often run their own internal apps that have access to sensitive data. They often have tools to enforce data protection and security policies on these apps, but an improperly implemented WebMCP tool may circumvent them. I wanted to create something that would allow them to have these same kind of policies for their WebMCP tools without forcing them to code it themselves. But it needed to do more than block data for the agent. I wanted it to control data access in a way that preserved the agent's ability to reason about the data. What it does WebMCP Guard is an SDK that wraps WebMCP functions written with the Imperative API and injects controls. It has a corresponding management console that allows the organization to define policies. It has the following types of policies Data Protection This gives the company control over what data the agent can see. It classifies sensitive data, including names, SSN, credit cards, and more, and transforms them before the agent sees it. It can replace this data with a unique token. If the same piece of data appears across multiple records, it will use the same token identifier, which allows the agent to reason about the data without actually knowing what it is. In some cases, it can contextualize the data while removing the specificity. For example, it can replace a DOB from a patient health record with an age range. Human confirmation To prevent errant destructive actions polices can be created that require the user to approve (via an on-page modal) an action before it can be completed. This is most often used before an agent takes an irreversible action, such as deleting a record. Posture Assessment It can restrict what types of agents can access the tools. For example, you can block unidentified agents or restrict it to agents from one provider, such as OpenAI. Justification Policies can require the agent to provide a written justification before a sensitive action runs — bulk export, for example. The requirement is injected directly into the tool's input schema, so the agent learns about it from the tool definition rather than from a refusal. The agent is instructed to stop and ask its user for the reason and relay it verbatim, and the justification is evaluated and stored on the audit record as the human's stated reason. How we built it TypeScript end to end, in a pnpm monorepo. The SDK splits into a browser half and a server half: the client package wraps document.modelContext.registerTool (with a navigator.modelContext fallback) and runs every call through a gate → execute → transform pipeline, while everything secret — the policy engine, the data classifier, the deterministic tokenizer, the encrypted token vault, and the audit writer — lives in a Node package the host app mounts as ordinary API routes. Tokens are deterministic by construction: HMAC-SHA256 over a canonicalized value under an org secret, so the same SSN or name yields the same token in every tool, every turn, even inside the free text of a clinical note. The vault encrypts originals with AES-256-GCM, using the token itself as authenticated data so a tampered row fails closed instead of decrypting to the wrong person. Storage is a small adapter interface (SQLite for the demo, in-memory for tests, both run against one shared conformance suite) so an organization brings its own database. This way the organization isn't reliant on SaaS infrastructure to protect their audit logs, etc. We also built an example medical app for the demo. It existing in the same repo. We used AI coding assistance for this project. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is brand new, and building against it seriously means finding the edges. Three real ones: tools' execute is invoked with no second options argument despite the typings declaring one (every tool crashed on its first real call); registering a live tool name again silently keeps the old tool, so policy-driven schema changes must abort-then-re-register; and feature detection has to cover both document.modelContext and the older navigator.modelContext surface. Tokenizing a structured name field is easy. A clinical note that says "Reached Tricia by phone" is not, and an agent can de-anonymize the token if information like that leaks. We fixed this by resolving bare name fragments to the same token as the full name (never hashed independently, which would split one person into two tokens), replaced only when the fragment maps unambiguously to one known person. Early on, the justification refusal told the agent what a justification should contain, so agents composed plausible ones themselves, defeating the control. The message now instructs the agent to stop, ask its human for the reason, and relay it verbatim. The denial text turned out to be as much a part of the security design as the policy engine. In the future, we will probably replace it with a modal like the approval workflow. Accomplishments that we're proud of The tokenization loop working end to end was a big win. An agent searches, gets tokens instead of names, reasons about them, passes one back into another tool, and the real value is swapped in server-side. The agent is actually able to reason about the data without access to the cleartext value. Getting the justification flow to work correctly was also a big win. Like I said earlier, a lot of agents just wrote the justification themselves, which isn't exactly what is intended. It's not foolproof, but this tool isn't supposed to be silver bullet for security; it is meant to complement other security measures for organizations that want to implement WebMCP. What we learned We'll still need some kind of control surface for the DOM. Agents that cannot accomplish their task via the WebMCP tool may fall back to DOM inspection. Currently, this requires a separate security tool to address, like an enterprise browser. But I think we could come up with some kind of native solution. Alternatively, this tool might be better as a browser extension, and then the SDK would merely enforce the use of the extension before serving the page. This would give us more control over what the agent can access, but it is also a bigger deployment than the current state. But when it comes to security, perfect can't be the enemy of good. Easily deploying controls on a WebMCP tool still greatly improves security and compliance, especially if it eliminates it as a path to circumventing other security controls. What's next for WebMCP Guard Smarter classification: NER-based name detection beyond the host-supplied dictionary, and free-text detectors for addresses and insurance ids. Structured export rows so bulk export gets the full transform treatment instead of leaning on the justification gate. Richer policy: combined confirmation-plus-justification actions, per-class control over inbound detokenization, and the pluggable LLM justification evaluator the interface already supports. Real identity: SSO/OIDC session resolution in place of the demo's mock personas. This allows the user to attach policies to specific people or user groups. LLM-as-a-judge: For justifications, I want the admin to be able to define what an acceptable justification is and use an LLM to determine if the justification given is adequate. Better agent posture controls: I want to determine a better way to identify agents so our posture controls are more reliable. End user notifications: Alert end users during WebMCP activity to prevent adversarial attempts to hijack the users session while hiding their activity. An optional browser extension: A stretch goal is to use a browser extension to better lock down the DOM so agents can't circumvent controls through DOM inspection. This will have to be optional since it significantly increases the deployment complexity, but it will close a major gap. Demo The live demo has two sites: Example EHR app: https://webmcp-guard-portal.onrender.com/patients Admin console: https://webmcp-guard-console.vercel.app/login?token=Nit52TvyXZWpgzot1UIqMV4ktAB3oCdFbrk5M5AFSYg%3D Built With chatgpt claude codex nextjs render sqlite vercel Try it out github.com webmcp-guard-portal.onrender.com webmcp-guard-console.vercel.app Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Andrew Akers Like Share this project: Updates Andrew Akers started this project — Sep 03, 2026 03:49 PM EDT

title: TaskBridge
pitch: Your AI-powered bridge to better job opportunities.
about_excerpt: Your AI-powered bridge to better job opportunities. Like 2 Comment Story Updates TaskBridge — A job workspace designed for humans and their AI agents Inspiration Job hunting is full of repetitive, low-judgment work: searching through dozens of listings, reading requirements, comparing them against your skills, and tracking interesting opportunities. As someone who has personally experienced this process, I started thinking about where AI agents could genuinely help. Agents are well suited to discovery, filtering, and repetitive tasks, yet most websites still force them to interact like humans, clicking through interfaces that were never designed for them. When I discovered the WebMCP Challenge, I wanted to explore the opposite approach: what if an application treated the AI agent as a first-class user? That idea became TaskBridge. TaskBridge is a job workspace where humans and AI agents collaborate. The agent discovers opportunities, compares them against a candidate's profile, and shortlists relevant jobs. The human remains responsible for judgment and final decisions. Saving a job can be automated. Applying for one is always the human's call. What it does TaskBridge allows users to browse and manage job opportunities through a familiar web interface while exposing structured capabilities to AI agents through WebMCP. The agent can: Search for job opportunities. Retrieve detailed job information. Access the candidate's profile. Save relevant opportunities. Retrieve saved jobs. Draft a tailored application. For example, a user can ask an agent to find remote jobs matching their experience. The agent retrieves their profile, searches available opportunities, compares requirements, and saves the strongest matches for the user to review. TaskBridge also supports live remote job listings and allows users to maintain an editable candidate profile. Users can upload a CV, which can be parsed to help populate their profile. The goal is not to replace the job seeker, but to reduce the repetitive work surrounding job discovery and applications. How we built it TaskBridge is built with Next.js, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS. The application registers six tools using the browser-native WebMCP API ( document.modelContext.registerTool ): search_jobs get_job_details get_candidate_profile save_job get_saved_jobs apply_job One of the key architectural decisions was making the human interface and AI agent tools share the same underlying logic layer. The dashboard and the agent therefore use the same search, ranking, and application-generation logic rather than maintaining separate implementations. Job matching uses a simple and explainable overlap score between a job's tags and the candidate's skills and interests: $$ \mathrm{match}(j) = \mathrm{round}\left( 100 \cdot \frac{|T_j \cap (S \cup I)|}{|T_j|} \right) $$ where Tj represents a job's tags, while S and I represent the candidate's skills and interests. Live remote jobs are fetched from the Remotive feed through a route handler, with bundled sample data acting as an automatic fallback so the application remains functional even if the external feed fails. Users can edit their candidate profile and upload a CV. PDF and DOCX files are parsed locally, with optional AI-assisted parsing available through the user's own OpenRouter API key. The apply_job tool can generate a tailored cover letter, but deliberately never submits an application. The user reviews the draft and decides whether to apply through the original job posting. The project itself was also built through human and AI collaboration. I directed the product and technical decisions while using an AI coding agent to help scaffold, refactor, and verify parts of the application. Challenges we ran into Working with an emerging browser API WebMCP is still an emerging standard, which meant dealing with browser implementation quirks during development and testing. Chrome's testing environment can return inputSchema as a JSON string and reject certain tool execution paths. I handled this by normalizing schemas and ensuring the same underlying handlers could execute consistently. React StrictMode also introduced double-mount behaviour that could interrupt tool registration. This required careful lifecycle handling using AbortController . Hydration-safe persistence Saved jobs, applications, and candidate profiles are stored using localStorage , but the application also needs to render correctly on the server. I used useSyncExternalStore with server snapshots to manage client-side persistence without introducing hydration issues. Unstructured job data Live job descriptions often arrive as messy HTML. Instead of injecting raw HTML into the application, I built a small parser that converts headings, paragraphs, and lists into structured content for safer rendering. Demo reliability A live external API can fail at exactly the wrong moment, especially when a demo is involved. Because computers apparently sense deadlines. To avoid this, every data layer gracefully falls back to bundled sample data. I also built a development-only agent demo using an OpenRouter tool-calling loop and a smoke script to verify all six tools end-to-end without requiring a WebMCP-capable browser. Accomplishments that we're proud of Building a complete human-and-agent collaboration workflow in less than a day. Successfully exposing six structured capabilities through the browser-native WebMCP API. Designing the agent with clear trust boundaries, allowing it to assist with discovery and drafting without autonomously submitting job applications. Creating a shared logic layer so the human UI and AI tools always operate on the same underlying functionality. Supporting both live job data and reliable fallback data for a resilient demo experience. Building an accessible interface with visible focus states, reduced-motion support, a skip link, and an aria-live agent transcript. Demonstrating that WebMCP can enable a more intentional relationship between web applications and AI agents. What we learned WebMCP changes the integration model There is no traditional integration layer to build between an application and an agent. The page declares its capabilities, and compatible agents can discover and use those tools directly. The application's responsibility is to expose clear, reliable, and honest capabilities. Tool descriptions are part of the user experience Agents don't navigate an application by looking at buttons. They rely on tool descriptions and JSON schemas to understand what they can do. Writing clear tool definitions turned out to be just as important as designing the human interface. Trust boundaries improve agent experiences Giving the agent the ability to search, compare, save opportunities, and draft applications while keeping final submission in human hands made the collaboration model clearer. Trust boundaries are not necessarily limitations. They can be product features. Designing for agents improves applications for humans too Thinking in terms of structured data, explicit actions, and predictable states resulted in a cleaner application architecture and a simpler interface for human users. What's next for TaskBridge TaskBridge is currently a proof of concept exploring how job platforms can be designed for both humans and AI agents. Future improvements could include: Integration with more job sources. Improved candidate-job matching. Application tracking. Interview and follow-up management. More advanced AI-assisted career research. Agent-assisted workflows across the entire job search process. TaskBridge started with a simple question: what happens when we stop forcing AI agents to navigate websites designed exclusively for humans? The answer I wanted to explore is simple: the future of the web may not be agents becoming better at pretending to be human users. It may be applications becoming better at working with both humans and their agents. title: WebMCP-Challenge
pitch: MODE lets anyone reshape a website by talking to an agent, turning cluttered interfaces into personal, accessible experiences stored in cookies.
about_excerpt: MODE lets anyone reshape a website by talking to an agent, turning cluttered interfaces into personal, accessible experiences stored in cookies. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The web is usually designed as a one-size-fits-all experience. A company decides where every element belongs, which promotions deserve attention, how much information appears at once, and what “accessible” means for the average visitor. The user can sometimes switch between light and dark mode or increase the browser’s text size, but those controls barely scratch the surface of what different people actually need. We were inspired by a simple question: What if a website could keep its trusted content and functionality while allowing each person to decide how that content should be presented? Someone with low vision may need larger text, stronger contrast, and fewer distracting elements. Someone with ADHD may want promotions and recommendations removed. A price-conscious shopper may want images hidden and products sorted by category and price. Another person may simply dislike the site’s visual design and want it reorganized into a calmer marketplace. Today, these changes often require browser extensions, custom CSS, accessibility tools, or technical knowledge. MODE explores a more natural interaction: the user describes the experience they want in ordinary language, and an agent adapts the website using capabilities intentionally exposed by the developer. MODE stands for My Own Display Experience . Its guiding principle is: The website owns the facts and functionality. The user owns the experience. What it does MODE is a WebMCP-powered preference layer that lets people reshape a website by talking to an agent. Our demonstration begins with Cartly , a fictional Amazon-style storefront. Its initial retail interface is intentionally dense: prominent promotions, crossed-out prices, sponsored products, recommendations, compact typography, multiple navigation regions, filters, product imagery, ratings, delivery information, and many elements competing for attention. The user opens the MODE sidebar and enters a request such as: “This page is overwhelming. Turn it into a calm, curated marketplace.” “Remove the crossed-out previous prices, but keep the promotional section.” “Make the text larger, use higher contrast, and reduce motion.” “I only care about comparing prices. Hide the images and sort from lowest to highest.” “Organize the products by category and then by price.” “Move the Cloud task chair before the Orbit LED desk lamp.” “Put the price above the title on every product card.” An agent interprets the request, inspects the state and capabilities exposed by the page, and applies only developer-approved actions. The result appears immediately on the same website without requiring the user to approve a separate preview. MODE can change: Page layout and information density Text size, contrast, color theme, and motion Visibility of promotions and sponsored content Visibility of product imagery, descriptions, ratings, filters, and crossed-out prices Product ordering Placement of products, sections, controls, and fields within safe structural groups Search terms and catalog filters Saved presentation profiles Cart contents and quantities through declared commerce actions The demonstration is not just a static redesign. Search, department selection, product filtering, sorting, add-to-cart, cart quantities, removal, and persistence all work as real interactions. At the same time, MODE preserves the developer’s authority over trusted information. The agent cannot invent or alter product names, prices, ratings, inventory, shipping promises, or checkout behavior. It also cannot execute undeclared actions, move elements across unsafe structural boundaries, or hide the controls needed to undo its changes. The page exposes 237 stable semantic element targets and 19 developer-approved WebMCP actions . Each meaningful region—including individual product fields—has a stable identity. This allows the agent to distinguish between concepts that may look similar in the raw DOM, such as a crossed-out previous price and an unrelated promotional banner. Preferences are remembered locally. Display settings, visibility overrides, and element positions are stored in first-party cookies, while named profiles and cart state are stored in local storage. A returning user therefore sees the experience they requested rather than being forced back into the original design. Every transformation is reversible: Revert last change restores the complete state before the previous agent request. A request containing several actions is treated as one transaction. Return to original restores the developer’s default storefront. Even the reset operation can be reverted if the user changes their mind. How we built it We built MODE as a React application using Vinext, Vite, TypeScript, and the OpenAI Sites-compatible project structure. The architecture has several connected layers. 1. A functional storefront We first built Cartly as a complete retail demonstration rather than a collection of placeholders. It includes a searchable product catalog, department navigation, ratings, price ranges, delivery filters, shipping filters, multiple sorting options, and a persistent cart. This was important because MODE needed to demonstrate that personalization can reorganize an application without breaking its underlying functionality. The products remain the same products, search remains search, and the cart continues working regardless of how the interface is presented. 2. A developer-controlled preference model We created a typed preference schema that defines exactly which presentation properties may change. It includes layout, density, text scale, theme, contrast, reduced motion, element visibility, product ordering, and related display preferences. Incoming values are validated against this schema. Unknown properties and invalid values are discarded. This means the agent is not given unrestricted access to application code or arbitrary CSS. It operates within an explicit contract established by the site. MODE also provides several complete experience presets: Retail default Calm marketplace Accessible shopping Price comparison These presets can be applied as starting points and then refined through additional natural-language requests. 3. A semantic element manifest One of the most important parts of MODE is its semantic page-element manifest. Rather than asking the agent to reason from anonymous DOM nodes, generated class names, or screen coordinates, the page describes its interface using stable identifiers such as: promotion.stage catalog.products product.cloud-task-chair.card product.cloud-task-chair.title product.cloud-task-chair.price product.cloud-task-chair.previous-price product.cloud-task-chair.add-to-cart Each entry includes information about the element’s role, hierarchy, visibility, protection status, and whether it can be repositioned. This semantic layer is what makes a precise request like “remove crossed-out prices” reliably different from “remove promotions.” 4. Safe element repositioning Repositioning introduced an additional structural challenge. Allowing an agent to place any element at any coordinate would create overlapping content, inaccessible controls, broken responsive layouts, and configurations that work at only one screen size. Instead, MODE uses developer-approved placement groups. An element can move before or after another element only when both belong to the same compatible group. For example: Products can be reordered among products. Product fields can be reordered within their product card. Major page sections can be reordered within the page flow. Header controls can be reordered within the appropriate header region. A product price cannot be moved into the footer. Protected recovery controls cannot be moved or hidden. The actual layout continues to use responsive CSS, while a persisted semantic order determines where movable siblings appear. This provides meaningful customization without turning the page into an unsafe free-form canvas. 5. A shared action layer The normal interface, the local agent, and WebMCP registrations all use the same validated action layer. This was an intentional architectural decision. We did not want one implementation for button clicks, another for the agent sidebar, and a third for WebMCP. A shared dispatcher means the same rules and protections apply regardless of how an action is requested. The page registers tools through document.modelContext when WebMCP is available. These include actions for inspecting page elements, changing visibility, repositioning elements, transforming the storefront, applying preferences, searching and filtering the catalog, and managing the cart. Because MODE uses progressive enhancement, the storefront remains usable even when WebMCP is unavailable. WebMCP adds agent discoverability and control; it is n

title: FormCoach — an AI coach that sees numbers, not your video
pitch: A workout coach that sees numbers, never frames: MediaPipe Pose tracks reps and form in-browser, and WebMCP tools let any AI agent coach you live — your camera stream never leaves the tab.
about_excerpt: A workout coach that sees numbers, never frames: MediaPipe Pose tracks reps and form in-browser, and WebMCP tools let any AI agent coach you live — your camera stream never leaves the tab. Like Comment Story Updates cover 04_approval_modal 02_agent_creates_plan 05_rest_gesture 03_live_rep_tracking 06_session_summary Inspiration Home workouts get people hurt because nobody is watching their form — and every existing AI fitness coach wants your video. We wanted a coach that knows how you're moving without ever seeing you . WebMCP made that possible: the camera can stay inside the browser tab, and the agent gets numbers instead of frames. What it does FormCoach turns your webcam into a privacy-preserving workout sensor. MediaPipe Pose runs on-device in the tab, measuring reps, joint angles, tempo, and form faults (like knee valgus) in real time. Those measurements — and the workout controls — are exposed as WebMCP tools, so any WebMCP-aware browser agent becomes your coach: Ask it to build a plan ("3x12 squats, 90s rest, my left knee is sensitive") It watches your live metrics and flags form breakdowns mid-set It can propose program changes — swap the exercise, cut reps, extend rest You confirm proposals with body gestures (raise both hands to accept, cross your arms to decline), because mid-set your hands are busy and sweaty During rest, show an open palm for one second to skip the timer How we built it Seven imperative tools plus one declarative form , registered on document.modelContext : Read tools ( getWorkoutPlan , getLiveMetrics , getSetHistory ) are annotated readOnlyHint so agents can poll freely. Write tools ( startSet , setRest , adjustProgram , endSession ) are gated by the human — adjustProgram returns a pending promise that only resolves after a gesture or a 20s timeout. The tool set follows the workout phase (idle → countdown → set → rest → done): registrations are scoped to AbortController s and swapped on every transition, so the agent only ever sees actions that make sense right now. createPlan is a declarative <form toolname> ; the handler reads SubmitEvent.agentInvoked to credit the plan to the agent or the human. The pipeline: webcam → MediaPipe Pose (33 landmarks/frame, on-device) → pose engine (rep FSM, form rules, gesture dwell) → session state machine → WebMCP tools. No backend, no accounts, no uploads — video frames never leave the <video> element. Challenges we ran into Detecting knee valgus in 2D: a naive angle threshold broke on front-view footage. We redefined it sign-based — the knee drifting past the ankle toward the midline — which survives both mirrored and non-mirrored coordinates. Background-tab timer throttling: browsers throttle timers in hidden tabs, which froze our replay engine mid-test. We rewrote replay as elapsed-time catch-up instead of tick-based stepping. Testing an API the test browser doesn't have: WebMCP isn't in stock Chromium, so we built an adapter layer with an internal tool registry, a window.__formcoach debug bridge that hits the same execute path a real agent does, recorded pose fixtures for camera-free replay — and a Playwright suite that mocks document.modelContext to verify the real API path (registration mirroring, {content:[...]} wrapping, AbortSignal cleanup). Confirming actions when hands are busy: buttons don't work mid-squat. Gesture confirmation ran through the same pose model, with on-screen buttons as a fallback. Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete human–agent loop with zero video leaving the tab, phase-scoped tool registration that keeps the agent honest, gesture-based consent for agent write actions, and a fully camera-free test story: 40 unit tests + Playwright end-to-end sessions, all green. What we learned WebMCP changes where capability lives. A server-side MCP with this job would need the video uploaded; in-tab, the agent gets a live numeric contract instead. We also learned that agent UX is mostly trust UX: an on-screen agent log of every tool call, explicit attribution badges via agentInvoked , and human confirmation for anything that changes the program. What's next Moving the "eyes" into a browser extension so any workout or rehab site can publish its own exercise spec and be coached by the same agent — and rehab verticals, where physiotherapy ranges-of-motion become first-class tool schemas. title: Agentic Sandbox
pitch: A deterministic factory decision lab where a human and a WebMCP browser agent safely replan the same live system together.
about_excerpt: A deterministic factory decision lab where a human and a WebMCP browser agent safely replan the same live system together. Like Comment Story Updates Current post-lock recovery with human Packaging lock, stale-write rejection, and receipt-backed evidence. Six narrow WebMCP Site Tools discovered in the live host. Scenario comparison: same output, cheaper standard-supplier plan passes the cost cap. Deterministic lock-bound proof: 9,252 < 10,937 under the human Packaging lock. The problem Factory planning decisions rarely happen in one place. They move through dashboards, spreadsheets, a simulation specialist, and an approval meeting, and each handoff loses context and authority. A generic assistant can make that worse by recommending a control that an operator has just taken off the table. What it does Agentic Sandbox makes the website itself the shared, inspectable decision surface. It is a deterministic factory decision lab where a human and a browser agent plan against the same versioned state. The demo mission is concrete: increase good output by at least 20%, keep total cost within 8% of baseline, add no machine, and do not increase defects. The agent reads the line, creates two bounded hypotheses, simulates a 16-hour shift, and compares immutable receipts. Scenario A reaches 11,114 good units but costs €47,670.51 and fails the cost cap. Scenario B reaches the same 11,114 units for €45,170.51 and passes all four constraints. Then comes the important moment: while the agent is working, the human locks Packaging. That click advances the factory revision and makes earlier evidence historical. The agent’s next write still carries the old revision, so it fails atomically with STALE_FACTORY ; nothing is applied or silently rebased. The agent re-reads the authority state, replans with only controls that remain available, and receives an auditable answer: under the Packaging lock, at most 9,252 good units are possible while the mission requires 10,937. The target is proven infeasible by deterministic evidence, not by model prose. That safe disagreement is the product. The human can change the admissible action space without restarting the conversation, and the agent can recover without overriding the new rule. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, the agent would have to infer state from pixels and click by coordinates, or the product would need a separate chatbot and backend with a second source of truth. Instead, the page exposes exactly six narrow Site Tools through document.modelContext.registerTool : get_factory_snapshot get_scenario_snapshot create_scenario apply_scenario_changes run_factory_simulation compare_simulation_runs The human interface and these tools share one application-owned command bus. Schemas are closed, handlers validate independently, and every mutation carries a request ID plus expected factory, scenario, and lock revisions. There is deliberately no agent-accessible lock, unlock, force, arbitrary patch, optimizer, ERP, PLC, SCADA, or machine-control tool. Human authority stays human. How it was built Agentic Sandbox is a self-contained React 19 + TypeScript + Vite app deployed on Vercel. The deterministic engine models 64 fixed ticks, uses integer/fixed-point arithmetic, and computes production, defects, energy, cost, constraints, invariants, and bottleneck evidence in the page. Each simulation creates an immutable, content-addressed SHA-256 receipt with exact operands, accepted/rejected operations, tick-level state, and an optional lock-bound proof. No displayed KPI comes from the language model. The hardest implementation problem was making a mid-plan disagreement trustworthy rather than dramatic: old authority must fail closed without erasing evidence that was valid when created. That required explicit revision precedence, atomic stale-write rejection, immutable receipts, and visible current-versus-historical states. The submitted flow was replayed against the public deployment in a supported WebMCP host, including discovery, comparison, the human lock, stale rejection, re-read, replan, and proof. What I learned WebMCP is most useful when a website already owns meaningful state, rules, and actions. Exposing those capabilities directly is more reliable than asking an agent to reconstruct them from pixels. A refusal can be more valuable than another recommendation: STALE_FACTORY proves that human authority survived concurrency, and 9252 < 10937 proves why the target cannot be met under the active lock. Potential impact and what’s next The first users I have in mind are plant planners, industrial engineers, and continuous-improvement teams working on line balancing, shift planning, and supplier what-if analysis. A production version could connect this exact capability, revision, lock, and receipt pattern to a validated digital twin, while ERP, PLC, SCADA, purchase, and physical-machine changes remain behind existing approvals. The broader pattern applies to any high-consequence planning interface: expose narrow capabilities, bind actions to explicit versions, preserve the human veto, and return evidence a machine can check. The agent reads the factory, creates two one-shift hypotheses, applies explicit settings, simulates both, and compares their evidence. Both scenarios reach 11,114 good units. Scenario A uses an expedited supplier, but the premium adds no output and breaks the cost cap. Scenario B uses the standard supplier and passes all four constraints. It is the best evaluated option under this policy, not a claim of global optimality. Every number comes from a simulator receipt, never from Model Pros. Then the human changes the rules. I lock packaging directly in the product. The factory and a factory revisions advance. Earlier evidence remains visible as auditable history, but it is no longer current. The agent intentionally retries its old scenario B right with the revisions it held before my intervention. A Gent Sandbox rejects the batch atomically with stale factory. No operational or scenario state is changed. After a fresh read, the capability map is explicit. Mixer, quality gate, and warehouse are available. Packaging is human locked. Supplier is phase closed. The agent creates a clean post lock branch and changes only available controls. The new receipt shows 9,114 good units, below the required 10,937. More importantly, the deterministic engine proves a conservative upper bound. 9,252 is less than 10,937. The target is proven infeasible under the current human constraint. The decision packet preserves the mission, human authority, revisions, receipt hashes, constraints, comparison claim, and proof. This is the agent native web. The human can change authority at any moment. The agent uses explicit browser native capabilities. Deterministic software owns the evidence, and both inspect the same state. Same page, clear authority, shared proof.

title: Net Slum

A new social web experience built for humans and their agents to create an experience they actually enjoy, not just engage with.

 Inspiration 

 Inspired by the netslum from the .hack conglomerate series, this web platform is meant to create a cyber social playground for both agents and humans alike. I was inspired to create a platform where agentic use is actually useful instead of time consuming. 

 What it does 

 Netslum is a web platform utilizing the at protocol that allows users and their agents to create public personal websites, as well as their own hyper personalized feed & homepage using webmcp. This web platform assumes agentic coding capabilites and leverages it so anyone can create a social experience that's built for them and their own personal needs without ever needing to actually program or prompt to program. Webmcp provides the lego building blocks for users to simply build out what works for them. This platform even supports webgpu (and webmcp tools to leverage them) so 3D objects and experiences can be rendered and built on people's sites. 

 How we built it 

 This entire project was built by me orchestrating a series of agents using a combination of pre built and custom harnesses. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Model intelligence (and therefore cost) played a significant factor in the speed of deployment when attempting to develop fully with agents. It was an incredible learning experience. And of course, time crept up on me faster than I could blink! 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Having my first major project deployed publicly! Most of my projects from hackathons were all privately submitted, but this time anyone can actually view my progress! This is the most feature-complete hackathon project i've ever done by mydelf that isn't a video game. 

 What we learned 

 I learned a lot about how the lynx framework functions, as well as how much effort it truly takes to build a platform vs. something more client-side like a video game. 

 What's next for Net Slum 

 I will continue to iterate over it, publish it around, and begin to experiment with seeing how many viewers and users I can get to enjoy this project live! i don't want to stop building and iterating with this - I want to keep going!

title: Cleanroom
pitch: Agent proposes, you approve, and your data never leaves the browser tab.WebMCP data-cleaning workbench where reads are free, every write is a diff you have to click,and the privacy receipt reads zero.
about_excerpt: Agent proposes, you approve, and your data never leaves the browser tab.WebMCP data-cleaning workbench where reads are free, every write is a diff you have to click,and the privacy receipt reads zero. Like Comment Story Updates Cleanroom What it does Cleanroom is a data-cleaning workbench for messy CSVs. You drop a file on the page and an agent in your browser profiles it, finds the concrete problems, queries and charts it, and proposes the fixes — without the file ever being uploaded anywhere. The design rule is one sentence: reads are free, writes are proposals. No tool mutates your table. When the agent wants to change something it computes the exact before/after diff, puts a card in front of you with its reasoning, and stops. You click Approve or Reject. undo is deliberately not exposed as a tool — the ability to walk a change back belongs to the person, not the model. The problem it solves Every analyst has the same bad afternoon. A CSV arrives and before you can answer one question you have to fix it: regions spelled five ways, amounts stored as ¥39,545 , four date formats in one column, duplicate rows silently doubling your revenue. An LLM is excellent at spotting exactly these problems. But letting one help has meant either uploading your data to a server or code interpreter — a non-starter the moment the file has customer names, salaries or anything your compliance team has an opinion about — or pasting a sample and hand-applying the suggestions yourself, which is the automation you wanted, gone. Cleanroom is the third option: the agent gets tools, not your data. Why this is WebMCP and could not be a server MCP This is not a remote MCP server with a web page bolted on. It structurally could not be one. The agent and the human operate on literally the same JavaScript object . One store is the single source of truth; the UI renders it and the tools operate on it. When the agent proposes a change the approval card appears in the human's rail in the same tick — no sync, no polling, no second copy that can drift. A remote agent cannot have that property, because a remote agent needs a copy. And everything a server MCP would need — upload, storage, auth, per-seat infrastructure — is simply absent. It's already your browser and already your session. The whole app is a static file. The privacy receipt The claim is "your data never leaves this tab," and a claim is worth nothing, so the page proves it. Before any other module loads, Cleanroom instruments fetch , XMLHttpRequest , sendBeacon and WebSocket and counts every outbound request. The count is in the header, and the agent can read it too, via a get_privacy_receipt tool — so when you ask "did my data go anywhere?" it answers with a verifiable number instead of a promise. It reads zero because there is nothing to send it to: no analytics, no CDN, no webfont, no charting library. Even the sample dataset is inlined as a string rather than fetched, specifically so the ledger stays honest. The deployed site also ships connect-src 'none' in its CSP, so the browser enforces it independently of our own code. Being straight about the limit: this counts requests the page makes. It cannot police the browser itself or a malicious extension, and it isn't a substitute for a security review. How I built it Vanilla JavaScript, ES modules, no framework and no runtime dependencies — a dependency that phones home would undermine the entire premise. Roughly 1,800 lines across eleven modules: a RFC-4180-tolerant CSV parser, type inference and column profiling, an issue detector, fifteen pure transform operations with a diff builder, the store that holds the undo stack, the WebMCP tool layer, the UI, and hand-rolled inline SVG charts. 14 tools are registered — eight read-only, six human-gated. Three implementation details did the most for how well an agent actually performs here: Every detected issue carries a suggested_fix — a ready-to-use propose_transform payload. The agent goes from "what's wrong?" to a queued, reviewable fix in one hop instead of guessing at an API shape. This cut the model's flailing more than anything else I tried. Errors are instructions. Every failure names the valid inputs — Column "reigon" does not exist. Available columns: order_id, order_date, region, … — and is returned as text rather than thrown, so the agent reads the recovery path instead of hitting an opaque host error. Results are context-window shaped. Profiles and aggregates are summaries by construction; raw rows are returned only on request and hard-capped at 200. A 100,000-row file is fully workable without a single row entering the model's context. Challenges WebMCP's API moved while it was being standardised — some hosts expose navigator.modelContext , the current spec draft uses document.modelContext , and earlier builds took a batch provideContext({tools}) instead of per-tool registerTool . Rather than bet on one, the registration shim feature-detects all of them and reports which it found, so the header tells the user the truth about their browser instead of failing silently. Tool results are returned in three shapes at once — MCP-style content , structuredContent , and a bare data object — so the same tool behaves identically across hosts. The harder problem was designing the pause . An agent that has to stop and wait is easy to build badly: it either blocks forever or barrels ahead assuming approval. propose_transform returns pending_human_approval with an explicit next_step , and a separate await_decision tool blocks on the human with a timeout and tells the agent what to say if it expires. Getting the agent to reliably not assume its change landed was most of the prompt-shaped work. What I learned Designing tools for an agent is interface design, and the same thing that makes an API pleasant for a junior engineer — good names, errors that say what to do next, results scoped to what you actually need — is what makes a model competent instead of erratic. The suggested_fix field was the clearest demonstration: same model, same data, dramatically better behaviour, purely from shaping the return value. The second thing: an approval gate makes an agent more useful, not less. Once a change is reviewable before it lands, you stop hedging your prompts and start letting it try things. What's next Multi-table joins under the same proposal model — the agent proposes the key and shows you the match rate before committing. Recipe export — the change log is already ordered and structured; emit it as a runnable script so a one-off clean becomes a repeatable pipeline. Approval policies — "auto-approve whitespace fixes, always ask about dropped rows." The gate exists; this is a rule layer on top of it. Try it In ChatGPT's browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled, open the page and ask: "What's wrong with this data? Don't change anything yet — just tell me what you'd fix and why." "Clean it up. Propose each fix separately so I can review them, and ask me before you touch anything that's a judgement call." In any other browser the built-in Agent Console calls the same registered tool objects a host calls — an inspector, not a mock — so you can see exactly what the agent sees. title: Agentic Service Dispatch
pitch: Five prepare. Human approval creates tool 6; use removes it.
about_excerpt: Five prepare. Human approval creates tool 6; use removes it. Like Comment Story Updates Native Chrome 151: baseline registry shows exactly five page-owned WebMCP tools. Reset restores the exact five-tool baseline with no runtime error. One successful commit consumes the approval and revokes the temporary capability. Human approval creates temporary tool 06: commit_approved_dispatch. Final candidate — TEST ADAPTER · APPLICATION EVIDENCE · NOT NATIVE: approval exposes only commit_approved_dispatch as tool 06. Final candidate — TEST ADAPTER · APPLICATION EVIDENCE · NOT NATIVE: one successful commit consumes approval and returns registry to five. REAL AGENT VERIFICATION | CODEX + OFFICIAL CHROME DEVTOOLS FOR AGENTS | Codex: commit_approved_dispatch after human approval; then 5. REAL AGENT VERIFICATION | CODEX + OFFICIAL CHROME DEVTOOLS FOR AGENTS | Human approves draft; commit_approved_dispatch appears (6). Inspiration Service coordinators cross asset records, prior work, provider qualifications, calendars, prices, deadlines, and a final dispatch system. Agents can prepare that work, but “don't submit until I approve” is only an instruction; it does not change authority. The entrant is a founder/operator of an automotive and service business. This fictional workflow is abstracted from firsthand work coordinating vehicle context, prior service history, provider qualifications, pricing, availability, constraints, selection, and final request authority. It tests a stronger boundary: human approval creates one narrow capability for one reviewed object, then use removes it. What it does A single request asks for a qualified fictional automotive detailer before Friday under ¥60,000, with history checked. Five WebMCP tools retrieve the vehicle, review history, compare three providers with exclusion reasons, check deadline availability, and create DRAFT — NOT SUBMITTED . The human reviews provider, slot, price, scope, rationale, and binding. Only then does commit_approved_dispatch appear as tool 06. One use commits the in-memory draft; after the result crosses the caller boundary, the registration aborts on the next task and getTools() confirms five again. Both public v1 and exact final candidate source ef35cfc separately verified that settlement timing in native Chrome. Reset returns to the exact five-tool baseline. Real-agent verification On 2026-08-31 (JST) , Codex + official Chrome DevTools for agents selected and executed the public page's registered WebMCP tools from a natural-language business request, without page-tool names or an execution order in the prompt. Actual order: get_active_vehicle → get_service_history → search_qualified_providers → check_provider_availability → create_dispatch_draft → human approval of the exact draft → commit_approved_dispatch . The five preparation tools produced DRAFT — NOT SUBMITTED . After human approval, the only added tool was commit_approved_dispatch . Codex rediscovered it with list_webmcp_tools , executed it once through execute_webmcp_tool , and verified revocation: 5 → 6 → 5 . All six page-tool executions completed. This is separate evidence from the on-page deterministic runner and the Playwright test adapter; neither was used in this real-agent run. It is not ChatGPT Site tools . Reset Demo was not verified through this agent route ; the separate human-operated native Chrome Reset check remains labeled as such. The fixed, fictional scenario demonstrates model-selected tool execution, not unrestricted planning or a real commercial booking. Environment: Chrome 151.0.7922.174 , official Chrome DevTools MCP 1.8.0 , Codex 0.151.0-alpha.7.2 , using an isolated Chrome profile. Recorded tool arguments, registry observations, and page screenshots . How it works The deterministic runner discovers and invokes the five registered preparation tools in order; it is a verification aid, not a simulated AI. Visible approval binds the canonical draft hash and creates tool 06 for 120 seconds and one use. Commit accepts only the bound approval ID, consumes in-memory authority, settles, unregisters tool 06, and proves the exact five-name baseline through getTools() . Why WebMCP The person sees the exact draft, count, countdown, and audit trace while an agent sees the same page-owned tools. The imperative document.modelContext API is the product mechanism: registerTool publishes five baseline tools and the approval-only temporary tool; getTools drives the visible capability panel and verifies appearance/revocation; executeTool invokes the deterministic proof sequence and one-time commit; toolchange refreshes the browser-truth display; and AbortSignal defines registration lifetime. Ordinary UI confirmation cannot prove the agent's commit capability was absent before approval or gone after use. A permanently available endpoint also misses the page-bound authority transition that human and agent inspect together. Human-in-the-loop safety Approval hashes the complete canonical draft with SHA-256 and binds IDs, lifetime, one-time nonce, idempotency, used state, and registration generation. Tool 06 accepts only the current approval ID; callers cannot alter vehicle, provider, slot, price, scope, or rationale. Before domain execution, the callback observes exact six and revalidates approval integrity, TTL, hash, generation, idempotency, and uncommitted state. Combined invocation/registration signals also protect asynchronous validation. Mutation, expiry, Reset, cancellation, malformed input, read failure, or stale work fails closed. Unmount makes no immediate physical-removal claim; remount re-verifies. The technical docs retain the full checks and non-atomic registry limitation. How we built it This is a one-screen Next.js 16 / React 19 app over a deterministic TypeScript store. useSyncExternalStore avoids stale component callbacks; registry work is serialized; UI reads are bounded, generation-safe, and single-flight; Reset epochs discard older lifecycle work. Production has one native adapter and no fake fallback. Missing document.modelContext yields an honest unsupported state. The visibly labeled Playwright harness exists only for application automation. Challenges Public v1 exposed the hardest browser issue: revoking tool 06 before its successful callback crossed the tested Chrome boundary produced UnknownError after a domain commit. After asynchronous validation, authority is consumed before the success result returns; next-task revocation is then verified with getTools() . Tests also attack remounts, duplicate/stale reads, concurrency, expiry, mutation, Reset, registration failure, and cleanup. Accomplishments Approval creates an inspectable capability rather than changing prompt text. Exact-draft authority cannot be widened by arguments; one success consumes it. The actual registry is the visual proof. Public v1 completed human-native 5 → 6 → 5 on 2026-08-27 without runtime error. Exact final candidate source ef35cfc completed human-native 5 → 5 → 6 → 5 → Reset → 5 on 2026-08-30; tool 06 was only commit_approved_dispatch , with no observed error, duplicate, stopped transition, or stuck state. Candidate automation is 290 automated tests, 10 E2E browser flows across 320–1920px, and 96.02/93.67/98.64/96.82% executable-source statement/branch/function/line coverage. It includes hostile inputs, hash races, cancellation, native-string/schema-runner compatibility, accessibility, and soak work—but the automated harness is not native conformance. What we learned Tool design is authorization design. Inputs constrain arguments; trust also needs capability absence, exact-object binding, lifetime, revocation, and evidence. WebMCP makes those decisions visible where the human reviews the work. Potential impact Customer Service coordinators in automotive, field service, maintenance, repair, inspection, installation, and similar operational businesses. Pain A coordinator may have to manually cross asset or vehicle context, previous service history, provider qualification, pricing, availability, multiple constraints, exclusion reasons, repeated data entry, and final submission authority before one consequential request can be released. Value The agent prepares one structured decision through page-owned WebMCP tools. The human reviews one exact draft. Approval creates one exact, temporary write capability. One approved action consumes that capability. It then disappears, while the reviewed object, capability lifecycle, and audit trace remain visible on the shared page. Practical impact The design targets fewer dropped operational constraints, visible reasons for excluding unsuitable providers, less fragmented coordination and re-entry, no permanently exposed broad commit capability, exact-object human approval, inspectable authority, and a shared operational state for the human and agent.
